#6372. 10 Magical Christmas Traditions Around the World

Living far away from family is hard at the best of times, but it becomes particularly difficult around the holidays. If there's one thing that makes it a little easier for me, it's being able to mix and match festive traditions from different countries to create something that's uniquely ours. As an Italian living in France with a British husband, I love bringing together the best of each culture for a rather extravagant Christmas. On Christmas Eve, we have oysters and Champagne, as per French tradition, followed by an Italian feast and plenty of Christmas crackers—although I draw the line at Christmas pudding, preferring a simple pandoro over anything else.

Whether, like me, you spend Christmas far from your family, are planning to chase the sun this December or are driving home for the holidays, one of the great joys of Christmas is making memories and indulging in nostalgic traditions. All over the globe, different countries and cultures celebrate the season in different ways, marking the holiday with long-established rites and rituals or merging heritage to create beautiful new traditions. Below, we run through some of our favourite Christmas traditions around the world, and ask the Traveller editors about their own personal festive rituals. From seafood feasts on Christmas Day in Australia to surfing Santa’s taking to the waves in SoCal, these are the most wholesome traditions for some festive joy this season.

Christmas is not recognized as a national holiday in Japan, but the festive season is still celebrated—albeit slightly differently from how you’d expect. As part of a marketing campaign launched in 1974, a few years after KFC first opened in Japan, the brand came up with the slogan ‘Kentucky for Christmas’, and it stuck. On Christmas Day, many Japanese families tuck into a full feast of fried chicken—a tradition so popular that you often have to order weeks in advance to make sure you’ve got your bucket guaranteed for the big day. The original Christmas meal even came with a bottle of wine. Christmas cake is just as surprising in Japan, too—strawberry shortcake, made with layers of sponge, whipped cream and fresh strawberries, is a festive favourite.

As you might imagine, food is at the heart of Christmas celebrations in Italy. Every region has its own traditions and dishes, enjoyed on Christmas Eve, Christmas Day and throughout the festive season. While northern Italians might tuck into tortellini in broth and other comforting dishes, in the south we go all out. In my family, we have twelve different dishes—mostly fish-based—served for Christmas Eve dinner, before indulging in traditional desserts and an unholy amount of nuts while playing tombola. If there is one tradition that the whole country shares, it's the rather quirky tradition of La Befana – a witch-like old woman who flies through the skies on a broomstick on the night of January 5, leaving gifts for children to discover on the morning of 6 January, known as Epiphany (Epifania in Italian). Well-behaved children receive sweets and presents, while naughty ones get coal – although these days it's usually sweet, sugary charcoal, which is actually delicious.

The real difference between the Scottish festive season and that of much of the rest of the world is Hogmanay. Once Christmas Day is done and dusted, the focus is on New Year’s—or, as the Scots call it, Hogmanay. Street parties in cities such as Edinburgh roll on until the early hours, Robert Burns’ Auld Lang Syne is sung at midnight, and the ‘first-footing’ custom takes place—the first visitor to a home after midnight is believed to bring good luck for the year ahead (along with traditional gifts such as whisky, shortbread or a lump of coal, of course). Traditionally, a tall, dark-haired man is considered the luckiest first-footer.

While much of the Northern Hemisphere is wrapping up against the cold, Christmas in Australia falls in the middle of summer, meaning festive celebrations often revolve around the beach, sunshine and outdoor gatherings. "The traditional Christmas lunch in Australia is usually seafood, a roast ham served cold, lots of salads and then a pavlova for dessert," explains Lauren Burvill, CNT’s senior commerce writer and resident Aussie. "After lunch the classic traditions are to play cricket in the backyard, or if you're lucky, on the beach. It's not unusual to see Santa on the beaches as well, often riding on an inflatable rescue boat from the local surf club. On Boxing Day the country's favourite pastime is to watch the cricket or the Sydney to Hobart yacht race."

Forget snowy landscapes and cosy fireplaces—in Southern California, you might spot Santa Claus swapping his sleigh for a surfboard during the festive season. "I grew up in greater Los Angeles, and though December isn't typically beach weather, something uncanny almost always happens on Christmas," explains Megan Spurrell, Conde Nast Traveler US’s associate articles director. "The temperatures spike to the mid-70s Fahrenheit with shining sun and many families, including my own, end up at the beach. But we also go to look out for a very SoCal figure, known as Surfing Santa. We keep our eyes out at Manhattan and Hermosa Beach, especially near the piers, though I've heard of surfing santas in Malibu and Santa Monica, too. Most are just local dudes with a Santa suit who reliably hit the waves on Christmas morning to entertain their neighbours (and get a surf session in)."

While many Western traditions see Santa leaving lumps of coal in stockings for badly behaved children, in Austria it's the terrifying Krampus who comes to punish them. As the folklore goes, the Krampus is a fearsome horned figure with a long, snake-like tongue, who accompanies Saint Nicholas on 5 December, otherwise known as Krampusnacht, the eve of Saint Nicholas Day. While Saint Nicholas rewards well-behaved children with sweets and small gifts, Krampus is said to frighten or punish those who have been naughty. Today, the tradition is celebrated with Krampuslauf parades, during which people dressed in elaborate horned masks and furry costumes take to the streets, particularly in Alpine towns and villages. The folklore even inspired a Christmas comedy horror film in 2015, starring Adam Scott and Toni Collette.

In Peru, Christmas Eve, known as Nochebuena, is the main event, with families gathering for a festive dinner and celebrations that often continue well past midnight. "We alternate years of spending Christmas in Southern California with my mom and sisters, and going to Lima, Peru, with my husband's family" says Megan. "Though Peru has plenty of traditions tied to Christmas, perhaps my favourite is the sheer fact (shared in many Catholic and Latin American countries) that the whole affair begins at midnight on the 24th. It can be torture waiting until midnight proper to dig into the feast of turkey and arroz arabe that sits out waiting, but the entire city explodes in fireworks when the clock strikes 12. And then the party doesn't stop until the wee hours of the morning, sometimes at a family member's house or at the city's bars and clubs. It almost feels like a preview of New Year's Eve, just a few days earlier."

Dumplings are a major part of Polish cuisine day to day, and Christmas is no exception. The traditional Christmas Eve supper, known as Wigilia, begins when the first star appears in the sky, with families gathering around the Christmas table for a feast that traditionally includes 12 meatless dishes. "My favourite part of seasonal eating has never been the Great British Christmas Roast, but instead 'Polish Christmas', celebrated by my family on Christmas Eve, a haphazard tribute to the Polish side of my family tree," says Olivia Squire, Traveller's features editor. "When I was a child, my grandmother used to make pierogi (Polish dumplings filled with mashed potato and cottage cheese) from scratch, which in more recent years has been taken over by my mum and I and usually involves a lot of swearing and tears. It's all worth it when we sit down to eat them alongside a vegetarian version of bigos (hunter's stew—an insult to my meat-loving ancestors), breaded fish and holy wafers, soundtracked by Carol's at King's, my English dad's addition."

Forget spending a fortune on Christmas presents—in Germany, the tradition of Schrottwichteln puts a rather amusing twist on exchanging gifts, with friends and family swapping unwanted, bizarre, or downright useless objects instead.

"For gifts, we follow the German tradition of Schrottwichteln (literally 'junk Secret Santa'), where everyone brings something completely useless, unwanted or gloriously ridiculous, often something they were given once and never knew what to do with. The more pointless, tacky or absurd, the better," Karin Mueller, Traveller's visuals director, tells us. "Our children have grown up with this ritual, and what began as a cosy dinner has become the highlight of the year. They never miss it. Now that they’re young adults, they bring their partners along, and it’s turned into this wonderfully chaotic, joyful, very-London celebration that I’m pretty sure they’ll keep going long after we stop hosting."

Across England, Christmas is celebrated with familiar traditions, from exchanging gifts to tucking into mince pies and singing Christmas carols. But each county and neighbourhood has its own customs, too. In some seaside towns, brave locals take part in a Boxing Day dip—sprinting into the freezing sea to shake off the Christmas excesses, often while raising money for charity. There's also the age-old custom of burning a Yule log, traditionally associated with good fortune and protection from misfortune. In Cornwall, some communities gather in local pubs for a traditional Cornish ‘shout’, joining together to sing folk songs and sea shanties.

"In the hazy betwixmas period, the days of lounging on the sofa and gorging on Terry’s chocolate orange are punctuated by one magical evening at a local pub for a Cornish 'shout'", explains Lucy Bruton, CNT's social media manager. "A shout refers to the community coming together to sing sea shanties and folk songs in the pub, and the Lerryn (where my family live in Cornwall) shout is a particularly special one to me. The tiny pub feels packed to the eaves with people of all ages belting out some of my favourite Cornish songs – from "Trelawney" to "Lamorna" and, of course, “Cornwall My Home”. It’s dark, cosy and a real slice of the magic of Cornwall."

We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

The surest way to get a scratch from a feline is to go for a forbidden tummy rub. But why do cats hate being touched on their bellies?

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Dogs typically love belly rubs and will roll on their backs to get more. With cats, it's a different story: Most are visibly uncomfortable when someone touches their belly, and the same applies to their feet and tail.

When a cat is petted in these areas, its body language often changes. "They might do a quick head turn, looking at your hand, or they might start moving away from you or wiggling around a lot, basically trying to get away from the petting," Mikel Delgado, a cat behaviorist and senior research scientist at Purdue University, told Live Science in an email. "If these early warning signs are ignored, they might escalate to biting, hissing or scratching."

But why do cats dislike it so much when humans touch these specific areas?

Although there has been little formal research into this question, animal behavior experts proposed a few ideas for why cats don't like to be touched in certain areas.

"Cats are prey animals as well as predators and so they can be very protective of areas that are particularly vulnerable to injury during attack, such as the belly area," Sarah Ellis, head of cat mental well-being and behavior at the cat welfare charity International Cat Care, told Live Science in an email.

A cat's belly houses vital organs ‪—‬ such as the liver, stomach and intestines ‪—‬ without the protective bony cage that the ribs provide for the heart and lungs. Although cats have evolved a special feature called the "primordial pouch" —‬ basically a flap of loose skin and fat on their belly —‬ which provides a little extra padding to protect vital organs during fights, most cats still feel threatened when humans touch or rub their belly.

Cats have extra padding on their stomachs to protect their organs.

Dogs have a similar anatomy to cats, but they have to worry less about falling prey to larger animals. Cats, meanwhile, can be hunted by dogs, urban coyotes, and even birds such as hawks and owls, making it natural for them to be protective of their bellies.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

The tail is also a vulnerable area for cats. "When a cat is chased by another animal, including other cats, the tail is often the part of the cat's body that is closest to touch," Ellis said, "and the risk of being bitten at the base of the tail is high." Therefore, cats may be skittish about having their tail stroked.

When it comes to foot rubs, there are two possible explanations for why most cats hate them. First, a cat's paws are essential in threatening situations. Running away from danger is a cat's preferred survival strategy, and they rely on their paws as a means of escape, Ellis explained. If they can't run away, "a cat may resort to repelling any threats through swiping and scratching and it needs its paws free to do so," she said. "It is therefore predisposed to not enjoy having its paws restricted in any way."

Another reason could be that cats' paws are very sensitive. They have wrist whiskers (also known as "carpal vibrissae") and toe pads that are sensitive to various types of stimuli, like pressure and heat, Delgado said, "so it's not surprising that many cats are sensitive about having their feet touched."

If you're interacting with a cat, it's generally a good idea to stick to the areas where most cats like to be petted: the base of their ears, around their cheeks and under their chin. These areas are rich in scent glands, and cats tend to rub them against other cats they are friends with, Delgado explained. So essentially, cats like being petted in those areas because "they treat us as they do other cats," Delgado said.

But some cats go against the grain. "I've had a few who enjoyed belly rubs," Delgado said. Others enjoy having their tail stroked briefly and show their pleasure "by pushing their rump into the hand of the petter and holding their tail up in the air," Ellis said. (This behavior is sometimes called "elevator butt.")

As puzzling as it may be to humans, these varied preferences are a reminder that "each cat is an individual," Delgado said. Positive responses to petting of the belly, feet or tail can also signal close bonding to a human, Ellis said.

She advises people to "always take the cat's lead, learn what each individual cat likes and dislikes and respect these preferences."

#6369. The 8 Best Trail Cameras for Hunting, Wildlife Watching, and Even Home Security

These expert-tested trail cams help hunters and wildlife watchers capture what happens off-grid.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Fall is peak season for those who want to gather last-minute information on deer and other game animals ahead of hunting seasons. Even if you’re not heading into the woods to hunt, it’s one of the most interesting times of year for observing wild animals. Whitetail deer, elk, bears, and other animals are becoming much more active due to seasonal mating periods while waterfowl and other birds migrate for the winter.

The advantage of having a modern trail camera is the ability to capture the action you’d otherwise miss, whether it’s an elusive buck passing by your stand in the night or the raccoon creating backyard mayhem. If you’re considering a trail camera that uses a cellular network to send photos and videos directly to your smartphone, the good news is these have gotten even easier to use.

While the trail cam experience improves every year, the cost of many units is more than $100, and cellular models require recurring data plan charges, making it trickier to assess value. Images from game cameras are better than ever, even in budget models, and apps add software features often.

Sorting out what matters most to you and how you plan to use your trail cameras can be a challenge, so we explain what to look for along with sharing our top recommendations selected from year-round testing of dozens of cameras evaluated side-by-side.

The Tactacam Reveal Pro 4.0 replaces the Reveal Pro 3.0 camera, our previous pick for Best Overall. Released this summer, the Pro 4.0 version keeps what made the 3.0 great and improves on it in two key areas: image quality and battery life. Reveal has one of the best apps in the space, with tons of settings and features to tweak your setup and manage your cameras and images. Updates to these basics are big usability improvements that demanding trail camera users will notice.

Cameras going dead in the field is a major gripe for users of these gadgets. You have to physically go and replace batteries, which adds hassle and cost to your experience. I tend to place cameras in early summer and let them run for several months until my hunting season starts. The problem is that active cameras can run through eight to 12 AA batteries in a month depending on the model and your camera settings.

Tactacam has tackled this issue in a few ways with the Pro 4.0 release. The brand told me it audited everything about camera operation that drained the battery and then made small tweaks to reduce power demands anywhere it could.

Tactacam has also developed sold separately R5 and R10 lithium battery packs that replace previous battery add-ons, which have the notable benefit of swapping into the same form factor as the AA battery tray, so they don’t add bulk to the camera.

Image quality in the Reveal cameras has always been solid, but the company took a unique approach to dealing with the challenge of getting both crisp day and night images by installing separate sensors for each. Photographers know that night images require different gear and settings than daylight shooting, so the split makes sense. The early returns from a month of testing confirm that the quality of both day and night is much improved.

The rest of this flagship Reveal camera is impressive, carrying over from the Pro 3.0 and now-discontinued Ultra camera. The Reveal lineup now has just two similar cameras: the Pro 4.0 and the X 4.0. The Reveal X 4.0 is basically the Pro 4.0 without a built-in display screen, which saves $30 and is a great option if you don’t value the screen for aiming and reviewing images at the device.

As mentioned, the robust app gives you remote control over everything including photo and video capture settings, transmission frequency, night image flash, trigger delays, and more. You’re also able to launch a live stream to follow up on interesting images, but there’s an additional subscription cost and it will drain the battery quickly. There’s also built-in GPS that shows the location of your camera on a map within the app—essential if you’ve forgotten where you placed it or if it’s stolen.

Cell-connected trail cameras are handy, but if you’re low on funds or trying to run a multitude of cameras, paying $150 and up per camera gets pricey fast. Spypoint’s Flex M2 trail camera keeps both the upfront purchase cost and recurring subscription fees reasonable. Spypoint even has a free data plan that gives you 100 images per month if you want to avoid subscription fees altogether. (The Flex M2 doesn’t have onboard memory, nor does it ship with an SD card, so you’ll have to spend at least another $20 per camera for a high-speed SD card.)

Despite the low price, the camera’s 32-megapixel photos and 1080p video are clear and well-exposed. The Flex M2 displays lower-resolution images in the app but you can request full-resolution images when you want more detail. This is beneficial because it keeps data demands low and shows up in the battery usage as well. After a month in the field, the eight AA batteries I was using displayed in the app at “High” strength.

Additionally, I appreciated that this camera is compact since I’m usually hauling my cameras several miles into the backcountry in a pack. If you want to run this camera year-round, I’d consider picking up the $60 five-watt solar panel add-on, which has a built-in battery and should allow you to leave the Flex M2 up indefinitely.

I was impressed with the overall experience with the Flex M2, but the highlight here is the cost to purchase and run this camera. Yes, you’ll need to pay up for video or a higher quota of images, but this is a great option if you want the excitement of getting trail camera images on your phone without the annoyance of yet another recurring subscription fee on your credit card.

The best way to cut down on battery costs for your trail cameras is running solar panels. While many cameras have the option to run on solar, it’s often an additional upfront cost. The new 2026 Moultrie Edge 4 Solar trail camera has it all smartly packaged together in an integrated unit that costs less than some standalone cameras.

Setting up solar often requires separate mounting as well as hauling out lots of separate pieces and cables to be connected. The Edge 4 Solar just straps to a tree as a single unit, ready to run indefinitely. The camera comes with a rechargeable lithium-ion battery powered by the panel, which enables you to place a camera and leave it running as long as you need. Having the solar panel integrated is convenient and compact, but you’ll need to choose spots wisely to ensure both good captures and sun exposure.

Beyond the solar power setup, the Edge 4 is a solid trail camera with crisp 40-megapixel photos and 1080p video. The app is polished and makes setup and use hassle-free even if you’re not particularly tech-savvy. The subscription plans are in line with the industry average, ranging from $8.99 to $22.99. The lowest-tier plan offers more than most other companies’ $5 plans (1,000 images and 10 videos) and the most expensive plan offers unlimited images and 50 videos and discounts steeply to $7.99 per month for each additional camera.

There are two significant recurring costs with a cellular trail camera: the data plan and batteries. Connected cameras can chew through batteries, which can add up, especially since you’ll want to use more expensive lithium batteries if you can. Sehmua’s 4G Solar Trail Camera comes with rechargeable batteries and a solar panel, which allows the camera to run indefinitely given adequate sun exposure.

The camera itself has a fast trigger and 2K photo and video that can be saved to an SD card, or to cloud storage for an additional cost. The app, which is a little clunky and can be confusing due to some quirky menus and word choices, works with images that show up quickly and reliably.

Notably, even though this is a 4G cellular-connected camera, you can still use the camera to record to the SD card if you decide not to pay for one of the data plans. This is another sneaky way this camera provides solid value for its low price point.

The convenience of cell-connected trail cameras is undeniable, but if you’re burned out on subscription charges and don’t mind checking your cameras manually, you can save a significant amount on your trail camera setup. The WOSPORTS Trail Camera is a budget option with impressive image quality and low one-time cost. The camera doesn’t ship with the required eight AA batteries, but it does come with an SD card.

This compact G600 records imagery to an SD card and lasts longer since it doesn’t use batteries communicating over cellular networks. You’ll have to walk into your hunting zone to swap cards, but the purchase price is a fraction of the lifetime cost of buying and operating a modern cell-connected setup.

The 56-megapixel images and 4K video aren’t Planet Earth–level quality, but I was still more than satisfied with the pictures and videos I got. I don’t put too much stock in megapixel numbers as a true measure of trail camera image quality because these numbers are mostly inflated with software enhancements. That said, the images and videos from the WOSPORTS camera were sharp enough for clear identification of details.

No matter how great your trail camera placement, it’s easy for cameras to miss animals. This is exacerbated in big open areas such as wetlands or crop fields where it can be hard to know precisely where animals might appear.

Muddy’s Trifecta 180 is built to minimize these misses. Three motion sensors and a rotating camera capture wide-angle 180-degree images. This is the perfect camera for the edge of large agricultural fields where animals could appear anywhere and often turn up in groups that can be hard to capture in a single image. You have the option for the camera to stitch together impressive panorama images (though they’re harder to appreciate on a phone screen) or the option to capture single-zone images like a regular trail camera would.

The downside of this impressive device is that it seemed to use more battery power than usual, likely attributable to the camera’s need to move and the usual drains of taking and transmitting images. If you’re planning on running it long-term, I’d consider picking up the solar panel accessory with integrated battery.

The Defend by Reveal 360 is not your traditional trail camera—it’s closer to a home security camera that’s designed to work anywhere. Ring and other doorbell cameras usually rely on WiFi for connectivity, which makes them impractical more than about 50 yards from your router. The Defend 360 uses cellular networks instead so you can place this camera anywhere with a decent cell signal.

In the field, the Defend 360’s biggest advantage is motion. Most trail cams are fixed in place, but this one adds remote pan-and-tilt control, allowing you to reposition the camera from your phone. Its 355-degree pan and 75-degree tilt effectively eliminate blind spots when combined with the wide-angle lens.

Like a regular trail camera, motion detection triggers photos only to conserve battery and data. A 1080p live view can be activated on demand when you need a closer live look. That approach makes sense for remote monitoring, though it feels different if you’re used to continuous video feeds from home security cameras.

A rechargeable battery and included solar panel allow for long-term deployment with minimal maintenance. Setup is straightforward via the app, and the camera automatically connects to the strongest available carrier via eSIM.

There are a few downsides. Night footage is serviceable but not amazing, and like most cellular cameras, it requires a subscription plan to unlock full functionality. Still, if your goal is reliable, wide-area monitoring in remote locations, the Defend 360 delivers better coverage and control than standard trail cameras.

A lifetime warranty usually isn’t reason enough alone to buy a product, but in the world of electronics generally and with trail cameras specifically, it’s unheard of and fairly compelling.

With Yellowstone.ai’s Y2 Camera and Solar Bundle, your upfront cost is on the higher side at $250, but the solar panel and rechargeable battery mean no recurring battery costs. You’ll also save on gas and time, since this is a cell-connected camera, and there’s no need to visit the camera unless you want to move it.

Compared to the big-name trail camera apps, the app is not quite as polished, but over several months of testing, I did not experience any of the quirks and bugs I’ve experienced with some trail cam apps from overseas companies (Yellowstone.ai is U.S.-based).

The image and video quality isn’t quite as sharp as the top tier of the cameras I’ve tested like the Reveal Pro 4.0 or Moultrie Edge 4 Solar, but it’s by no means unacceptable. I was impressed by features such as built-in GPS, automatic cell network selection, and remote settings adjustments.

The solar bundle comes with the panel, Y2 camera, and two rechargeable battery packs. If you want to keep the upfront cost down, the camera alone is half the price at $125.

I’ve assembled my choices in this guide based on years of firsthand testing, and I continue testing new trail cam options every season to keep up with the constant rollout of new features and improvements. For decades, I’ve been hanging trail cameras with professional hunters and friends to capture wallowing elk, nursing moose, and scavenging bears on camera.

Historically, I’ve preferred inexpensive, simple cameras that I monitor manually, which keeps my trail camera budget in check, but as connected cameras have gotten more reliable and affordable, I’ve shifted to using cell cams almost exclusively. I hunt in three different states as well as in spots several hours from my home in Colorado, which makes manually checking all my cameras nearly impossible. I still employ “manual” cameras around my property where pulling memory cards frequently isn’t a pain.

One of the main divisions in the trail camera market is whether your trail camera connects to a cellular network, which, if it does, is what allows you to wirelessly send images over great distances. Connected models are so common now that AT&T and Verizon offer monthly service plans that often come bundled with the camera.

This connectivity means that you don’t have to physically visit your camera to check out the imagery it has captured—a benefit that’s most tangible when cameras are placed in far-flung hunting spots, but less valuable if you’re using the camera closer to your house. The cellular connection also makes the cameras easier to operate since most cell-connected cameras can be controlled via your smartphone through apps. These allow you to use remote-control camera settings to switch between photo and video modes, adjust camera sensitivity, and check battery levels.

Networked cameras are addictive to use because they can provide instant, or at least frequent, gratification from your camera(s). However, there’s usually a recurring data plan cost in addition to setup complexity. Bottom line: Be sure you really need the connectivity. There also may be legal restrictions on wirelessly connected cameras that limit how you can use them. Be sure to double-check your state’s regulations before buying.

All trail cameras store images locally on the device, whether or not they have the ability to transmit them wirelessly. More often than not, that storage comes in the form of an SD or micro SD card, which you can remove to download your photos. Cameras with wireless support, however, now often feature an internal hard drive, which stores data more reliably, since you no longer need to physically “pull cards” to collect your footage.

If you’re planning to only use a networked camera, I recommend choosing a camera with internal memory. The No. 1 source of problems I’ve had over the years of testing dozens of different trail cameras and helping others set up many more is memory cards. These plastic chip-like cards are fragile, easy to lose, and can be formatted incorrectly. Even when there’s nothing wrong with a card, cheaper SD cards with slower transfer speeds can cause errors when processing larger images and videos.

The only advantage of having a camera with removable memory is if you want to use the camera without a data plan. This is required for the increasingly rare non-networked cameras, but even connected cameras can be used manually if they have physical cards. Some cameras with internal memory also have an optional SD card slot, such as the Reveal Pro 3.0, which gives you the option to expand storage capacity and use the camera without paying for a data plan.

This might seem like a minor detail, but given that many people want their trail camera to capture their subjects without alerting those subjects to the camera’s presence, the camera’s exterior color can be a critical factor. Since a majority of trail cameras are marketed to hunters and are intended to be used outdoors, these devices generally come in solid earth tones or camouflage patterns.

If you’re a hunter, you probably already have a good sense of what patterns are most appropriate for your area. If not, snap some photos of the trunks of the trees where you intend to mount the camera; then compare them to the patterns on the cameras you’re considering.

Cameron Shrum, avid bowhunter and co-owner of C&K Archery in Frisco, Colorado, says, “People will get a good deal on a camera and not realize how important it is to have [it] match [their] habitat. The goal is to get pictures of animals without them knowing they are being watched, and when something is out of place, game animals have a tendency to figure it out.”

As a professional photographer and videographer, the first thing you need to know about judging the quality of a camera is that there is no single metric that easily tells you which camera will record more clearly. At a glance, checking specs like the number of megapixels in a camera’s sensor gives you a decent clue as to what you can expect.

Ultimately, the best way to gauge the quality of a trail camera is with your eyes. Take a minute to look at sample photos posted by customers on retailers such as Amazon, which give you a practical way to evaluate images taken under natural conditions.

Trail cameras rarely take print-worthy shots, but that isn’t what they’re for. If you’re just patterning animals, image quality isn’t as crucial as simply detecting them. Trophy hunters trying to identify certain calibers of animals or monitor a specific animal across multiple cameras will want to be more picky about image quality and clarity.

Even if you don’t need great fidelity, a better image makes using trail cams more useful and rewarding. I’ve come to appreciate having modern trail cameras that deliver clear images and 4K videos over the crude, fuzzy work of older, lo-fi models.

I recommend using only lithium batteries in trail cameras. Especially with cheaper cameras, I’ve found that regular alkaline batteries don’t provide enough voltage for the IR flash, and many times a trail camera may not record video with underpowered batteries (alkaline batteries start decreasing in voltage as soon as you start using them). Lithium batteries deliver higher voltage consistently, and they work better in the cold.

If you’re setting up a cellular trail cam, make sure you check signal strength in the area. If you have a camera that offers an app or website (as many now do) that lets you view images on your smartphone, try triggering the camera and see if you receive the notification and image.

Since trail cameras are often left alone for days, weeks, or even months at a time, setting them up properly is important. Shrum recommends testing your trail camera before you walk away. “Have it snap a few pictures with you walking by and then review them. Sometimes you may not have the right angle; it may be too high or too low. Try to set the height and angle to capture the game in the center of the camera’s view.”

Trail cameras are usually strapped to a tree and most come packaged with a long strap for this purpose. If you’re placing a camera somewhere without convenient trees for the angle you want, look into a camera stand or even a tripod. Most trail cameras have a standard tripod plate mount (¼-20) and stands or stakes are available from most manufacturers.

A common spot to place cameras is along well-traveled game trails. A tip I picked up watching champion archer Levi Morgan put up cameras on one of his hunting leases: rather than pointing the camera down a trail where it’s likely to be in the line-of-sight of animals as they walk it, put the camera off-trail between 10 and 30 feet away perpendicular to the trail. This will usually give you broadside images of animals instead of head-on and puts the camera in their periphery.

Once you’ve tested your placement (and image transmission for connected cameras) by viewing a test photo on the app or the camera itself, scan the camera’s field of view for new-growth vegetation. Plants and tree branches can result in a near-constant stream of false triggers on a windy day. I like to place any plants or branches I cut behind the camera for a bit of concealment, making sure they can’t blow in front of the camera.

Since trail cams are motion-activated, a fast trigger seems important. You don’t want an animal to pass by the camera before you get a photo, right? In my experience, the real problem is taking the photo too quickly, which results in seeing just the nose of a slow-moving deer. Still, many brands tout their fast trigger speeds as if they solve an important problem.

“It’s kind of a BS spec, frankly,” Gregg Farrell, vice president of marketing for Tactacam Reveal, told me. “The goal is to capture the animal in the center of the frame and our cameras do that through the operating system working with the [motion] sensor.”

Most trail cameras have listed trigger speeds around a half second, which can work well, but are often too quick if implemented poorly. I almost always switch my cameras to shoot a multishot burst, if available, to give the camera more opportunities to grab a well-framed shot. Keep in mind, though, that this will double or triple the number of images you receive, so it may not be a solution if you’re using a cell-connected camera and trying to save with a limited-data plan.

Some cameras have detection delay settings that let you set a period of time after an image is captured before it’ll take another. This can cut down on look-alike images if an animal is hanging around in the detection area, especially if you’ve enabled a multishot mode.

Connected trail cameras make scouting convenient, but they come with hidden costs. Almost all cellular trail cameras require a monthly data plan to cover the cost of cloud storage and image transmission.

Many companies tack on extra fees for features such as live streaming, which eat up a lot of data and cost the companies money with their network provider partners. Like sitting at a blackjack table, it’s easy to get caught up in the excitement of scouting and click your way to hundreds of dollars in recurring monthly charges. You can review the details of each company’s data plans before you buy and decide what features you want to use in advance. You can save money on a camera if you decide you don’t need all the latest features and avoid the temptation of activating those extra charges in the process.

Common game animals such as whitetail deer and elk tend to settle into routines during the summer months which often persist into early fall. The change of seasons and seasonal mating windows will help throw routine out the window in the fall, but if you can identify high-traffic areas in the spring and early summer, that will likely continue all summer.

The best practices for finding a good spot and setting up the camera properly are the same in any season. Spring in some ways makes it easier to identify animal travel patterns since the ground is often wet and recent activity is more obvious. Hike your zone and look for fresh signs to identify intersections, pinch points, and frequently visited locations. If you’re able to access your cameras easily and often, use the early season to experiment with different locations for a few weeks and try new spots you hadn’t considered before that show promise based on animal signs. Half the fun of placing these cameras is finding that perfect location and image framing that yields a ton of exciting wildlife images.

There are plenty of things that can trigger a trail camera other than the type(s) of animals you’re looking to capture, including squirrels, lights, and vegetation moving in the wind. “False triggers,” as we call them, are not only disappointing, but waste storage and burn through your data plan. It’s hard to eliminate them completely, but there are lots of ways to minimize them.

The most important is proper camera setup. Once you’ve got it framed up the way you want and have a successful test image, look for branches and weeds in the frame, primarily in the foreground. A single goldenrod stalk or pine bough can burn through a month’s data allotment on a windy day, so take your time to clear the immediate area in front of your camera.

You can’t always clear cut in front of a camera, so if you find you’re still getting more false triggers than you’d like, adjust the camera’s trigger sensitivity down. Many cameras only offer high or low, but if you have a more finely graded adjustment such as the 1 through 10 sensitivity settings on the Reveal Pro 3.0, adjust slowly down until you stop getting false triggers so you don’t overcorrect and miss animals.

Some cameras also use recognition software to reject images that appear to be empty. Moultrie’s Edge cameras allow you to only accept motion triggers in selected zones of an image, effectively blocking triggers from, for example, a corner of a detection zone with moving tree branches.

Most states have some sort of regulation with the use of trail cameras, especially when used on public land and as they relate to hunting activities. Arizona, where game animals tend to congregate around limited water sources, banned trail cameras for hunting statewide in 2021. Colorado, where I live, has few restrictions on trail camera use before your hunting season begins, but limits employing them while you’re actively hunting.

Using trail cameras on your own private property doesn’t usually involve too many restrictions, but be sure to check the regulations from your state’s wildlife management organization to confirm, as private land practices can still be regulated through the hunting codes since wildlife are considered a shared public resource.

There are so many options for security cameras dedicated to home use, and because of that, most of the time it makes more sense to just buy a security camera from a brand that specializes in that application, such as Ring or Google Nest.

These products generally have superior apps and software to hunt-focused trail cameras. Since they're designed for home use, they effortlessly connect to your home WiFi network, don’t require a data subscription, and will have features trail cameras won’t such as two-way communication.

That said, if you already own trail cameras and don’t need specific features, most trail cameras can serve a security purpose. The best trail cameras to employ for security are the newer “live” trail cameras that transmit imagery instantly via cell networks and notify you on your phone when the camera has been triggered.

Another option is WiFi-enabled trail cameras that can connect to your phone without a cellular network to transmit images. However, these cameras don’t usually transmit if you’re not within range of the camera (i.e., at home), so they’re limited to general monitoring rather than real-time notification when you’re away.

Jamie, Senior Reviews Editor, joined the Hearst Enthusiast Group in 2021. She has covered technology and consumer lifestyle gadgets since 1995—and shared her expertise in print, digital, and in broadcast originating the role of The Gizmo Girl for ESPN’s Cold Pizza. She has written about, tested, and reviewed everything from turkey fryers to high-definition TVs. Her byline has appeared in TWICE, Sound & Vision, Consumer Reports, and many others. In her free time, Jamie is in a yoga class, searching for the perfect matcha latte, or walking the boards.

#6368. Sea to Sky Highway Named One of the Best EV Road Trips in the World

Most people know the Sea to Sky Highway as one of Canada’s most beautiful drives. It winds from the edge of Vancouver along Howe Sound, climbs past waterfalls and mountain viewpoints, and continues toward Whistler and Pemberton.

Now, it has another reason to be on your road trip list: it has been named one of the best EV road trips in the world.

According to a study by iSelect, British Columbia’s Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally among the world’s most EV-friendly road trips. The study analyzed 48 iconic road trips across six continents and scored each route based on factors such as charging infrastructure, distance, estimated charging cost, and traveller reviews.

For Canadian travellers, that is a big deal. EV road trips are no longer just about whether you can make it from one charger to the next. The best routes now combine scenery, reliable charging access, reasonable costs, and places you actually want to stop along the way.

Yes. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of the best EV road trips in Canada because it is relatively short, scenic, well-travelled, and supported by charging options along the route. iSelect ranked it seventh in the world for EV road trips, with 49 chargers available across its 121-mile route and a road trip score of 88.15 out of 100.

The route is ideal for electric vehicle drivers because it connects major destinations like Vancouver, Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton without requiring a long, remote drive through charging gaps.

Electric vehicles are becoming a bigger part of travel planning. The International Energy Agency expects global electric car sales to reach 23 million in 2026, representing 28% of total car sales. That means more travellers are thinking about charging stops the same way they used to think about gas stations, rest areas, and coffee breaks.

Charging infrastructure is also expanding. The IEA reported that the worldwide stock of public charging points reached more than 7 million at the end of 2025, with nearly 1.8 million public chargers added in 2025 alone.

That shift matters for road trips. A few years ago, EV travel could feel like a math problem with scenery attached. Now, on the right routes, it can feel much closer to a normal road trip — as long as you plan ahead.

The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh globally in iSelect’s study. The route stretches from Horseshoe Bay toward Pemberton, passing through some of British Columbia’s most famous scenery, including Howe Sound, Squamish, Whistler, and the Coast Mountains.

Chart idea: create a simple horizontal bar chart titled Top 10 EV Road Trips in the World, using the Road Trip Score column. This would work well just below the table.

One of the most interesting parts of the ranking is that Canada appears twice in the global top 10.

The Kootenay Highway ranked second in the world, with a score of 99.24 out of 100. The Sea to Sky Highway ranked seventh, with a score of 88.15. That gives Canada two of the highest-rated EV road trip routes in the world according to iSelect’s index.

That should not be surprising to anyone who has road-tripped through British Columbia. Canada’s western mountain routes already offer some of the best scenery in the world. The difference now is that EV infrastructure is starting to make those drives more accessible for electric vehicle owners.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not a long cross-country endurance test. That is part of what makes it such a good EV route.

The drive from Vancouver to Whistler is short enough for many modern EVs to handle comfortably, but scenic enough that you will want to stop anyway. Instead of treating charging as an inconvenience, you can build it into the trip.

Stops like Squamish, Shannon Falls, Brandywine Falls, Whistler Village, and Pemberton give travellers natural breaks along the way. For EV drivers, that means charging can happen while you eat, hike, shop, or take photos instead of sitting around watching a battery percentage crawl upward.

Horseshoe Bay is a great place to start if you are coming from Vancouver. It has waterfront views, ferry traffic, cafes, and a relaxed village feel before the highway begins climbing toward Squamish.

Shannon Falls is one of the easiest scenic stops on the Sea to Sky Highway. The short walk to the waterfall makes it a perfect break on the way to Squamish or Whistler.

Squamish is one of the best stops on the route. It has food, coffee, outdoor shops, hiking access, and views of the Stawamus Chief. It is also a practical place to stop, stretch your legs, and check your charge before continuing north.

The Sea to Sky Gondola is one of the most popular attractions along the route. It offers sweeping views over Howe Sound and the surrounding mountains, making it an easy way to turn the drive into a full day trip.

Brandywine Falls is another easy stop between Squamish and Whistler. The walk is short, the waterfall is impressive, and it is a good reminder that the Sea to Sky Highway is not just about getting to Whistler.

Whistler is the main destination for many Sea to Sky road trips. In summer, it is great for hiking, biking, patios, lakes, and mountain views. In winter, it becomes one of North America’s most famous ski destinations.

Pemberton is a quieter extension of the trip beyond Whistler. It offers mountain scenery, farmland, and a slower pace for travellers who want to continue past the busiest part of the route.

Even on EV-friendly routes, it is still smart to plan your charging stops ahead of time. Check charger locations, charging speeds, plug types, and whether stations are available or out of service before you start driving.

The Sea to Sky Highway is not the place to play battery roulette. Mountain roads, weather, traffic, and detours can all affect range. Keep a buffer so you are not stressed if a charger is busy or unavailable.

EV range can drop in cold weather, heavy rain, strong winds, or mountain driving. The Sea to Sky Highway includes elevation changes, so it is better to plan conservatively.

The best EV road trips are the ones where charging fits naturally into the route. Stop for lunch in Squamish, explore Whistler Village, or take a scenic break while the car charges.

Do not wait until you are in a parking lot with weak signal to download a charging app. Set up your accounts, payment methods, and route planning tools before you leave home.

For an EV road trip, we would use a mix of navigation, charging, and general travel apps.

For more trip-planning tools, see our guide to the best travel apps for 2026.

Absolutely. The Sea to Sky Highway is one of Canada’s great scenic drives whether you are driving an electric vehicle, hybrid, or gas-powered car.

The EV ranking simply shows that the route is becoming more accessible for modern travellers. The scenery was already there. The charging infrastructure is what makes it easier for EV drivers to enjoy the route with more confidence.

The Sea to Sky Highway’s global ranking is part of a bigger shift in travel. Sustainable travel is no longer just about choosing trains over planes or staying in eco-lodges. For many travellers, it now includes how they drive, where they charge, and whether road trips can be done with lower emissions.

Canada has the scenery. The challenge has always been distance. As charging infrastructure improves, more Canadian road trips will become realistic for EV drivers.

That is good news for travellers, but it is also good news for smaller communities along the way. EV road trips encourage people to stop longer, spend locally, and build their route around towns, restaurants, viewpoints, parks, and overnight stays.

Before driving the Sea to Sky Highway in an electric vehicle, make sure to:

The Sea to Sky Highway has always been one of Canada’s most spectacular drives. Now it is also being recognized as one of the best EV road trips in the world.

That combination makes sense. The route is scenic, manageable, practical, and packed with places worth stopping. For EV drivers, that is exactly what makes a great road trip. You do not want to plan your entire day around charging. You want charging to fit into a journey you already wanted to take.

From Vancouver to Squamish, Whistler, and Pemberton, the Sea to Sky Highway proves that EV travel does not have to mean giving up adventure. It just means planning the route a little smarter.

And honestly, if your charging stop comes with mountain views and a coffee in Squamish, that is not exactly a hardship.

#6367. The Best Airbnbs in Colorado, Including a Ski-In Chalet and a Cliffside Cabin

I’ve always found Colorado a little hard to resist. After a handful of trips, I’ve explored everything from Aspen’s glitzy streets to Denver’s spirited food and cocktail scene to the many smaller towns in between—and somehow, there’s still more to discover. With four national parks; miles of hiking and biking trails; world-class ski resorts; and cities brimming with independent shops, restaurants, and bars, Colorado is a year-round playground with plenty to keep you busy (and plenty of reasons to come back).

Finding the right Colorado Airbnb is part of the fun. Think tucked-away mountain cabins with front-row seats to the snow, sprawling homes made for group getaways, and character-filled apartments that put you right in the middle of the action. While there are plenty of gorgeous Colorado hotels, there's something pretty wonderful about having your own Airbnb to return to after a day of chasing fresh powder, hiking, or exploring a new town. Whether you're plotting a winter ski escape, a summer adventure, or a fall foliage getaway, these are the 13 best Airbnbs in Colorado to add to your wish list.

We've selected these listings based on Superhost and Guest Favorite status, ratings, amenities, location, decor, editor stays, and previous guest reviews.

Number of guests: 9Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: In-ground pool, firepit, outdoor shower, dedicated office space, rooftop with mountain views

Don’t let the university neighborhood fool you—this south-of-downtown oasis is ideal for a quieter, family-friendly stay. It's close to the light rail, making it easy to get around when you so choose. With succulent-filled rooms, large paintings, five cozy bedrooms, and two-story windows, there’s lots to love about this space.

Madi Allen was 12 years old when she almost died from flu. Now 28, she shared her story with Live Science.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In February 2011, Madi Allen, a healthy 12-year-old in Central Illinois, who loved playing sports, almost died from the flu. The influenza B virus resulted in her developing necrotizing pneumonia, where the infection triggers inflammation that destroys the tissue of the lungs, methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), and her kidneys shut down. She was put on life support and dialysis, and was intubated for five weeks. She spent another two months in hospital and a decade recovering from the damage caused.

Allen, now 28, shared her experience with Live Science.

I was 12 years old when it all started. I was just a normal seventh grader, I played soccer and basketball. I didn't really have any health issues beforehand — just sports-induced asthma.

That weekend, I started to feel a little sick, but nothing too bad. My mom kept giving me over-the-counter medicine and it would work for a bit, then once it wore off, it would get really bad. I'd planned to go to one of my friend's birthday parties then spend the night with my best friend. I went to the party, but I texted my mom saying I should come home because I really wasn't feeling well, which was not usual for me at all. That night I asked my mom to sleep with me because I just felt terrible.

That was Saturday. By Sunday night, the only position that I could get comfortable in was my mom holding me like a baby. My mom just held me all weekend. My whole body just hurt and I started feeling like I couldn't breathe properly. That got way worse Monday morning.

We were waiting for my pediatrician to open up and my mom suggested taking a shower, saying, "Maybe that will help you feel a bit better before we go to the doctor." She had to help me take a shower because I was so weak, I couldn't stand by myself. She stepped away for a second just to grab a towel and said that when she came back, my lips were turning gray and my eyes were starting to look sunken in. She knew that something was not right so she called my dad, who was at the grocery store, and told him to just leave everything, that we need to get to the hospital.

Allen was put on life support and had to be intubated for five weeks after getting sick with flu.

Our local hospital is just a small rural hospital — everybody gets transferred out. They diagnosed me with double pneumonia and then sent me to a different hospital 30 minutes away that specialized more in kids.

My dad rode with me in the ambulance while my mom went home and grabbed a few things — she thought we'd just be there for a few days. By the time we got to the second hospital, I was in respiratory distress. They wanted to intubate me straight away but were waiting until my mom got there so she could talk to me — my dad did the best he could, but my dad didn't know how to calm me down.

I don't think the doctors even told me that they were putting me to sleep. My mom had to be the one to tell me. I remember being very scared. They put this mask on my face for the BiPAP [bilevel positive airway pressure machine, which delivers pressurized air to a patient] and I felt like that was suffocating me. It didn't feel like it was helping at all, which, I guess, at that point, it wasn't. They were just trying everything they could. I was begging them to take it off of me, crying and just saying, "one minute, just take it off for one minute."

Finally my mom tried to calm me down and she's like, "They're gonna have to put you to sleep now." I remember her telling me, "You're just gonna go to sleep for like a couple of hours and then you're gonna wake up and you're gonna feel a lot better."

My mom had to leave the room while they were doing that. As she was walking out the door, the last thing I said was "Mom" and then I put my hands in a heart shape. That was the last thing I did and the last time my mom heard my voice for five weeks.

After I was intubated, things got worse. I had to be put on life support so needed to be moved to a bigger hospital in St. Louis, Missouri. The flight team came to evaluate me and they later told me they didn't think they were ever going to get me to Saint Louis. They thought I wasn't going to make the trip. But they said my mom was begging them to help me, everyone in my family was begging them, so they did everything they could to get me on the helicopter. They worked on me for several hours — every time they tried to move me something would go wrong — but eventually they got me there.

The doctors had to call my parents to get permission to do surgery and put me on life support. My mom said that every time she heard my dad's phone ring, she thought they were calling to tell them that I didn't make it. They were told twice that it was more than likely I was going to pass than make it. They were trying to prepare my parents that I wasn't going to make it.

After getting out of hospital, it took years for Allen to recover, eventually having part of her lung removed that had been badly damaged by the virus.

I woke up five weeks later, and it was very confusing. Everybody was told if I asked what day it was, just to tell me the day of the week. When someone accidentally told me the date, I started crying because my aunt was supposed to be getting married a few weeks later and I was worried about being at her wedding. My mom wasn't there, so my dad had to calm me down and then he told me the wedding had been pushed to October so I could be there.

The second thing I was worried about was that I was supposed to take a test on the Constitution and that I'd missed it. I ended up taking it in the hospital. I was there for 93 days. I got out the very last week of school, so I got to go in on the last day of school and surprise my classmates and my teachers.

That summer, I didn't really do anything besides go to doctor's appointments. I was doing physical therapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy — literally all my time was spent at the hospital in therapy. I'd missed three months of school, but I got to start eighth grade with all my friends, and I ended up playing basketball again. But the next several years was a lot of hard work of trying to get back to my normal.

It probably took the rest of junior high and high school to get back to how I would have been before. It was a very long process and during that time I got sick a lot, so I ended up back in the hospital several times. And it was hard going through that as a teenager — I felt like everybody else is living their normal life, and I felt like I missed out on a lot. Looking back now, I still feel like I did miss out a lot. But I think we made the best of the circumstances.

During COVID, when I was 22, I kept getting sick, and the doctors finally told me that part of my lung was so damaged from the flu it was causing infections, so they gave me an option of getting part of my lung removed. It was a major surgery, but I did it and that was probably the best decision I ever made, because it's been five years and I have not been in the hospital once.

I moved to Florida about three years ago, and I started working as a medical assistant in a pulmonary clinic. This semester I got accepted into respiratory therapy school, so for the next two years, I'm going to be in school for respiratory therapy. It's kind of a full circle moment, to come back into the medical field, because there was a point in my life where everybody was asking me, "Oh, do you want to be a doctor? Do you want to be a nurse?" And I'm like, "Absolutely not." I was still so sick that I was there all the time. I never wanted to be there.

I went to college and I got a degree in criminal justice, but I never really knew what I wanted to do. I ended up getting a job at our local hospital — that first hospital that I went to. Every time they put me in the ER I just loved being there. That job made me realize that this is what I wanted to do.

When people hear my story, they don't realize that if I don't tell the end — after the hospital until now — they don't realize that my life didn't go back to normal after. It's taken 10 years. And it's hard. Some of the other family members that we've gotten to know through Families Fighting Flu, it's difficult listening to their stories. Sometimes I feel like I have this survivor's guilt. Their stories sound exactly like mine — but their kids didn't make it.

Before I got sick I got the flu shot every year, but that year we just got busy and it got put on the back burner. Since getting sick I have always made it a priority to get the flu shot every year. I know it is not a guarantee that I will never get the flu again — but hopefully it will reduce the chances of it ever getting that bad again.

With thanks to Families Fighting Flu, a non-profit organization that promotes flu vaccination and raises awareness of the severity of the infectious disease through families that have been affected.

#6364. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!
