#6322. Review: KLM 787-10 Business Class (Amsterdam – Los Angeles), Still A Solid Choice

I don’t need an airline to surprise me every time. Sometimes I want to know what I’m getting. My KLM 787-10 business class flight from Amsterdam to Los Angeles reminded me why I keep choosing KLM…and why I still wish it would turn down the heat!

I recently flew KLM’s Boeing 787-10 in World Business Class from Amsterdam to Los Angeles once again, about a year after the flight reviewed below. The seat and overall experience have changed little, so I’ll offer a more abbreviated review of my latest flight. My comprehensive review follows, with a detailed look at the cabin and seat features. In short: nothing has changed at KLM, for better or for worse.

Yes, especially for 60,000 Flying Blue miles (though I’d probably now pay the extra to get out of “light” class). The seat was comfortable and the food was excellent. I enjoyed the flight even though I knew almost exactly what to expect.

The warm cabin remains my biggest complaint, particularly because I encountered the same issue on this route last year. Individual air vents would help accommodate those of us who prefer a cooler sleeping environment.

Even so, this was a comforting way to get home to Los Angeles. Familiar and even boring does not have to mean disappointing.

The detailed review below covers my April 2025 flight on the same aircraft type and route. It includes more detailed info on the seat features, inflight entertainment, Wi-Fi, lavatories, and amenity kit.

My 11-hour KLM flight from Amsterdam to Los Angeles on the 787-10 in World Business Class was smooth, comfortable, but a little warm…

I’ve reviewed the KLM A330, 777, and 787-9 in business class and also the 787-10 in economy class, but this was my first time flying the 787-10 in business class.

I arrived at the KLM Crown Lounge quite early to get my work done for the day, just in case the internet did not function on my flight. While the lounge gets crowded, I quite like it.

Boarding began at 9:05, 45 minutes before departure.

I entered via door 2L and proceeded through the galley and turned left to my seat in 4K.

The KLM 787-10 business class cabin features 38 Jamco America Venture seats arranged in a 1-2-1 reverse herringbone configuration. These Japanese-made seats are 10-15% lighter than traditional reverse herringbone seats.

Seat pitch is generous and seats convert into a fully lie-flat bed (75 inches long). There’s a side storage compartment, seat controls on the armrest, two USB-A ports (one on the side and one under the screen), and a universal power outlet.

My left armrest could be raised (for use when seated) and lowered (to give more space for sleeping).

Interestingly, I noticed the seat looked a bit tattered…at least cosmetically. The paint was chipped on the armrest and under the monitor and the (faux) leather shell around the seat was discolored. There was also noticeable dirt and grime. Everything functioned, but it really looked like an old product, even though my aircraft, PH-BKG, was only delivered five years ago.

Bedding on KLM is comparatively average, with a large pillow and soft duvet-style blanket. There is no day blanket or mattress pad.

I tried to sleep after lunch but the cabin was warm and there were no personal air vents. I did manage a few hours of sleep, but I would have loved to sleep eight hours…a cool cabin and a plush mattress pad would have helped.

The retrofitted 777 World Business Class cabins offer suites with closing doors; the 787-10 do not have this extra feature.

The 11-hour journey to California included lunch after takeoff, a midflight snack, and a meal before landing. Menus were waiting on each seat and KLM continues to print menus for each flight (you’ll notice on the backside of the menu lists your flight number and flight date).

Pre-departure beverages were offered before takeoff, including beer, sparkling wine, orange juice, and “Royal Blue Legend,” the KLM signature cocktail with lemon, ginger, and spirulina…which I had to try.

Lunch began after takeoff, with a refreshing amuse bouche (I don’t even know what it was, but the green thing was topped in a toasted walnut and was very nice) and a drink (I enjoyed “The Very High Fashioned” cocktail, a riff on an Old Fashioned).

I had chili shrimps with pickled watermelon and beetroot mousse and fresh watercress for my appetizer…a great collection of flavors. I was served with a small green salad and bread with Dutch butter. I switched to a Boschendal Boschen Blane 2023 (white wine from South Africa).

For my main course, I chose salmon à la Flamande with Hollandaise sauce, served with white asparagus, scrambled eggs, and potatoes. The salmon filet was very small, but it was a good choice.

For dessert, cheese (blue cheese and Beemster Royaal Fenugreek cheese) with crackers, grapes, and a raisin salad with pine nuts, followed by a tart raspberry mousse topped with sunflower seeds, topped with passion fruit crumble.

About halfway through the flight, passengers were offered a vegetarian croquette sandwich with mustard (I tried that) or a mini club sandwich. Both were served with cherry cheesecake ice cream, which I skipped.

A self-serve station was also set up in the galley with Dutch snacks:

105 minutes before landing, a Caesar salad with pulled chicken, egg, tomatoes, Reypenaar cheese, and pine nuts was offered along with a side of pumpkin ravioli in cream artichoke sauce. A very nice pre-arrival meal, though the pasta was served wrapped in aluminum foil…that could have easily been removed.

The internet worked well on the flight (the flight pass was €22) and it turned out to be a very productive flight when it became clear I could not sleep.

I also managed one movie on the flight, an old Brad Pitt, Kevin Spacey, and Morgan Freeman film called Seven. A little jarring, to say the least…

The KLM IFE library includes music, movies, TV shows, games, and a moving flight map.

KLM’s 787-10 has two lavatories in the front of the cabin reserved for business class passengers (and also for crew use). As always on KLM, I appreciate the tulip flower and the Delft Blue House wallpaper. Soap products were from Marie-Stella-Maris.

The amenity kit also had products from Marie-Stella-Maris (face cream and lip balm) and also included socks, a pen, earplugs, and a dental kit (with tootpaste tablets instead of a tube of toothpaste).

As we approached LAX, the purser came around with Delft Blue Houses, the signature “souvenir” of KLM World Business Class. I was hoping for house 98, which was the parental home of Anthony Fokker in Haarlem (Fokker went on to become one of the world’s greatest aircraft builder in the late 1920’s with factories in the Netherlands and the USA) and I got it!

Then the lady in front of me did not want a house, so I asked if I could have hers and got a second one, 89.

The crew was very seasoned/mature (as always on KLM, it seems) and also very lovely. Very attentive service with a smile and I appreciated so much that flight attendants roamed the cabin throughout the flight, not just during the formal meal services.

It was a beautiful morning (yes, still morning) when we landed at LAX 11 hours later and we flew right over downtown LA and the iconic In-N-Out next to LAX.

KLM offers a very average business class, which is to say a very solid business class. I enjoyed good service, great food, and a comfortable seat on the flight, though the lack of air vent and warm cabin made sleeping difficult. I like the 787-10 and look forward to flying KLM again.

KLMs wines are consistently bad. Embarrassingly bad, especially given what Air France serves. In general, the meal quality continues to decline on KLM, you can really feel the cheapness.

KLM has not been a great experience for us even in Biz Class!! Never got a house on one flight!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!!

I find the lack of adequate bedding concerning, makes the product all very mediocre, average at best. It’s not only for comfort, but brings peace of mind to know one is not sleeping directly on the (very probably) very dirty seat.

Ah, yes. Three saucy thirst trap pics! There is a God after all.

I’m surprised that you find Matthew’s selfies “saucy”. He’s an attractive chap but he’s hardly posing provocatively, and is completely covered from neck to ankles.

Great review as always. It will forever be a mystery to me why mainline carriers cheap out on not having individual air vents. Thankfully most of the AC aircraft have that feature (the airline I primarily fly). This seems rather shortsighted and something I’d expect with Ryanair (or insert LCC or ULCC here) as opposed to the likes of KLM. That said, those Delft houses are a nice touch – very cute!

Do you think they are just being cheap? I don’t understand why anyone would opt out of them to save a few bucks?

“KLM offers a very average business class, which is to say a very solid business class.”

“Average” and “solid” are not even the same. They are not synonyms.

Jesus H. Christ. Look it up in a dictionary.

I just arrived in SIN from DPS & business class was all right. My FA was good but the rest of the crew was very average.

You really can be a dimwit. In my view, an “average” business class (typical or normal) product is “solid” (dependable or reliable). KLM has a consistent, reliable, quality product with attentive, senior cabin crews and a great seat. That makes it “solid”. The wankery of products like Qatar is lost on most frequent fliers. No reason why I would pick KLM if an Air France flight was available. [Although I do love my Delft house collection!]

#6320. Defiant Ritz-Carlton Singapore Joining Marriott Bonvoy… Finally!

The world’s only Ritz-Carlton that doesn’t participate in the Marriott Bonvoy program will finally be joining, which seems long overdue. I can’t imagine the hotel will be particularly generous, but we’ll see!

The 608-key Ritz-Carlton Millenia Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program as of December 1, 2026. So as of that date, Bonvoy members will be able to earn and redeem points, and take advantage of Bonvoy elite perks, when staying at the hotel (admittedly Bonvoy elite perks at Ritz-Carlton properties are fairly limited, as breakfast isn’t a benefit for any elite tier).

As I covered in late 2025, this property is the only Ritz-Carlton in the world that doesn’t participate in the Bonvoy program. The backstory here is that the hotel opened back in 1996, and at the time, Ritz-Carlton didn’t have any sort of a loyalty program that awarded points.

In 2010, the Ritz-Carlton Rewards program started awarding points for hotel stays, as a parallel program to Marriott Rewards. The ability to earn and redeem points came at a cost to individual hotels, but it was intended to boost occupancy and average daily rates.

Initially, hotels had the option of whether they wanted to opt in or out of the program. Most hotels bought into the concept, though the Ritz-Carlton Osaka and Ritz-Carlton Singapore were the two hotels that opted out. The Ritz-Carlton Osaka eventually decided to participate, leaving the Ritz-Carlton Singapore as the only hotel that’s not participating.

Ultimately when the Marriott Bonvoy program formed as the combination of Marriott Rewards and Starwood Preferred Guest, the hotel could still stick to its legacy contract of not having to participate in the program. Clearly the owners of the hotel have now had a change of heart… or something!

Obviously we don’t have any sort of an official explanation for the reason that this Ritz-Carlton property is finally backtracking. I can’t imagine that Marriott gave the owners an ultimatum, given that Marriott is known for letting hotel owners get away with anything, as long as they get paid.

My guess is that the competitive realities just finally caught up with this hotel — Singapore is an increasingly competitive hotel market, this is a massive hotel with 600+ rooms to fill every night, and the hotel is also a bit past its prime.

The truth is that loyalty programs exist for a reason, as they’re a great tool for getting heads into beds. Obviously the hotel will be on the hook for some additional loyalty fees, but I imagine this will make the hotel more appealing to people who otherwise wouldn’t have considered it.

I also have to imagine that even though the hotel did a decent job communicating its lack of participation in Marriott Bonvoy, I still suspect many guests didn’t realize this, and ended up being disappointed.

As of December 1, 2026, the Ritz-Carlton Singapore will be joining the Marriott Bonvoy program. This is the only Ritz-Carlton hotel in the world that hasn’t participated in Bonvoy, so this is great to see.

The backstory is that the hotel opened before Ritz-Carlton had a loyalty program, and then when a program was finally formed, participation was optional. Literally every other Ritz-Carlton in the world saw value in this… except this one, apparently.

Fortunately they’ve now come to their senses, or something, so it’s great to see that this will be changing.

What do you make of the Ritz-Carlton Singapore joining Bonvoy?

United Airlines is connecting its two West Coast hubs to northern Michigan.

Next summer, the carrier will launch nonstop service to Traverse City, Michigan, from both Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

The two routes will launch on June 19 and run through the peak summer season, according to details shared Thursday by Cherry Capital Airport (TVC). The airport touted the service as something that would give TVC its "first-ever coast-to-coast nonstop footprint."

Traverse City is a popular summer destination, situated on the banks of Grand Traverse Bay, an arm of Lake Michigan.

The region is also home to the famous National Cherry Festival each summer. That century-old extravaganza — which includes an air show — will feature the U.S. Navy's Blue Angels in 2027.

United will operate its California service to Traverse City on Saturdays through the summer.

However, the carrier will also offer flights on select Wednesdays — including before and after the cherry festival.

United will operate a Boeing 737-800 on the route, according to the airport.

That aircraft features 16 domestic first-class recliners across four rows up front, and 150 seats in the main cabin (the number of extra-legroom Economy Plus seats vary from one jet to another)

While United’s Los Angeles and San Francisco routes to TVC are new, the carrier is no stranger to the region.

United already offers service to the airport from each of its other mainland U.S. hubs — including Chicago, Denver, Houston, and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD).

On top of the two Traverse City routes, United announced additional new service from San Francisco.

The carrier will launch flights to Jacksonville International Airport (JAX) on March 29. That route will operate twice per week, year-round.

Traverse City and Jacksonville give United a total of seven new routes from its Bay Area hub in just the last couple of weeks.

Several of those flights are new transcontinental service, including routes to Hartford, Conn.; Richmond and Norfolk, Va; and Charleston, S.C.

#6318. My First “New” Chase Sapphire Reserve Travel Redemption Blew My Mind

There’s… a lot… of coverage surrounding the revamped Chase Sapphire Reserve Card. As per usual these days, the hot takes are plentiful and people are fired up. It’s either the apocalypse or the beginning of something great, depending on which attention seeker you read. As a long time cardholder, I’m really intrigued by the new changes.

The changes really fit my profile and sure, the card will cost more, but I won’t have to introduce any behavior change to get more, unlike some other cards. I’ll do most of my spending on this card. I’m a keeper just from the fee credit and earning multipliers.

Well, if my first Chase Sapphire Reserve redemption is any indicator, this card may single handedly change the redemption game and just about everyone should take note — including airline and hotel transfer partners. It’s already a huge win.

Chase Travel’s ‘The Edit’ is a curated selection of nice hotels, which offer benefits similar to those provided by a travel agent or other luxury credit card booking platform. When booking a ‘The Edit’ property, you can expect breakfast for two, a $100 F&B credit, late check out and an upgrade subject to availability.

Which leads me to the important bit! With the revamped Sapphire Reserve Card, there’s a new “Points Boost” feature, which offers up to two cents per point (25,000 points would cover $500, etc) for some flight or hotel purchases.

This can be amazing value, with flights of $3,000 being grabbed for just 150,000 points, with no taxes and fees and the ability to still earn frequent flyer miles and elite status points, since the airline treats it like a cash ticket.

Previously, the Sapphire Reserve card offered a steady point redemption opportunity directly on Chase Travel at 1.5 cents per point (100,000 points would cover $1500, etc). But with the new version, some travel purchases you want to redeem for will either offer less value than before, the same, or more, with this new ‘Points Boost’ at 2 cents per point. We like more!

I am in New York and wanted to do a little staycation, so I fired up Chase Travel and found one of my more reliable upper mid-scale hotels, The Thompson Central Park was on as part of ‘The Edit’. My two options became a very clear singular, third option.

Typically, I’d consider paying cash or transferring my points from Chase to Hyatt to pay for a stay like this. Hyatt has “fixed” points rates, meaning the points price is largely irrespective of the cash price and only changes by seasonal dates. For this season, it was 25,000 points per night for the Thompson Central Park.

If I were to transfer my points, I’d get a free night (the cash rate was around $500) and have a really solid points redemption at exactly two cents per point. I’m not loyal to any hotel chain really, so I wouldn’t get any breakfast or “elite” benefits, but a free night is a free night.

BUT — Chase Travel had a ‘Points Boost’ option to book the hotel directly on their platform and not transfer points to Hyatt. Chase Travel was offering this property for circa 25,000 points and that would cover the $500 cash rate, but unlike transferring points to Hyatt, because I was redeeming a ‘The Edit’ property on Chase Travel, I’d receive…

Yep, by NOT transferring my points (and dealing with the fractured transfer journey) I was able to get myself basically $200 in additional value added to my stay with the breakfast and $100 property credit, not factoring in the value of late check out or a category room upgrade. In addition, I’ll be able to earn elite nights and Hyatt Points on the stay.

A mere 25,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards Points got me a “free” $500 hotel night, breakfast for two, and $100 to spend at the hotel. That’s a pretty stunning redemption, giving more than two cents per point of value and still allowing me to earn on the stay, unlike when you transfer your points to a loyalty program. I wish I could’ve stayed longer.

For the first time I can remember, transferring points to Hyatt was not the best option here and that’s something to stand up and take notice of.

If Chase can keep up this Points Boost game, it can really send ripples through rewards. For the first time, people can easily receive tremendous value for their points through a credit card portal while still earning elite status and points with the hotel or airline of their choosing.

You can check out the new 100,000 point + 500 travel credit offer for the Sapphire Reserve. It’s 200,000 points for Sapphire Reserve Business Cards.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

#6317. I Found $1.70 Burritos At Denver Airport. Thank You, Taco Bell.

While I usually just make a beeline for the Capital One Lounge while in Denver International Airport, I recently noticed that Taco Bell is back…now airside instead of landside..and from a cost perspective, probably the best deal for food in DEN.

If you’ve flown from Denver for years, you might remember that there used to be a Taco Bell in the Jeppesen Terminal in the food court above the security checkpoint. At some point that closed while the airport was refurbishing that area and did not re-open.

But was I (very pleasantly) surprised to see a Taco Bell Cantina in Concourse A (near Gates A47 and A49) during a recent trip through DEN. I had no idea!

Even better? The prices were street pricing, not airport pricing. $1.70 for a burrito? What a lovely way to get your junk food fix without breaking the bank.

And street pricing not ubiquitous in the airport. I had a salad with some pulled brisket at Brothers BBQ and it was almost $20….

I also want to note that I tried the more “local” option, called Denver Street Eats, located in The B Gates, which offers street tacos. A steak taco was $6.25. That may seem reasonable at first glance, but it was just a small flour tortilla with very little to it: a bit of steak, a couple spinach leaves, and a few tiny slices of picked onions. It was good, but sorry, Taco Bell is better.

So if you’re looking for an affordable meal at Denver Airport, Taco Bell is your best bet.

And for new readers, yes, I have a strong affinity for Taco Bell…wherever I am in the world. Check out the archive.

#6316. American Airlines Quietly Removes Trump From West Palm Beach Gate Monitors

American Airlines has updated the gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach, and they no longer mention President Trump. This seems like a sensible change (unrelated to politics), and the timing sure is… interesting.

Over the summer, we saw Palm Beach International Airport (PBI) renamed President Donald J. Trump International Airport. We knew that Trump wanted an airport named after him, and some conservative politicians in Florida came together to make it happen.

It’s interesting to see how airlines handled this. At the time, American updated its gate monitors for flights to West Palm Beach. The monitors initially read “West Palm Beach, FL.” American then updated the monitors to say “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach.” Now JonNYC reports that as of this week, the airport name listed on the monitors has been changed again, and is back to the original name, with no mention of Trump.

so… has anyone noticed that AA has changed the gate monitors from “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach” back to “West Palm Beach, FL” ? https://t.co/IG2mPA3zgG

JonNYC specifically emphasizes that he’s not claiming there’s any connection between this and the election results, though the timing of it happening this week sure is interesting.

Personally I’m not a fan of airports being named after even semi-controversial figures, and particularly politicians. It’s something I’ve said over and over, regardless of the party affiliation of the person. Unless a city has multiple airports, I think it’s also stupid to identify the airport based on the name rather than the place.

Like, it makes sense to clarify London Heathrow (LHR) vs. London Gatwick (LGW), but it’s not like there are multiple airports in West Palm Beach. For that matter, saying you’re “flying to President Trump” just sounds a little weird, in my opinion.

JonNYC notes that he’s not suggesting that this had anything to do with the recent election, though everything about the timing here is interesting:

American Airlines CEO Robert Isom: "From a commercial aviation perspective, the eyes of the world have been on us, and we've certainly delivered… No doubt, it's a result of the economy and the job market." https://t.co/28JzoEf4Z3 pic.twitter.com/BcgYJbChNz

American Airlines seems to have quietly reversed course on how it refers to West Palm Beach’s airport on its gate monitors. In recent months, the airline has referred to the airport as “Pres DJT, W Palm Beach,” while now it seems to be back to “West Palm Beach, FL.”

This change comes the same week as the midterm elections, though everyone can decide for themselves to what extent these points are related…

What do you make of this American gate monitor change?

#6315. A Flight Only Bookable With Points Offers Amazing Winter Sun

I often tell people that the best unkept secret with Avios is, in fact, the Avios app. Separate to the British Airways app, the Avios app allows users to set flight alerts and goals, but also gives a heads up about opportunities before they appear anywhere else.

Case in point: before a press release had even hit my inbox, the Avios app alerted me that an ‘Avios only’ flight had just launched. This isn’t the first time Avios has launched a flight only bookable with points, but it is the first time they’ve done one to CAPE TOWN, during peak winter break time.

British Airways and Avios have collaborated on a flight only bookable with Avios, where every seat on the plane is available for sale with points. First, business, premium and economy, all available using Avios. The flights depart as follows…

As noted, these flights are now bookable and if history repeats itself, they won’t be available for long. This plane only has 8 seats in first, so get in quick! One amazing thing about Avios is that they aren’t just the currency of one airline, but a whopping seven. If you have any points with Finnair, Iberia, Qatar, Aer Lingus, Logainair, Vueling or British Airways you can pool points together to book these flights.

Avios is also a transfer partner of Amex, Bilt, Capital One, Chase and plenty of other global financial institutions, so there should be ample opportunity to convert bank points into Avios and get these booked. Hot tip though, ensure there are seats available before you make your transfer, since this will be a hot commodity.

I love any airline rewarding members with flights entirely bookable with points. What makes this one different is that it’s not some off peak, off season destination. It’s Cape Town, easily one of the toughest tickets with any currency, during peak time, perfect for people looking to ditch the weather for the holidays and catch NYE in one of the best cities on earth.

Yes, Cape Town is by far one of my favorites and for any oenophiles, a trip to nearby Stellenbosch or Franschoek is a must. Standard luggage limits apply, so definitely bring enough suitcases to haul back wine. Fin. Head to British Airways website to book.

#6314. Can Dubai Become the World's Fittest City?

At 6 a.m. on Sunday, November 22, Dubai's Sheikh Zayed Road will fall silent. For one morning only, the city's six-lane superhighway—usually a blur of Nissan Patrols, taxis, and delivery scooters—will belong to tens of thousands of competitors as Dubai Run takes over the city’s skyline at dawn, following in the footsteps of a record 307,000 participants last year.

Leading the charge is usually Dubai's Crown Prince Sheikh Hamdan bin Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the driving force behind the Dubai Fitness Challenge (DFC) and one of the city's most ambitious experiments: to turn itself into the fittest city in the world.

"The people of Dubai have created an inspirational fitness movement, sending a powerful message that traveled far beyond our city,” Sheikh Hamdan said during a previous edition of the challenge. “Together, let us transform Dubai into the fittest city in the world.”

An athlete himself, the Crown Prince has long championed cycling, diving, and long-distance running, but the challenge—now in its tenth year—is his most visible legacy. Launched in 2017, it calls on residents and visitors alike to commit to 30 minutes of exercise every day for 30 days each November. Since its inception, more than 16 million people have taken part, transforming what began as a simple invitation to get moving into one of the world’s largest community fitness initiatives.

This year’s landmark edition is running until Sunday, November 29 under the theme What’s Your 30x30?, inviting residents and visitors to find their own way to complete 30 minutes of daily activity. With four flagship events, three free Fitness Villages, and more than 30 Community Fitness Hubs, the program is among the most ambitious yet, transforming everything from beaches and public parks to shopping centers and major roads into places to exercise.

The first Dubai Fitness Challenge took place in 2017

Four major events headline the 2026 calendar: Dubai Ride, which opened the challenge on Sunday, November 1 with thousands of cyclists taking over Sheikh Zayed Road; Dubai Run, the world’s largest free community fun run, on Sunday, November 22; Dubai Stand-Up Paddle, a two-day festival of paddle boarding, kayaking and yoga at Hatta Dam on Saturday, November 7 and Sunday, November 8; and Dubai Yoga, which returns for its second edition on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands together for a mass sunrise session beneath the DIFC Gate Building.

Three Fitness Villages—at Kite Beach, Zabeel Park and Al Warqa’a—act as free, all-day wellness hubs offering everything from boxing and beach volleyball to spin classes and meditation. More than 30 neighborhood Community Hubs have also been set up across the city, bringing fitness closer to home with pop-up runs, rooftop yoga, skateboarding lessons, padel tournaments, and family-friendly bootcamps.

The calendar aligns with a packed line-up of international sporting events, from the Dubai Premier Padel P1 and T100 Triathlon to the DP World Tour Championship and Emirates Dubai 7s. This year also brings the return of the Dubai Sail Grand Prix, with high-speed catamarans racing off the city’s coastline, while HYROX Dubai will see athletes tackle a grueling combination of running and functional fitness challenges. Elsewhere, the program includes obstacle races, mountain trails in Hatta, and community running events across the city.

It’s all part of what His Excellency Saeed Hareb, Secretary General of the Dubai Sports Council, describes as a lasting change in the city’s relationship with exercise. “It has helped establish a culture of active living, bringing communities together and making sport and physical activity an integral part of life in Dubai,” he said as the challenge marked its tenth anniversary.

Ahmed Al Khaja, CEO of Dubai Festivals and Retail Establishment, says the anniversary is an opportunity to reflect on how far the initiative has come. Speaking at the launch of the 2026 program, he credited the collaboration between government bodies, private businesses, and local communities with making exercise increasingly accessible across Dubai. The aim, he said, is to inspire healthier habits that continue long after the 30-day challenge ends.

The numbers suggest it’s working. Last year’s edition attracted a record three million-plus participants, up from 2.73 million in 2024. More than 307,000 people took part in Dubai Run alone, while Dubai Ride welcomed 40,327 cyclists. Since the challenge launched in 2017, cumulative participation has exceeded 16 million, a remarkable figure for an initiative that began with a simple invitation to exercise for half an hour a day.

The Dubai Ride closes the city's busiest highway for one morning each year

Ethan Matthews, Chief Operating Officer at Reset Fitness and a former professional rugby player and coach in Portugal and Italy, says that Dubai’s greatest fitness asset is its variety. “There are world-class facilities on every block now—not just gyms, but parks, cycling tracks, and sports complexes,” he says. “Try as many things as possible—team sports, group sessions, individual training. It’s about finding what challenges you physically but also what you actually enjoy. That’s how you stay consistent, especially on the tough days.”

For Matthews, the social aspect is just as vital. “The moment you find something you like—padel, CrossFit, running, whatever—you meet people. It opens doors, both personally and professionally. That’s what keeps Dubai’s fitness culture alive.”

Anthony Lee, a personal trainer and owner of Activ8 Lifestyle & Fitness who has spent nearly two decades as part of Dubai’s fitness scene, thinks the timing of the challenge is part of its success. “It’s clever,” he says. “It's just before Christmas, when everyone wants to feel a bit fitter before heading home for the holidays, and when the weather’s perfect for being outdoors.”

He describes the month-long initiative as “a push that gets people back into routine,” and a rare opportunity to sample new workouts without cost or commitment. “You can try boxing on Kite Beach one day, yoga in Zabeel Park the next. It breaks the monotony.” What stands out most, he adds, is accessibility. “You don’t have to be an athlete. It’s about being a better version of yourself—you versus you.”

For visitors, the challenge offers a very different way to experience Dubai as, during November, the city’s hotels, cafes and shopping centers adopt a surprisingly sporty rhythm. At Kite Beach, sunrise yoga sessions fill up fast, while the public running track buzzes with tourists and locals alike, and Zabeel Park hosts evening workouts beneath the skyline. There's no need to sign up—just show up on the day.

Outside of November, the spirit of the challenge remains. Dubai has built more than 557 kilometers of cycle tracks, with a goal of 1,000 kilometers by 2030, and the urban planning department is adding shaded walking routes to make exercise feasible for longer stretches of the year.

Lee, the personal trainer, believes Dubai’s fitness drive has found fertile ground because of the city’s demographic and design. “It’s a young place,” he says. “Most people are working-age expats, and with the beach and pool culture here, people want to look and feel good.”

But vanity isn’t the whole story. “Every new residential tower has a gym and a pool, so exercise is built into daily life,” he says. “When I moved here 18 years ago, you had a handful of hotel gyms and a couple of Fitness First branches. Now every neighborhood has options, from boutique studios to outdoor circuits.” He has also noticed a social shift: “Fitness has become a way to meet people. For newcomers, joining a class or trying padel is how you find your tribe.”

This year’s Dubai Fitness Challenge runs under the theme What’s Your 30x30?

The fitness calendar's cleverest invention, however, might be the Mallathon. With summer temperatures soaring past 45°C, nine of the city’s biggest malls were converted into indoor running routes between June and September, attracting 100,000 participants.

Dr Amir Firouzjaei, a general practitioner and traditional Chinese medicine expert who has lived in Dubai for three years, believes the movement taps into something deeper. “When a city moves, its energy moves,” he says. “It’s not only about training the body but refreshing the mind and spirit.”

He explains that the city’s blend of high-intensity exercise and restorative practices “keeps the balance between energy and recovery,” preventing burnout and encouraging people to “stick with it.”

The trend is filtering into Dubai's hospitality scene, too. New-generation hotels such as SIRO One Za’abeel pitch themselves as “fitness and recovery” spaces, complete with in-room stretching areas, altitude chambers and performance coaches. In Al Quoz, the Matcha Club—a blend of padel courts, co-working space, and cafe—has become the new social hang-out for the health-minded. Even Dubai’s famously indulgent brunches are getting lighter, with restaurants like Eat Well dishing up bowls, turmeric shots, and cold-brew coffee instead of the traditional Champagne towers.

Matthews, who moved to Dubai in 2017—the same year the first Dubai Fitness Challenge launched—says he’s watched the city’s attitudes shift dramatically. “Post-Covid, the appetite for fitness just exploded,” he says. “Gyms, studios and open-air facilities have multiplied, but more importantly, people’s reasons for exercising have changed. They’re doing it to feel good, not just to look good.”

He believes that’s partly because of education and access. “The government has played a big role through campaigns like 30x30, but accessibility is the real game changer. Whether it’s walking paths, beach gyms or purpose-built cycling tracks, there’s always somewhere to move.” For Matthews, that accessibility underpins a healthy, sustainable economy. “When people feel better, they perform better—at work, at home, everywhere. Fitness has become part of Dubai.”

Residents and visitors alike are invited to discover new ways to move, connect and build healthy habits that last beyond the challenge's 30 days

Firouzjaei, the doctor, sees Dubai’s fitness boom as part of a wider cultural shift. “It’s a fast city, and that creates pressure,” he says. “People here work hard and compete hard, so they need ways to recharge and reset.”

He points out that the city’s international mix has made wellness more mainstream. “Residents come from everywhere—Asia, Europe, the Middle East—and many already know yoga, acupuncture, or functional medicine,” he says. “They’re open to new ideas and they understand that health is an investment rather than a luxury.” In his clinic, he’s noticed that even patients who once focused purely on appearance now talk about sleep, stress, and balance.

Behind the lifestyle messaging lies the emirate's urban agenda. Dubai wants to be a ‘20-minute city,’ where every resident can reach work, shops, and recreation within a short cycle or walk. The health argument is compelling. Obesity and diabetes are major public health concerns across the Gulf, and studies show only one in five UAE children meets recommended daily activity levels. City officials believe that building infrastructure—parks, cycle paths, open gyms—is the surest way to shift behavior.

Already, habits are changing. Park footfall has risen 20% year-on-year, while corporate wellness participation has grown by 30%. The once-novel sight of commuters jogging to metro stations has become almost ordinary.

According to experts, Dubai's mix of international residents has made wellness more mainstream

For tourists, taking part couldn’t be easier. The Dubai Fitness Challenge app lists daily events, classes, and pop-ups across the city, most of them free.

Looking back on 18 years in Dubai, Lee says the transformation has been “massive.” When he first arrived, “there were far fewer gyms, and fitness wasn’t part of daily conversation.” Now, he says, it’s as visible as the skyline itself. “Sure, some people join the big events just for the photos—you’ll always have that—but for others it’s the start of something lasting,” he says. “Even if they only do the challenge for a month, it plants a seed. And that’s what counts.”

Matthews agrees, though he cautions against seeing Dubai’s fitness scene as something reserved for the elite. “The biggest misconception is that you have to be in peak shape to take part,” he says. “You don’t. Fitness here is for everyone, from people training for Ironman to those who just want to walk their dogs or join a weekend bootcamp.”

Dubai has always been a city in motion, but now it wants its progress measured not by the height of its towers or the size of its megaprojects, but by footsteps, pedal strokes and heartbeats. It's a city that’s, quite literally, on the move—and inviting the world to keep up.

Dubai’s biggest community running event transforms Sheikh Zayed Road into a traffic-free running track, with participants choosing between a 5km route through Downtown Dubai or a longer 10km course finishing beneath the DIFC Gate Building. More than 307,000 runners took part last year.

Where: Sheikh Zayed Road, starting near the Museum of the FutureWhen: Sunday, November 22, 6.30 a.m.How to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Marking the finale of Dubai Fitness Challenge, thousands of yoga enthusiasts will gather beneath the iconic DIFC Gate Building for a mass sunrise session. The program includes guided breathwork, a sound bath and a 30-minute yoga session, with dedicated areas for families and women.

Where: DIFC Gate BuildingWhen: Sunday, November 29, sunriseHow to take part: Register free at at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Dubai’s largest beachfront Fitness Village returns with everything from spinning and yoga to padel, beach volleyball, basketball and cricket. There are dedicated activity zones, bookable courts and daily fitness classes, with the Arabian Gulf providing a rather spectacular backdrop.

Where: Kite Beach, JumeirahWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 3 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends 7 a.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Zabeel Park’s Fitness Village returns with boxing, spinning, basketball, padel, and daily group workouts, alongside dedicated children’s activities. The village also serves as the official bib collection point for Dubai Run.

Where: Zabeel Park, Gate 2When: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; weekdays 4 p.m.–11 p.m., weekends noon–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

Set among palm trees and parkland, this neighborhood-style Fitness Village combines outdoor exercise with family-friendly activities. There’s a 2.8km running and cycling track, bike rentals, daily fitness classes, dedicated ladies-only areas and courts for padel, volleyball, football, and basketball.

Where: Al Warqa’a ParkWhen: Saturday, October 31 to Sunday, November 29; daily 4 p.m.–11 p.m.How to take part: Register free on-site, with selected activities available to book at dubaifitnesschallenge.com.

#6313. American Airlines Vs. United First Class: Boring Chicken Dinners That I’d Happily Order Again

I realize if you just read my blog it looks like I’ll eat anything thrown in front of me and to some extent that is true on airplane, but a pair of flights, one on American Airlines, the other on United Airlines, featured chicken dinners much closer to my what I usually eat at home. Let’s compare them in this week’s Meal of the Week.

Let’s start with American Airlines. I was flying from Los Angeles to Chicago and received a same-day upgrade (as a mere Advantage Gold!) and thus was not able to pre-ordered. Onboard the choices were chicken or pasta (described as a chicken breast with rice or pasta shells with tomato sauce). I chose chicken.

The chicken breast was covered in a white sauce and served with white rice on the side and green beans on top. On the side, a small green salad with sun-dried tomatoes and a ramekin with what appeared to be parsnips, carrots, and cabbage with croutons…at least I think so (whatever it was, it was nice).

While not an exciting dinner, I really appreciated just eating a lean chicken breast and green beans…it’s very similar to what we eat at least a couple nights per week at home.

Dessert was raspberry sorbet…I miss the Häagen-Dazs ice cream that used to be on these flights (and the real ice cream sundaes before that).

On to United. Same route. The current “signature entree” out of Los Angeles is described as:

Pollo asado chicken thigh Pollo asado chicken thigh with charred corn farro, street corn style zucchini and asado sauce

The AA dish was fine, but this folks was excellent. The flavor of the chicken was excellent and the corn farro and zucchini were really nice…we grow zucchini in our garden at home and cook it in the oven with our chicken so this really felt close to home. The corn was a nice treat and I ate every bit of it.

The sale on the side had sun-dried tomatoes and sliced cucumbers and the meal also came with a cornmeal roll and a slice of “hot chocolate” cheesecake, which I passed on.

Both were rather boring meals, but both were very delicious. Simple is often better.

My Meal of the Week feature examines an airline meal from my travels over the years. This may be a meal from earlier in the week or it may be a meal served over a decade ago.

Matthew is an avid traveler who calls Los Angeles home. Each year he travels more than 200,000 miles by air and has visited more than 135 countries. Working both in the aviation industry and as a travel consultant, Matthew has been featured in major media outlets around the world and uses his Live and Let's Fly blog to share the latest news in the airline industry, commentary on frequent flyer programs, and detailed reports of his worldwide travel.

Cool comparison. The entrée and dessert look better on UA; the sides better on AA. Probably within a few shekels of each other cost-wise.

Matthew, you had me at “if you just read my blog”…

Sun dried tomatoes needed to die with the 80s.

You’re easy to please. I’ve found that 9/10 dishes served in domestic First Class across UA, AA, and DL range from meh to throw it in the trash.

I expect it to be bad and am surprised when it is at least mediocre.

Exactly how I feel about your hot-takes, ironically.

I love the meal reviews. One of my favorite things about LALF.

#6312. KLM Plans 15% Workforce Reduction And Simpler Fleet: “Future Not Guaranteed”

It’s obviously a tough time for aviation in general, given the impact of high jet fuel prices. For that matter, Dutch national carrier KLM has faced its own unique challenges, given increasing limits placed on the carrier’s Amsterdam Schiphol (AMS) hub, plus all the competitive challenges (increased competition from regional low cost carriers, Gulf carriers, etc.).

In recent years, we’ve seen KLM introduce initiatives intended to improve economics. The airline is now taking that to the next level, and has just announced an absolutely massive project intended to improve economics by €1 billion per year.

KLM has unveiled the details of a project that it expects will contribute to annual earnings improvements of €1 billion per year, which it hopes will allow the company to invest in fleet, customer experience, and people.

KLM’s plan is to focus on its core strengths, which it describes as a global network of 160 destinations served nonstop from Schiphol, and reliable operations supported by a modern fleet. The company wants to become a smaller, simpler, and more agile organization, through restructuring, outsourcing, and closer collaboration with Air France-KLM.

Here’s how KLM CEO Marjan Rintel describes this initiative:

“Every day, we all work with incredible dedication, commitment, and pride. But KLM’s future is not guaranteed. The environment we operate in is becoming increasingly complex, with global instability, high fuel prices, and growing pressure on the aviation industry. That’s why, at this pivotal moment for KLM, we’re taking far-reaching, sometimes painful measures. Every department and every division will be asked to contribute.”

“We’re doing this with a clear vision for the future: one where KLM remains a great airline that connects customers to the world, a company people want to work for, and one the Netherlands can be proud of.”

How does KLM plan on improving economics by so much over the coming years? For one, the airline will simplify its fleet.

The long term plan is to have a fleet of 185 Airbus, Boeing, and Embraer aircraft. The latest changes particularly center around the European network, where just about all network carriers in Europe struggle to make money, given the costs and competitive landscape.

KLM plans to change the balance between larger and smaller aircraft on European routes. In the long run, the airline will fly a mix of 227-seat Airbus A321neos and 132-seat Embraer E195-E2s. The company no longer plans to acquire Airbus A320neos, which were part of a larger Air France-KLM order, as those planes are instead going to Transavia. Furthermore, in the coming years, we’ll see Boeing 737s and Embraer E190s retired.

Next, the airline hopes to achieve greater flexibility, higher productive, and lower costs, with its labor agreements. As you’d expect, this will be the most painful change. For one, KLM plans to reduce its workforce by around 15%, meaning that around 5,000 positions will be “reorganized.”

This follows the company’s number of staff already declining in recent years. The good news is that there aren’t expected to be mass layoffs — KLM expects to limit the impact on employees through natural attrition, voluntary arrangements, and transfers to other positions.

The airline also emphasizes that employment terms and conditions need to become simpler and more competitive, noting that “continuing on the current path is not sustainable.” KLM wants to work with unions to establish new collective labor agreements, and the company aims to achieve a structural productivity increase of at least 8% by 2028.

This decrease in headcount will come through a combination of Air France and KLM cooperating more closely, outsourcing catering and maintenance, and reducing planned growth of the fleet.

The airline industry is tough in the first place, and among the major network carriers, KLM is perhaps in the toughest spot, when you consider the overall industry dynamics:

KLM is planning to majorly cut costs and simplify things, which is probably necessary in light of how the situation has evolved.

As part of this, the carrier’s short haul fleet will eventually consist of just Airbus A321neos and Embraer E195-E2s. On top of that, we’ll see the airline reduce its workforce by around 15%, through a combination of increasing efficiency, outsourcing jobs, and more. The company will also be looking for some concessions from existing employees.

In total, the company hopes that these changes will contribute €1 billion per year. While aviation is tough across the board, it’s especially tough to be KLM, where you’re reliant on one hub (which regulators keep trying to shrink) with very high costs, and that hub isn’t a market that’s as lucrative as somewhere like London, Paris, etc. I’m a fan of KLM, and I hope these changes don’t do too much to change the quirky spirit of the airline.

What do you make of these major KLM changes?

I get asked some version of the same question all the time: what’s the best travel credit card to actually keep in your wallet?

For me, the answer has changed over time. As my travel habits have evolved, so has the mix of cards I rely on. Some help me earn points quickly, others offset travel costs with built-in credits, and a few simply make traveling more comfortable.

While getting outsize value from a travel credit card often means paying an annual fee, I've found that the right perks can more than justify the cost. And one of the cards I'm looking to add to my wallet next doesn't charge an annual fee at all.

These are the travel credit cards I keep coming back to — and in some cases, the ones I'm planning to add next — based on their earning potential, flexibility and benefits I actually find useful.

I chose these cards based on the value they can provide travelers. In particular, I considered:

I've also included cards for different types of travelers, from beginners and those seeking premium perks to airline and hotel loyalists and travelers who don't want to pay an annual fee.

Purchases that qualify for the $300 annual travel credit will not earn points.

*The top brands are Airbnb, Vrbo, Plum Guide, HomeAway, Homestay.com and Vacasa

*Welcome offer value is an estimated value based on TPG's November 2026 valuations and is not provided by the issuer.

The newest premium travel card in my wallet is the , and after just a few months, it's already become one of my favorites.

While the $795 annual fee is steep, I've been getting plenty of use out of the card's travel perks. One of my favorite benefits so far has been the up to $500 in annual credits for The Edit, Chase’s curated hotel booking platform (issued as two credits of up to $250 per calendar year for stays of two nights or more).

I recently used one of those credits for a luxury stay at At Six in Stockholm, where I also enjoyed some of the other perks when you book with The Edit, such as complimentary breakfast for two and a $100 property credit. The hotel's impressive breakfast spread was a particular highlight, and I was able to use the property credit to cover a couple of dine-in meals.

Lounge access has also been a major benefit. I frequently fly through Dulles International Airport (IAD) when visiting family on the East Coast, and the Etihad Lounge, which is part of the Chase Sapphire Lounge network, has become one of my go-to spots to relax before a flight.

I've also booked other hotel stays through Chase Travel, where the card earns 8 points per dollar spent on eligible purchases. Between the hotel benefits, lounge access and $300 annual travel credit, I've found plenty of ways to put the Reserve to work in a short period of time.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Related: Chase Sapphire Reserve: Earn 100,000 valuable points

The was the first travel card in my wallet — and that goes for a lot of us here at TPG. It’s also the card I recommend most often to beginners or casual travelers who want flexible points without a sky-high annual fee.

With beginner-friendly perks like a $100 annual hotel credit and strong travel protections, it delivers real value without overwhelming complexity.

The card also makes it easy to get quick, upfront value. After earning the welcome offer and maximizing bonus categories — like 3 points per dollar spent on dining and 2 points per dollar spent on travel purchased outside the Chase Travel portal — I was able to build a sizable stash of points within a few months.

I ultimately redeemed those points for a trip through four European countries, which felt like a pretty great return for my first year with the card.

I'm also particularly excited about the card's newer earning category for vacation rentals. As someone who's stayed in more than 60 Airbnbs, I love that I can now earn 3 points per dollar spent on eligible vacation home rentals, including Airbnb bookings.

It’s the travel card I recommend over and over again to friends and family because of its ease of use, strong earning potential and outsize value relative to its modest $95 annual fee.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Sapphire Preferred.

Related: 6 ways to maximize the Chase Sapphire Preferred as a beginner

Best for: Straightforward premium rewards

Another top contender in the premium space — and one that’s firmly earned a place in my wallet — is the Capital One Venture X Rewards Card. For me, its biggest selling point is how easy it is to get value from the card without having to overthink my spending.

Part of the reason I added the card was to diversify my points and miles beyond Chase Ultimate Rewards. Up until recently, I’d been almost exclusively earning Chase points, but as I’ve gotten deeper into the points and miles world, I’ve realized how valuable it is to have access to multiple transferable currencies and transfer partners.

At the same time, the Venture X fits naturally into my everyday spending habits. Cardholders earn a flat 2 miles per dollar on nearly every purchase, which removes the need to track bonus categories or optimize every swipe. It’s become my go-to catch-all card and the one I reach for whenever a purchase doesn’t neatly fit into a bonus category on another card.

I've also gotten great use out of its travel benefits. I recently used the card's $300 annual Capital One Travel credit toward a three-night stay at the DoubleTree by Hilton London Marble Arch, bringing the cost down from $1,096 to $796. I also appreciate being able to relax in Capital One Lounges and participating Priority Pass lounges when I travel.

For me, the Venture X works because it combines straightforward everyday earning with travel benefits I actually use, making its $395 annual fee easier to justify.

To learn more, read our full review of the Capital One Venture X.

Related: 5 reasons why I’m applying for the Capital One Venture X

For travelers who regularly fly a single airline — especially those based near one of that carrier’s hubs — a cobranded airline card can make a lot of sense.

That’s been true for me with United, but I think the same general strategy applies to frequent Delta and American Airlines flyers as well. If you consistently fly one carrier, the right airline card can make your travel experience cheaper, smoother and more comfortable through perks like travel credits, free checked bags and priority boarding.

Despite its $350 annual fee, the offers several easy-to-use benefits that help offset the cost. The $200 annual United travel credit, for instance, has helped offset flights home to visit family. And the two free checked bags for me and a travel companion have already saved me a significant amount in baggage fees.

The card also offers award flight discounts, anniversary bonus miles, priority boarding and improved award availability, which make the card feel like a keeper for the long term.

That said, I do wish it included lounge access — especially at this price point.

Still, the Quest has made flying United more affordable and convenient for me, which is exactly what I want from an airline credit card.

To learn more, read our full review of the United Quest.

Related: I just changed my airline loyalty — here's how the United Quest Card sealed the switch

Not every worthwhile travel rewards card needs to charge an annual fee. The is one I'm interested in adding to my wallet because it could fill an important gap in my Chase strategy without adding another annual fee.

On its own, the Freedom Unlimited earns cash-back rewards. But when you pair it with an eligible Ultimate Rewards-earning card like the Sapphire Preferred or Sapphire Reserve, you can combine your rewards and potentially get more value by redeeming them for travel or transferring them to Chase's airline and hotel partners.

That's particularly appealing to me because I'm working toward building the Chase Trifecta, a strategy that combines multiple Chase cards to maximize earnings across different types of purchases.

With no annual fee, the Freedom Unlimited could give me another way to earn rewards on everyday spending while letting my Sapphire cards handle travel purchases and unlock more valuable redemption options.

To learn more, read our full review of the Chase Freedom Unlimited.

Related: The best beginner Chase card combo for travel rewards

Best for: Hilton perks without the premium price tag

The is the newest addition to my wallet — and my first hotel credit card.

For years, I've prioritized flexible rewards over hotel-specific points because I didn't want to commit to a single hotel program. But as I've started traveling more and spending more nights in hotels, I realized I was leaving some valuable perks on the table.

After comparing several hotel cards, I ultimately chose the Hilton Surpass because it struck the right balance between cost and benefits. One of the biggest draws for me is automatic Hilton Honors Gold status, which gives me meaningful hotel perks without requiring me to earn status through stays.

I'm also a fan of the card's up to $200 in Hilton statement credits each calendar year, issued as up to $50 each quarter. And Hilton's large footprint means I'm much more likely to find a property where I can actually put those benefits to use when I travel.

For me, the Surpass is a relatively approachable way to test-drive hotel loyalty while getting useful benefits from the start. As I spend more nights with Hilton, I'll be able to see whether a hotel card deserves a permanent place in my travel strategy.

To learn more, read our full review of the Hilton Surpass.

Related: How I chose my first hotel credit card — and the 4 cards I considered

Choosing the right travel credit card ultimately comes down to how you travel, where you spend your money and which perks you'll actually use.

For beginners, the Chase Sapphire Preferred remains one of the strongest entry points thanks to its balance of value, flexibility and simplicity. Frequent travelers looking for a more premium experience — especially when it comes to lounge access and travel perks — may get more value from the Chase Sapphire Reserve.

Meanwhile, the Capital One Venture X is a great fit for travelers who want premium benefits without overcomplicating their rewards strategy, and the United Quest offers a strong value proposition for frequent United flyers who prioritize convenience and United-specific perks.

For travelers who don't want to add another annual fee, the Chase Freedom Unlimited can be a useful complement to a Sapphire card, particularly if you're building a Chase trifecta. And for travelers who want hotel-specific perks, the Hilton Surpass offers a relatively accessible entry point to hotel loyalty with automatic Hilton Gold status and useful Hilton credits.

You certainly don't need all six cards on this list to get good value from travel rewards. But whether you're looking for your first travel card or considering adding another to your wallet, I'd start by thinking about which benefits you'd use most often — and whether they're worth the annual fee.

#6310. 11 Gorgeous US Ski Vacation Homes Built for Fresh Powder and Easy Slope Access

I’ve been skiing my entire life, venturing out for nostalgic winter weekends on the East Coast and fresh powder-chasing adventures out West. Yet somehow, the anticipation of a new ski season never gets old. Like clockwork, every winter brings a new mountain to explore, a favorite run to revisit, and plenty of reasons to start dreaming about the next snowfall. With El Niño in the conversation and ski resorts across the US gearing up for opening day, there’s no better time to get your winter plans in order.

After all, a memorable ski vacation isn’t just about finding the right mountain (though I take my terrain very seriously). It’s also about the cozy ski towns, the lively après-ski scenes, the snow-covered scenery, and of course, the splendid place to retreat to when it’s time for boots to come off. When it comes to the best ski vacation homes, there are some amenities that really do take these trips to the next level: a hot tub to soothe your muscles, an in-unit washer and dryer to freshen up base layers, a nice fireplace or firepit to cozy up around, and a kitchen for easy meals at home—especially ideal after working up a big appetite on the mountain.

Some of the best ski vacation rentals in the US are every bit as enticing as the mountains themselves. Think glass-walled chalets, design-forward A-frames, and tucked-away cabins with easy access to the lifts. From New England favorites to Western powder havens, these 11 standout stays are worth building your next ski or snowboard getaway around.

Number of guests: 12Bed and bath: 5 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Hot tub, cedar barrel sauna, pool and ping-pong tables, arcade games, boot warmers

If you’re an avid East Coast skier, you’re likely no stranger to Killington’s buzzy ski resort, home to over 200 ski trails of terrain for any level shredder. This five-bedroom cabin makes a great launchpad for those staying in the area. The amenity-filled gem sits only four minutes away from Killington Resort, and comes with a game room, cedar barrel sauna, and mountain views for days. Use the boot warmers in the closet before hitting the mountain, then leave all your gear in the ski shed for storage once you’ve returned. In the evenings, fire up some food on the patio grill then cozy up around the wood-burning fireplace.

Where to ski: Killington Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: Killington Skyeship Base Lodge, The Lookout Tavern, Killington Village, Gifford Woods State Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: Floor-to-ceiling windows, mountain views, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

I’m adding this Vermont gem to my ski bucket list for a dozen different reasons, starting with the fact that the mountain access is second to none: This spruced-up, slopeside penthouse apartment sits steps from the ski lifts, less than just a five-minute walk to Stowe Mountain Resort’s six-passenger Over Easy Gondola. It’s also a 15-minute drive to one of my favorite mountains, Smugglers’ Notch, where the vibes are always high and the terrain is suitable for all kinds of skiers.

Back at “home,” this modern mountain aesthetic will refresh you after a long day on the slopes. A picture-perfect gas fireplace hangs in front of floor-to-ceiling windows that provide mountain views for days. Tasteful pops of color complete the dining space, comfy blankets line the couch, and the small-but-mighty kitchen has all the appliances you might need for cooking dinner.

Where to ski: Stowe Mountain Resort or Smugglers’ NotchThings to do nearby: Stowe Village, Matterhorn, Cliff House Restaurant, Gondola Skyride (to Mount Mansfield’s peak), The Club at Spruce Peak

Number of guests: 6Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Firepit, wraparound deck, dining area with grill, mountain views, wood-burning fireplace

Perched 60 feet above New York’s buzzy Hunter Mountain, with a ski (or hiking) trail just across the street, this rental is ideal for a fun-filled New York ski trip not far from the city. In true log cabin fashion, guests can admire the vaulted ceiling made of cedarwood beams, indoor fireplace, and mountain-facing sliding doors which open to a wraparound deck with a firepit. There are odes to nature everywhere, from framed landscape paintings to horns and antlers as wall decor.

The home’s slopeside location is the real draw: As one previous guest wrote in an Airbnb review, “you’ll feel like you’ll have your own backdoor to Hunter Mountain.” While it’s not a true ski-in/ski-out property, the home sits a quick drive or walk away from the Hunter North area, where you can gear up and take off.

Where to ski: Hunter Mountain Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Tannersville, Hunter Mountain Brewery, Ze Burger Wine Bar, Fellow Mountain Cafe

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedroom, 3.5 bathsWhy we love it: California king bed, laundry facilities, wood-burning fireplace, patio with private hot tub

This extra-luxurious abode has the look and feel of an upscale hotel—à la The Cloudveil—but it’s actually a private townhouse at the base of Jackson Hole Mountain Resort with three bedrooms that sleep up to seven. While the prime location may be one of the biggest selling points, the decor and design make it even more enticing: The living room, for example, has classic Jackson Hole touches (note the antler chandelier and cozy fireplace), balanced out by light linens and airy textures. You might be hard-pressed to leave this homey adobe, but if and when you do decide to venture out, you can enjoy the two hot tubs and pool at the nearby Sundance Tennis and Swim Club.

Where to ski: Jackson Hole Mountain ResortThings to do nearby: JH Sports (for gear rentals), Teton Village, Moose Creek Quad Chair, Mangy Moose Jackson Hole

Number of guests: 4Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 1 bathWhy we love it: Hot tub, wood-burning sauna, gas grill, indoor fireplace, kid-friendly amenities, fully equipped kitchen, in-unit washer and dryer

Where to ski: Breckenridge Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Hoosier Pass, Peaceful Valley Lodge, Downtown Breckenridge, Boreas Mountain, Quandary Peak, BreckConnect Gondola

Number of guests: 8Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Fully equipped kitchen, mountain views, hot tub, firepit, central location

This corner of the Rockies, roughly 45 miles south of Bozeman, Montana, is a choose-your-own-adventure kind of city. And Big Sky Resort sits at the top of many Montana itineraries for good reason—especially come wintertime. Ski days here mean inviting terrain of wide-open slopes, steep chutes, and picture-perfect runs beneath the hulking silhouette of Lone Peak. Just 10 minutes from the resort itself, this gorgeous mountain home sits on a sprawling 23 acres of land in the Lower Beehive Basin neighborhood—a backcountry ski destination in and of itself.

Inside the home, you’ll find modern cowboy country design and swanky amenities in the places that matter. For one, each of the two bedrooms feature king beds with mattress warmers to keep you cozy during winter nights. Take advantage of the big patio space for stargazing, relaxing in the hot tub, and cooking up some s’mores before heading inside for a movie night. The house can technically host up to eight guests, but it’s more ideal for families or smaller groups. Aside from the two bedrooms, the living room offers one sofa bed and two bunk beds.

Where to ski: Big Sky ResortThings to do nearby: Lone Mountain Ranch, Gallatin Peak, Big Sky Mountain Village, Fan Mountain, Beehive Peak, Madison Base (at Big Sky Resort)

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4.5 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski out access, hot tub, indoor fireplace, fully equipped kitchen

When it comes to access to Utah’s renowned slopes and cool ski towns, you can’t get much better than this four-bedroom luxury penthouse. At the base of Park City Mountain, this condo boasts ski-in/ski-out access directly from the mountain's Silver Star lift. Spacious living areas, a chef’s kitchen, a hot tub, and a balcony overlooking the golf course and icy lakes create a refined on-mountain experience. The penthouse’s proximity to both ski runs and downtown makes for a seamless mix—not to mention you’ll be just a 10-minute drive to Deer Valley Resort, accessible from the condo via a free ski shuttle. With bunk beds for families and plenty of lounge areas for après-ski downtime, this Park City gem accommodates groups seeking easy access to slopes in style.

Where to ski: Park City Mountain; Deer Valley ResortThings to do nearby: Kimball Art Center, Old Town Main Street, Creekside Park, Iron Mountain Trailhead, Thaynes Canyon

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, firepit, fully equipped kitchen, game area, in-unit washer and dryer

New Mexico ski trips mean a real change of scenery, and this year there’s an extra reason to have this underrated mountain range on your radar. The state is one of the southern mountain regions set to see a spike in snowfall this winter thanks to El Niño. Lucky for those who book this cabin, you’ll be just 23 miles from Taos Ski Valley, and practically at the front door of Angel Fire Resort, a hidden gem famous for wide, smooth, groomed cruiser runs and gentler slopes. (It’s a great one for beginners, featuring the renowned Heading Home 3.2-mile green run that traverses all the way from the summit to the base.)

This home is only around 100 yards away from that exact ski run, with slope access right out the door. Inside, there’s a ton of space to sprawl out and indulge in simple creature comforts: soaking in the hot tub, roasting marshmallows around the firepit on the expansive deck, and playing board games (or one of the vintage arcade games inside the den).

Where to ski: Angel Fire Resort; Taos Ski ValleyThings to do nearby: Oeste Vista Trail, Summit Haus, Cabin at Southwest Flyer Lift, Liberation Park

Number of guests: 10Bed and bath: 4 bedrooms, 4 bathsWhy we love it: Wraparound deck, sauna, firepit, unique design, opt-in grocery delivery, Koyo massage chair

Mammoth is another mountain with an El Niño forecast worth keeping an eye on. Rising to 11,053 feet, the Eastern Sierra resort boasts California’s highest ski-resort summit and 3,500 acres of terrain, with plenty of room for everyone from first-timers finding their ski legs to seasoned riders chasing steeper lines. This unique mountain home near the base of the mountain takes its design cues from Japanese ryokans the host has frequented, with a soaring ceiling, dramatic dome-shaped window framing the surrounding peaks, and a loft-like den. The amenities are equally enticing: a hot tub, sauna, massage chair, optional tatami-and-futon sleeping quarters, yukatas, and an enormous shower room. Locationwise, it’s hard to beat: Canyon Lodge is less than half a mile away and walkable, while the Village and Eagle Lodge are both under a mile from the house. On especially snowy days, you may even be able to ski right down the hill and back home.

Where to ski: Mammoth Mountain Ski AreaThings to do nearby: Twin Lakes Vista, Mammoth Creek Park, Sherwin Lakes Trailhead, Mammoth Brewing Company, Canyon Lodge, Whitmore Hot Springs

Number of guests: 7Bed and bath: 3 bedrooms, 2.5 bathsWhy we love it: Slopeside and central location, heated pool, hot tub, private balcony

Where to ski: Aspen Mountain Ski Resort; Aspen Snowmass Ski Resort; Aspen Highlands Ski ResortThings to do nearby: Aspen Art Museum, Main Street, John Denver Sanctuary, White House Tavern

Number of guests: 5Bed and bath: 2 bedrooms, 2 bathsWhy we love it: Ski-in/ski-out access, hot tub, gas fireplace, mountain views, outdoor seating on the patio

There’s something pretty splendid about staying at 8,300 feet, especially when the mountains are quite literally at your doorstep. This standalone cabin in Big Sky’s iconically named Cowboy Heaven neighborhood is a haven for folks who wish to spend their days outside, whether that means skiing straight from the deck in the winter or taking advantage of the area’s wildlife spotting in general.

It’s especially ideal for couples, small families, or friend groups, with one caveat for your crew: The second bedroom has a queen-over-twin bunk, so five adults looking for equal amounts of space may want to book elsewhere. A big plus? Big Sky’s tiny but endearing town center is less than a 10-minute drive away.

Where to ski: Big Sky Ski ResortThings to do nearby Lone Mountain Ranch, Moonlight Lodge, Big Sky Town Center, Gondola Mid Station, Montana Jack, Beehive Basin Trailhead

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Epic Pass?

The Epic Pass offers skiing and snowboarding at a sprawling collection of USresorts. Major destinations include Vail, Beaver Creek, Breckenridge, Keystone, Crested Butte, Park City, Heavenly, Northstar, Kirkwood, Stevens Pass, and Stowe. There are also regional and partner resorts with more limited access, so check the specific pass tier before booking a trip. Do note that blackout dates and access limits vary by pass, so read the fine print!

Which ski resorts in the US are on the Ikon Pass?

The Ikon Pass has a tempting lineup as well, especially if your winter plans involve chasing snow across the Rockies and Sierras. Its US destinations include Mammoth Mountain, Palisades Tahoe, Steamboat, Winter Park, Aspen Snowmass, Copper Mountain, Big Sky, Jackson Hole, Taos Ski Valley, Deer Valley, Alta, Snowbird, and Sun Valley. Out east, you can head to Killington, Sugarbush, Stratton, Loon Mountain, Sugarloaf, or Sunday River.

Where is El Niño predicted to bring snowfall this season?

For the 2026-27 season, a strong El Niño is shaping the forecast, with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) expecting wetter-than-average conditions across the southern US, from California and the Southwest through the Southeast, as well as along the East Coast. This could mean more opportunities for snowfall in higher-elevation ski destinations, particularly when temperatures cooperate.

However, wetter doesn't automatically mean snowier: NOAA also expects warmer-than-average conditions across much of the West and northern US Seasonal outlooks predict precipitation patterns, not specific snowfall totals, so keep an eye on shorter-range forecasts before planning a powder chase.

Read more about how El Niño is impacting ski resorts here.
