#6309. Emirates Profits Plunge Due To War… But The Airline Still Made Money?!

It goes without saying that it has been a tough year for airlines, due to the United States getting into a war with Iran. All airlines have been dealing with higher jet fuel prices, but airlines in the Gulf region have of course been dealing with additional issues, as all kinds of airports in the region have been attacked, making some people reconsider traveling through the region.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note that Emirates has just released its financial results for the first half of the fiscal year (April 1 through September 30, 2026). Yes, Emirates’ profits decreased massively, but surprisingly, the airline still turned a healthy profit, and the numbers look much better than I would’ve guessed.

Prior to this year, Emirates was the world’s most profitable airline for two years in a row, as the carrier really is incredibly well run.

That’s why I think it’s interesting to note how the airline performed over the first six months of the current fiscal year, which coincides entirely with the current Iran conflict. While there are results for the overall Emirates Group (which also includes dnata, etc.), I’m focusing on the airline specifically, since I find that to be most telling.

Emirates reported a half-year profit of $1 billion, down 68% compared to the previous year. Interestingly, revenue was $15.5 billion, down “only” 13% compared to the same period the previous year. The airline didn’t actually cut back its total capacity that much — available seat kilometers (ASKM) decreased by 17% compared to the previous year, while the passenger load factor decreased to 72%, from 79.5% the previous year. Emirates carried 21.8 million passengers over the six months, down 22% from the same period last year.

As of September 30, 2026, Emirates is operating 91% of its pre-disruption network, with the passenger and cargo network spanning 150 airports in 78 countries. However, that reflects the number of destinations, rather than the total actual capacity (in other words, many destinations are being operated with reduced frequencies).

Emirates CEO Sheikh Ahmed bin Saeed Al Maktoum reflected on this as “a demanding six months,” and said that “once again our business model and our people stood up to the test.” He explained that the company is entering the second half of the fiscal year “with measured optimism,” “while keeping a close watch on costs and geopolitical developments.”

One would think that Gulf carriers are in the toughest spot of any airline, given that they’ve been so reliant on connecting people traveling between other regions, and at least among some people, their willingness to travel through the region has decreased, assuming it can be avoided.

Admittedly many people also just live in this region, so it’s not like there are endless options. But when you consider all factors, I’d say these are very encouraging results, much better than I would’ve expected.

I know there’s often a lot of skepticism when it comes to the reported financials of Gulf carriers. I do think at some Gulf carriers, there’s reason to be skeptical about the math, based on what is and isn’t reported.

In the case of Emirates, though, the airline is legitimately very profitable and well run. The airline has managed to efficiently scale its operation in a way that no other airline really has, and that’s where credit goes for the carrier’s success.

Of course we have to acknowledge that there’s a difference in underlying economics. Dubai (DXB) is much lower cost to operate out of than somewhere like London Heathrow (LHR) or New York Kennedy (JFK), and Emirates Group owns both the airline and the ground handling company. Furthermore, the cost of jet fuel is lower in Dubai than it is in somewhere like London, and I imagine the airline also has access to more attractive financing opportunities, given that it’s owned by the government.

However, that’s hardly anything that’s super hidden or secret. I mean, economics in US aviation are also sort of lopsided. Airline profits are largely reliant on everything except actually flying, which is a privilege and upside that most foreign carriers can’t fully unlock.

I think it’s also interesting to note how well Emirates’ yields have held up during this time. For example, just based on looking at fares through Google Flights, it seems like Etihad’s strategy has just been to publish incredibly low fares to fill seats, including in premium cabins. I haven’t found that to be the case with Emirates, though, as the airline has managed to maintain pricing power despite reduced demand.

Emirates has reported its financial results for the first half of the 2026-2027 fiscal year. As you’d expect, this was a generally tough time for a Gulf carrier, given the current war with Iran. While Emirates’ profits were cut by around two-thirds, the airline still turned a healthy profit of around $1 billion.

Honestly, the actual operating figures don’t at all reflect what you’d expect during a crisis, so it seems like the airline is weathering this story pretty well, all things considered. I do feel like Emirates is uniquely positioned among its competitive set, and I’d be shocked if the story is similar at Etihad or Qatar Airways.

What do you make of Emirates’ financial results?

#6308. Cheers At The Gate As American Airlines Pilots Save My Flight From Cancellation

Never have I been so happy to board a delayed American Airlines flight…because we actually took off when I thought we were certain to face cancellation. And it culminated in a way that left me smiling.

American Airlines is famous for its rolling delays and I recently encountered one on a flight from Chicago to Los Angeles. While AA has promised that it going to do a better job of communicating delays and trying to predict actual departure time based on aircraft placement, it still has some work to do.

My flight was originally supposed to leave at 7:10p but I received a text message in the afternoon that it would be delayed until 8:15p, which actually was idea for me. I showed up to the airport at 7:30p, had a quick bite to eat in the Admirals Club, and prepared to board…but boarding never began. Instead, the delay was pushed to 8:45p. Then it was pushed to 9:00p. Then 9:30p. Then 10:15p. Then 11:30p. Then 11:55p.

The other AA evening flight to Los Angeles was facing similar delays.

Why? The aircraft was on the ground and at the gate. It had been there since 7:45p.

One of the agents in the Admirals Club turned her screen to me and said, “See look, you’ve got no pilots.”

Sure enough, no pilots were assigned to my flight, though it made no sense to me…this was an A321 and were in Chicago O’Hare, a hub. Does AA have no reserve pilots there that can fly an Airbus?

During this time I went back and forth between the gate and the lounge, because the rolling delays notifications often came late and while I know you usually get a text message when boarding starts, that is not always the case and I did not want to miss the flight (like Andrea Sachs).

The poor gate agents were fielding the angry mob…people were livid and many were freaking out that the flight would not cancel. The gate agent didn’t exactly help by stating his belief the flight would cancel, but I appreciated his candor.

Back in the Admirals Club, suddenly the pilot positions were filled. They were being flown in from Dallas, said the agent.

Seems like a product of poor planning, but okay. I was offered a hotel room if I wanted to bail and rebook for tomorrow (“But it aint gonna be at the Hilton”) but I really wanted to get to LA without a short night in a hotel room.

Back at the gate, we were told that though the pilots had been assigned, it would be up to them determine whether they wanted to accept the overtime assignment and fly the flight…the gate agent once again was on the pessimistic side. Many passengers were (understandably) irate.

But around 11:15p, the Dallas flight pulled up to the gate. We all waited anxiously.

Suddenly, a first officer rounded the corner and the whole gate area broke out into cheers. Someone called out, “Are you our pilot?!” and he flashed the thumbs up sign.

Moments later, the captain showed up to another chorus of cheers.

The trip was on! Boarding soon commend and we were on our way…very late, but on our way.

And as an added bonus, since so many passengers bailed, I got a first class upgrade at the gate, minutes before boarding. Better than three seats in economy class? Probably not, but certainly better than just an open middle in Economy Extra and I ended up enjoying a delicious salmon dinner enroute to LAX and still enjoying a nap for a couple hours due to the late hour.

I wish AA would get their act together, but after hours of rolling delays, I was just thankful to get home without having to overnight in ORD.

#6307. Why The Boeing 747-400 Was A Turning Point For Two-Pilot Cockpits

Vytautas Kielaitis | Shutterstock | Simple Flying

For almost two decades, operating the Boeing 747 meant having three people on the flight deck. Alongside the captain and first officer, a dedicated flight engineer monitored the jumbo jet's complex systems, managed fuel distribution, checked engine parameters, and ensured its electrical, hydraulic, and pneumatic systems operated correctly. But the introduction of the 747-400 changed this longstanding arrangement, demonstrating that even one of the world's largest commercial aircraft could be operated by just two pilots.

However, the 747-400 was not the first commercial aircraft to adopt a two-pilot cockpit. Boeing 757 and 767 had already demonstrated the advantages of computerized flight decks, while other manufacturers had experimented with similar arrangements on four-engine aircraft. Nevertheless, the 747-400 represented a major milestone in bringing two-pilot operations to the jumbo-jet category. How did Boeing eliminate the flight engineer, what happened to the responsibilities previously assigned to that position, and how did the change influence subsequent generations of commercial aircraft?

When the original Boeing 747 entered commercial service with Pan American World Airways on January 22, 1970, its flight deck reflected late-1960s technology. The aircraft was considerably more complex than previous commercial jetliners, featuring four engines, extensive fuel systems, multiple hydraulic circuits, and sophisticated environmental controls. As a result, Boeing designed the original 747-100 to operate with three flight deck crew members: a captain, a first officer, and a flight engineer. This arrangement continued with the subsequent 747-200 and 747-300 generations. Boeing's official 747 historical overview identifies these three aircraft as the original Classics generation.

On most aircraft, the flight engineer sat in a dedicated seat behind the two pilots, facing a large instrument panel with hundreds of switches, gauges, indicators, and circuit breakers. While the captain and first officer concentrated on flying, navigation, and communication, the flight engineer monitored the aircraft's technical condition and performed numerous operational tasks. This included checking engine performance, managing fuel transfers between tanks, monitoring electrical generators, maintaining hydraulic pressure, and controlling cabin pressurization. On a four-engine aircraft as large as the 747, these responsibilities created a considerable workload, especially during departure, cruise, and abnormal operating conditions. The Boeing 747 flight deck historical overview compares the original cockpit arrangement with its modern successor.

Importantly, the flight engineer was not an additional pilot. The position required specialist technical training and a detailed understanding of aircraft systems, allowing the two pilots to concentrate on their primary flying responsibilities. The arrangement was also common across earlier generations of four-engine commercial aircraft, including the Boeing 707 and Douglas DC-8. However, as electronic systems became more sophisticated, aircraft manufacturers began to question whether a dedicated third crew member was still necessary. Boeing's subsequent 757 and 767 programs would answer that question.

The transition toward two-pilot commercial aircraft was already underway when Boeing began developing its 757 and 767 programs. Both aircraft entered service in the early 1980s, introducing advanced digital avionics and electronic flight displays that significantly reduced the need for conventional cockpit instrumentation. The 757 entered commercial service with Eastern Air Lines in January 1983, while the 767 followed later that year. Their integrated systems demonstrated that many functions previously requiring dedicated monitoring could be handled through computerized aircraft equipment. NASA's historical research into cockpit automation documents the technological changes introduced with the two aircraft, showing that the development was not entirely straightforward.

Boeing initially faced regulatory and industry resistance to operating larger aircraft with only two pilots. The 1981 Presidential Task Force on Aircraft Crew Complement examined whether advanced automation could safely absorb the responsibilities traditionally assigned to flight engineers. Its findings supported two-pilot operations and helped establish the regulatory foundation for aircraft such as the 767. NASA's publication, Human Factors of Advanced Technology Aircraft, explains how Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System (EICAS) technology became central to this transition. The system was even described as an electronic flight engineer because it could monitor aircraft systems and alert pilots when intervention was necessary.

Contrary to popular belief, the Boeing 747-400 was not the first four-engine jet aircraft certified for two-pilot operation. That distinction belongs to the Lockheed JetStar, the first quadjet designed for two-pilot operation, introduced into service in 1961. Meanwhile, the British Aerospace BAe 146, which first flew in 1981 and entered commercial service in 1983, is recognized as the first commercial passenger quadjet certified for a two-pilot flight deck. Before these developments, four-engine mainline jetliners traditionally required a flight engineer. Thus, the 747-400 did not invent the concept, but it extended that philosophy to the jumbo-jet market.

First quadjet overall with two-pilot operations

First commercial passenger quadjet certified for two-pilot operations

Established integrated systems monitoring

Extended two-pilot philosophy to the jumbo jet

Boeing already had the technological foundations in place when it decided to modernize its flagship aircraft. However, transferring the concept to the 747 required a much more extensive redesign than simply removing the flight engineer's seat.

As the last remaining commercial 747 aircraft near retirement, it still represents one of the most iconic eras in American aviation.

The Boeing 747-400 introduced a completely redesigned flight deck that replaced the traditional analog instrumentation with a computerized glass cockpit. Instead of presenting aircraft information through hundreds of individual gauges and switches, the new arrangement consolidated essential data into six cathode-ray tube (CRT) displays. Two primary flight displays and two navigation displays provided the pilots with essential flight information, while the central displays presented engine parameters and aircraft systems information. According to Airport Technology's technical overview of the 747-400, these displays measured about eight inches by eight inches and incorporated flight control, navigation, engine indication, and crew alerting information.

One of the most striking changes involved the number of instruments and controls in the cockpit. The integrated digital avionics systems reduced the number of flight deck lights, gauges, and switches from approximately 971 on the 747-300 to just 365 on the 747-400. This represented a reduction of more than 60%, illustrating how much information had been consolidated into electronic displays. The Aviamagazine Boeing 747 factsheet documents this transformation.

The aircraft's development also benefited from technology introduced on the 757 and 767. Boeing incorporated integrated avionics, computerized flight management, and more sophisticated monitoring systems, allowing information previously distributed across the flight engineer's panel to be presented directly to the pilots. The 747-400 entered commercial service with Northwest Airlines on February 9, 1989, marking a significant departure from the original jumbo jet's cockpit philosophy. Boeing-747.com's flight deck history explains how the redesigned cockpit absorbed the functions of the traditional engineering station.

As a result, the working environment for pilots changed substantially. However, the most important question was not how many instruments Boeing removed, but how the aircraft continued performing the responsibilities previously assigned to the third crew member.

Boeing did not transfer every flight engineer responsibility to the captain and first officer. Instead, it redesigned the aircraft's systems so that computers could continuously monitor many operating parameters and present the information requiring attention to the remaining crew members. One of the most important technologies was the Engine Indication and Crew Alerting System (EICAS), which consolidated engine information and aircraft system alerts into electronic displays. EICAS could identify abnormal conditions and communicate relevant information to both pilots, thus replacing a flight engineer who monitored hundreds of individual instruments.

The flight engineer's traditional responsibilities extended well beyond engine monitoring, and the new automated system had to cover them. The 747-400's integrated systems provided information about fuel distribution, electrical power, hydraulic systems, environmental controls, and other essential aircraft functions. Pilots could access additional system information through dedicated display pages, while alerts helped prioritize conditions requiring their attention. The Boeing 747-400 technical overview describes the integrated avionics architecture, including systems supplied by Rockwell Collins and Honeywell. In other words, the functions once spread across numerous instruments were consolidated into fewer electronic displays.

Nevertheless, automation did not eliminate the need for pilots to understand the aircraft's technical systems. The captain and first officer remained responsible for monitoring the aircraft, interpreting warnings, and deciding how to respond to abnormal situations. The computers could identify problems and provide information, but they could not replace the judgment required when making operational decisions. This distinction was important because the introduction of advanced avionics also created new human-factor challenges, including the possibility of pilots becoming overly dependent on automation. NASA's research into the introduction of new cockpit technology examined precisely these issues, including pilot workload, training, and the interaction between flight crews and computerized systems.

In short, the 747-400 redistributed responsibilities rather than eliminating an entire operational function. Integrated aircraft systems began performing the flight engineer's traditional monitoring tasks, while the remaining crew members supervised them. This also changed the economics of operating the jumbo jet, particularly on long-haul routes where crew scheduling and staffing represented significant recurring expenses.

Technological advancements in the cockpit enable modern aircraft to fly with only two pilots.

Many airlines had important commercial implications with the introduction of the two-pilot 747-400 configuration. Removing the dedicated flight engineer position meant operators no longer needed to roster a third specialist for every flight, reducing cockpit staffing requirements and simplifying crew scheduling. On long-haul operations, where extended duty periods could require additional pilots, this was particularly valuable. It also made the 747-400 more consistent with the two-pilot philosophy already established on the Boeing 757 and 767, helping airlines operating multiple Boeing aircraft families benefit from a more standardized approach to cockpit operations.

The 747-400's commercial success demonstrated the importance of this modernization. Boeing produced 694 examples of the variant, making it the most commercially successful passenger generation of the jumbo jet family. Its appeal was not based exclusively on the new cockpit, as the aircraft also introduced winglets, improved engines, greater range, and other aerodynamic and structural refinements. Nevertheless, the two-pilot flight deck was among its most consequential operational improvements. The aircraft's success helped establish the expectation that even large four-engine widebodies could operate without a dedicated flight engineer.

Boeing continued this philosophy with the 747-8, the latest production generation of the jumbo jet. Introduced in passenger and freighter configurations, the 747-8 retained the two-pilot flight deck while incorporating further advances in avionics and electronic displays. Its cockpit included technology derived from the Boeing 787 program, although Boeing maintained sufficient commonality with the 747-400 to support a shared type rating following appropriate differences training. The aircraft therefore continued the transition that had begun with the -400, rather than returning to the three-person flight deck of earlier generations.

The 747-8 ultimately demonstrated that the two-pilot arrangement was not a temporary solution specific to the 747-400. It had become the established operating philosophy for the entire modern jumbo-jet family. However, the broader question remains relevant as commercial aircraft become increasingly automated: how much responsibility should be delegated to computers, and how can manufacturers ensure that pilots remain fully capable of managing the aircraft when those systems encounter problems?

The Boeing 747-400 demonstrated that technological advances could fundamentally change how airlines operated their largest aircraft, replacing extensive manual monitoring with integrated computer systems and electronic displays. The transition also helped establish a new relationship between pilots and automation, with computers handling routine monitoring tasks while flight crews retained responsibility for aircraft control and operational decisions.

The contrast between the 747-300 and 747-400 remains particularly striking. The former required three flight deck crew members and analog cockpit lights, gauges, and switches, while the latter operated with two pilots and a glass cockpit. The subsequent 747-8 continued the two-pilot configuration, confirming that Boeing considered the arrangement integral to the jumbo jet's modern design philosophy.

Although the older Lockheed JetStar and BAe 146 had already shown that four-engine aircraft could operate with two pilots, the 747-400 took this concept to an entirely different level in commercial aviation. It proved that aircraft size and engine count did not automatically determine cockpit crew requirements. The 747’s greatest legacy was demonstrating that computerization could transform even the world's most recognizable jumbo jet.

#6305. Bizarre: Lufthansa Group Now Requires Travel ID For Online Check-In

Most airlines encourage travelers to check-in online, given that it’s mutually beneficial — it saves time for the traveler, and saves resources for the airline. Well, Lufthansa Group is implementing a new policy that makes it more difficult to check-in online, as flagged by aeroTELEGRAPH, and that strikes me as rather backwards.

Lufthansa Group has the concept of a Travel ID, whereby customers have an account they can use to log-in across digital platforms belonging to all carriers, including Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian, Brussels Airlines, Edelweiss, Discover Airlines, etc. This is separate from the Miles & More program, as the idea is that it simply creates a unified log-in for digital services across the airlines.

So along those lines, Lufthansa Group is progressively rolling out an initiative whereby customers need to have a Travel ID account in order to check-in online via the website or app.

Lufthansa Group is rolling out this requirement gradually. The Travel ID is required to check-in online as follows:

There are a limited number of exceptions for the Travel ID requirement. Specifically, you don’t need a Travel ID if you’re a traveler checking in at the airport counter or machine, if you’re traveling on a ticket issued by another airline, or if you’re on a flight operated by another airline with a ticket issued by Lufthansa Group.

Airlines love data and being able to market to customers. It’s one of the reasons that airlines create such strong incentives to sign-up for their loyalty programs (or in this case, a log-in that allows the airline to market to you). We’ve seen countless airlines roll out free Wi-Fi for those who are loyalty program members, and the logic is easy enough to follow.

However, in this case we’re talking about online check-in, which is something that arguably helps the airline more than it helps the customer. I can understand an airline wanting to add a step for something that entirely benefits the customer (like free Wi-Fi), but doing it for a basic function that saves the airline money? Well, that’s quite the approach to take.

In fairness to Lufthansa, I’m not sure this is actually a bad idea, or will backfire that much. Yes, it’s a minor annoyance, but:

Now, it’s still rather customer unfriendly, in my opinion, but that’s not exactly the first time we’ve seen something like that in the airline industry…

Lufthansa Group will start requiring passengers to sign-up for a Travel ID in order to check-in online. This is progressively being rolled out through November 30, 2026. Making it more complicated to check-in online seems counterproductive.

At the same time, clearly this is intended to encourage travelers to register for a Travel ID, so that Lufthansa can better track customer data and market to travelers. Usually we see incentives created to encourage this kind of registration, but in the case of Lufthansa Group, the airline is instead threatening to take something away if you don’t register.

What do you make of Lufthansa Group’s new online check-in requirement?

#6304. Denver Airport Taco Bell Worker Sues Over Unpaid Security Time. So Much For My $1.70 Burritos?

I had barely finished celebrating $1.70 burritos at Denver Airport when View From The Wing highlighted a lawsuit that might help explain why airport food usually costs so much more. No, we did not coordinate our Taco Bell coverage. Apparently, we just had different concerns about what happens before someone hands me a burrito.

A former Taco Bell food preparer at Denver International Airport is suing the restaurant’s operator over allegedly unpaid time spent passing through security and traveling to the restaurant before clocking in. The Colorado state court lawsuit also alleges failures to provide paid rest breaks, according to Law360.

Meanwhile, I had just written about finding surprisingly affordable Taco Bell food in Concourse A. A reader noticed the coincidence and wondered about the relationship between my cheap burritos and Gary’s discussion of employee compensation.

My first instinct is to distinguish getting to work from doing the job. Most employees do not get paid for their commute, even when traffic makes it miserable. An airport restaurant operator does not control the security checkpoint, either.

But Colorado’s wage rules give the worker a substantial argument. They specifically include security or safety screening, and waiting for it, among activities that can constitute compensable time worked. The rules also provide circumstances in which travel between work locations must be paid once work has begun.

That raises a question beyond the checkpoint itself: if required screening starts the paid workday, does the subsequent journey to the restaurant count too?

At Denver Airport, getting through security does not necessarily mean you are anywhere near your workstation.

Taco Bell can reasonably argue that the screening and journey remain part of the commute and the lawsuit, on its own, does not establish that wages were unlawfully withheld. Still, Colorado’s express inclusion of security screening makes this a claim worth taking seriously.

I often roll my eyes at airport food prices. My recent Denver visit included a nearly $20 barbecue salad and a $6.25 street taco that left me much less satisfied than Taco Bell.

But this dispute illustrates a genuine expense associated with operating inside an airport.

If employees must be paid while waiting for screening and making their way to the restaurant, the operator is paying for time before anyone starts preparing food or serving customers. That expense has to be absorbed somewhere. Some of it could end up in menu prices. Indeed, it must.

Every overpriced airport meal is not suddenly justified, but workers should not forfeit compensation required by law so I can enjoy a cheap lunch. It is a more convincing explanation for a price premium than simply charging more because passengers have nowhere else to go…

I hope those $1.70 burritos stick around. After praising them, I would prefer not to discover that I had written their farewell tribute.

But if airport employees must be paid for additional time getting through security and reaching their workplace, higher operating costs will put pressure on those bargains. I can appreciate affordable food and recognize that providing it inside an airport comes with expenses the neighborhood Taco Bell does not face. Gary and I managed to cover both sides of that equation without even comparing notes!

#6303. Where to Eat Gluten-Free in Montreal

Recently I’ve noticed more and more food people going to Montreal—and who can blame them? This laid-back bilingual gem on the St. Lawrence River is one of North America’s very best food cities. Personally I’ve loved it since my first visit almost 20 years ago. Montreal’s wonderful food scene draws me back year after year, sometimes multiple times,and by now the six-hour drive from my home in New York City feels like a breeze. It helps to know that my top meals of the year are waiting just across the border.

But for the past two years, following my wife’s celiac diagnosis, I have been navigating the city a little differently. When I was younger, trips to Montreal meant poutine, bagels, smoked-meat sandwiches, and a plethora of other canonical Québécois favorites that happen to be full of gluten. These days we prioritize other local favorites and have developed a dependable roster of businesses we trust—and that don’t feel like a compromise. Luckily there are a ton of them; we’ve been thrilled to discover that Montreal is a paradise for gluten-free eating.

In my opinion the only gluten-free Montreal-style bagels worth sampling are located in Burlington, Vermont. But Montreal is a city that takes its baked goods seriously, and it’s home to a handful of excellent dedicated gluten-free bakeries. You will not miss the bagels. Instead how about a croissant?

Any gluten-free eater knows croissants are one of the hardest pastries to get right without gluten. As a rule my wife and I don’t really bother—unless we’re in Montreal. At Boulangerie Le Marquis, near Jean-Talon Market, and sister business Le Marquis Signature Santé, in Old Montreal, magnificent pains au chocolat and gluten-free croissants—available in plain, almond, and chocolate-almond varieties—arrive hot out of the oven all morning long. Flaky laminated pastry is a near-impossible feat in the gluten-free world, but Le Marquis has perfected it. We favor the pains au chocolat and almond croissants, but it’s tough to go wrong.

Even more unique is the gluten-free manouché at La Bolo à Lolo, a GF market and takeaway in the Plateau. Chef and owner Gordy Moufarrej emigrated from Lebanon to Montreal as a boy and uses his mother’s homemade za’atar in these addictive flatbreads. Made from Moufarrej’s proprietary GF flour blend, they are topped with a paste of olive oil and za’atar, plus cheese if you want (you do). A number of sandwiches made with the same base are available, but we’ve never gotten past the manouché—on our last visit to Montreal, we went three days in a row.

Perhaps unsurprisingly for a French-speaking city, crepes are another great option, and Montreal boasts an amazing spot for 100% buckwheat Breton-style galettes. At Crêperie du Marché, a bustling stall at Jean-Talon Market, cooks turn out a dedicated gluten-free menu of lacy galettes with both savory and sweet fillings. It’s a personal choice, but we like the cheeky selections that mix both: ham, cheese, eggs, potatoes, and a drizzle of maple syrup. Why not?

Nearby is cheery, quirky Cantine Panella, a dedicated gluten-free bakery and café run by the Peruvian chef Alessandra Perona. Her South American sensibility means breads are made with flours like quinoa, cassava, and sweet potato, which gives them a delightful chewiness. We like to stock up on a few of these to bring home, though they sometimes don’t last the drive.

Of all Montreal’s classic foods, rotisserie chicken might be my favorite. At Québécois-style rotisseries it’s slow-roasted on a spit and accompanied by gravy; at Portuguese spots it’s often spatchcocked and grilled over charcoal, then served with piri-piri sauce. In both cases gluten sometimes spoils the fun: Traditional establishments like the legendary Chalet Bar-B-Q and Portuguese eatery Ma Poule Mouillée both use wheat flour in their sauces. No matter—these are far from your only options.

Piri-Piri Chicken at Rôtisserie Coco Rico

At Rôtisserie Coco Rico, a Plateau institution open since 1970, the chicken is spit-roasted and served with GF piri-piri in a mélange of the two dominant local styles. On the side fries from a dedicated GF fryer are among the city’s best (and this is a city with great french fries), but don’t sleep on the roasted potatoes, full of savory chicken flavor.

More refined, and representing the French Canadian tradition, is Little Italy’s Rôtisserie La Lune, from the team behind überpopular restaurant and wine bar Mon Lapin. Gorgeous, plump birds are served with rich gluten-free gravy and excellent fries that come from a blessedly dedicated fryer. The same fryer is also responsible for the unbelievable Croqu’Ailes Farcies XL, which are deboned chicken wings stuffed with more chicken and deep-fried. Every meal here should start with these. But the kitchen has an equally deft hand with seasonal salads and veggie-focused sides—almost always gluten-free and an essential counterweight on the table.

Down the street from La Lune, Mon Lapin is equally adept at catering to gluten-free diners: On two recent visits most of the menu was in play. Dishes change with the seasons, but friendly servers will guide your choices (and help you navigate the impressive wine list). Make sure to save room for the restaurant’s signature buckwheat layer cake, accented with buckwheat honey caramel, fromage blanc, and crisp shards of buckwheat tuile. I’m not sure there’s a better gluten-free dessert on the continent.

Mon Lapin’s co-owners, chefs Jessica Noël and Marc-Olivier Frappier, and wine director Vanya Filipovic, are all alums of the trendsetting Little Burgundy eatery and wine bar Vin Papillon, whose chef and owner happens to be celiac. Best known as half of the duo that opened Montreal icon Joe Beef, Fred Morin now presides over those two restaurants, plus the rotisserie McKiernan and gastropub Liverpool House. His kitchens have airtight allergy protocols and are particularly sensitive to gluten-free diners because of Morin’s own celiac status. And because so many Montreal chefs have passed through Morin’s kitchens, his influence looms large over the city’s fine dining scene—and its spirit of hospitality toward those with allergies and intolerances.

While all of Morin’s restaurants are fantastic, Vin Papillon is the one we come back to every year—its Jambon de la Petite-Bourgogne is one of the world’s great meat-and-cheese plates, featuring house-cured ham, the Quebec sheep-milk cheese le Fleur des Monts, and a sneaky application of brown butter that brings together all the nutty, savory notes. For dessert the restaurant often serves a gluten-free carrot cake ice cream sandwich with caramel sauce in a silver goblet.

Another Joe Beef group alum, Ariel Schor, runs one of our favorite Verdun neighborhood spots with his brother, Pablo. Both natives of Argentina with Jewish roots, the Schors run a restaurant called Beba with a particular affinity for offal (organ meats) and a surprisingly light touch with creative veg dishes that change seasonally. Swiss chard leaves are stuffed with zucchini and chard stems and served with a sweet-and-sour condiment of onions, raisins, and pine nuts. Medjool dates are impishly filled with foie gras and topped with pistachio. Elsewhere on the menu expect things like tongue, rabbit, chorizo, and tripe—dishes that tend to be gluten-free.

When you’re craving Gallic comfort food, Montreal overdelivers. I used to think there were Leméac people and L’Express people, that one couldn’t possibly love Montreal’s two most prominent old-school bistros equally. I was wrong. The late local architect Luc Laporte designed both dining rooms, and they each have the buzzing, joyful energy most restaurants covet.

L’Express is my first love, a Montreal stalwart open since 1980 that I’ve been to more times than I can count. Its main virtues for gluten-free eaters are a dedicated fryer and incredibly good french fries—available as a stand-alone side or, even better, as part of steak frites. There are plenty of other GF mains and entrées, but room must be saved for the enormous île flottante, a classic French meringue-based dessert encased in a hardened caramel dome and surrounded by shards of candied almond. For something on the lighter side, try the unique crème brûlée with wild sweet clover from Quebec, sometimes called boreal vanilla.

Leméac does not have a dedicated fryer, so fries don’t work for celiacs. But I promise you won’t miss them. We favor the textbook duck confit, served with roasted potatoes and a bright green salad. For dessert there’s an unmissable gluten-free chocolate-and-banana moelleux, a decadent cake served with caramel and popcorn ice cream, along with many other classics, including crème caramel.

Montreal is also home to a number of fabulous Middle Eastern and North African restaurants, some of which can cater to gluten-free diners—albeit with asterisks. We love the standout Damas, a Syrian fine-dining spot on a pretty corner in Outremont, though gluten-free choices are limited. Still, it’s worth the trip for the ground lamb and eggplant kebab grilled over open charcoal and accompanied by charred pepper, tomato butter, and gobs of garlic labneh and the dreamy hummus topped with lamb shawarma and pine nuts, which can be served with crudités rather than pita. Both are among the best things I’ve eaten in recent memory.

Le Petit Alep, a neighborhood institution near Jean-Talon, offers more Syrian and Armenian options. The marvelous mezes are largely gluten-free and served—upon request—with crudités; savory, comforting mujaddara is made with lentils and rice, no bulgur, barley, or other glutenous grains. End with the house herbal tea, a beautiful floral mixture of cardamom pods, mint, rosewater, and orange blossom. I’ve tried to make it at home, but I can’t quite replicate it. That’s okay—I’ll be back next year.

#6302. Lufthansa Realizes 28 Business Class Seats Isn’t Enough For Boeing 787

In recent times, Lufthansa has started taking delivery of factory fresh Boeing 787s, featuring the carrier’s all-new Allegris cabins. Management at the airline has reportedly decided that the configuration of these planes isn’t quite right for many routes, so now it’s planning some updates.

That’s a sensible change, but it always just feels like Lufthansa is a step behind when it comes to acting logically and catching onto trends, no?

Lufthansa currently has a fleet of 20 Boeing 787-9s. Four of these were acquired secondhand (they were former Hainan Airlines jets), while 16 are brand new, and feature Allegris interiors. Not only that, but Lufthansa has at least another 22 of these planes on order, which will be delivered in the coming years.

In the long run, the Dreamliner is supposed to be the carrier’s primary long haul aircraft based in Frankfurt, complementing the Boeing 747-8s and Boeing 777-9s. Meanwhile Munich (MUC) is primarily getting Airbus A350s (including the A350-900 and A350-1000).

Lufthansa’s 787s are configured with 287 seats, including 28 business class seats, 28 premium economy seats, and 231 economy seats. Keep in mind that three of those seats aren’t even certified yet (but should be certified before the end of 2026), so actual business class capacity is currently just 25 seats.

Anyway, even with all seats certified, Lufthansa Group management has decided that the capacity doesn’t actually match demand on many routes, with CEO Carsten Spohr indicating that the airline is working on installing more business class and premium economy seats on upcoming Dreamliners.

Reportedly nothing has been finalized yet, as this is still in negotiations with suppliers, but the idea remains that the current configuration doesn’t offer enough premium seats.

Given the eventual size of Lufthansa’s Dreamliner fleet, it would also be reasonable to think the airline may have two configurations in the long run, to reflect the demand of different destinations. For example, one would assume that the potential customer demand profile would be different to New York (JFK) than to Columbus (CMH), both of which are going to be Dreamliner routes in the coming months.

I know ragging on Lufthansa is just too easy, from its challenging labor relations, to its botched Allegris rollout, and more. However, I can’t help but feel like the airline is a little behind on trends.

I mean, for how long have we been talking about the surge in premium travel demand? American is taking delivery of 787-9s with 51 business class seats, United is taking delivery of 787-9s with 64 business class seats, and British Airways is reconfiguring 787-9s with eight first class seats and 38 business class seats.

So Lufthansa just taking delivery of dozens of factory fresh 787s with just 28 business class seats seems a little off, especially since Lufthansa only recently started adding these planes to its fleet.

I get that demand differs between markets, and the 787 is actually supposed to be the less premium plane in the fleet, in the long run (with the Boeing 747s and 777Xs being the most premium Frankfurt-based planes), but still, 28 seats just doesn’t seem like a lot by any metric. Heck, the Airbus A330s that are slowly being retired have 42 business class seats, and that’s an overall smaller plane.

Of course the whole Lufthansa Allegris and SWISS Senses situation is just sort of messy, from the 3.5-seat first class cabin that makes no sense, to the need to install a weight on SWISS A330s to balance out the weight of first class, to the new Allegris seats delaying entry into service for planes by years, despite it not actually being that cutting edge at this point.

Lufthansa Group CEO Carsten Spohr has indicated that the airline is considering a new configuration for many upcoming Boeing 787s. Management has decided that 28 business class seats and 28 premium economy seats isn’t sufficient, which strikes me as a rather obvious, when you look at trends. Heck, these Dreamliners are partly replacing planes with 50% more business class seats.

I’m curious to see what Lufthansa eventually settles on for a premium Dreamliner configuration, because I agree, 28 business class seats isn’t a lot!

What do you make of Lufthansa reconsidering its 787 layout?

Your statement that ‘ragging on Lufthansa is almost too easy’ sums up the situation nicely. Can anyone really remember a time when this airline, and LH group in general, wasn’t a joke? Remember when Lufthansa itself could seriously claim to be among the most premium and reliable brands on earth? It’s long been a trope that British Airways is the airline that most severely shredded its premium image, especially under Cruz. But he lasted less than 5 years running BA, and they’ve spent the last 6 years doing (just) enough to recover some of that, and are arguably about halfway there at best in terms of repairing the damage. Spohr has had a dozen years to wreck Lufthansa, with no end in sight, and they clearly cannot start repairing the damage until he goes. The fact they continue to get the most basic planning wrong, misreading or ignoring clear industry trends, just underlines this. Among the flagship European carriers, LH is just so far behind Air France, and even BA as things stand, it’s hard to imagine when they can actually try to catch up, saddled with their current leadership.

Nah they just knew all the premium travelers were going to spend their money elsewhere. Smart. :D

......yet still there is no accountability. Now that AA seem to have finally seen the light, LH must be out on their own as the most incompetant managemnt for a major airline

The whole Allegris philosophy was a gamble on one very specific aspect: segmenting customers with different seat types. The allegris business class seat is a very inefficient seat. It is essentially the same concept as united’s Polaris, except with more seat pitch, and every second row, just one middle seat instead of two. Lufthansa thought they could segment their business class customers, upsell certain seats (especially the throne seats, the long bed and the mini-first class at the bulkhead) and make up for the lost revenue of having such an inefficient layout and shrinking the size of the cabin (to maintain a large economy class cabin). But this gamble failed, because Lufthansa didn’t realise that by upcharging so many business class passengers even to simply select a window seat put a bad taste in many people’s mouths. Look at BA, AF and KL. all business class seats in their cabins are created more or less equal with the exception of the bulkheads. Furthermore, Frankfurt is a business heavy market, but has less point-to-point business traffic, and a lot of connecting traffic. It is easy for travellers who are not star-alliance loyal to simply connect elsewhere, or fly united across the Atlantic. Lufthansa wanted to create a segmented business class cabin, but instead created a business class “lite” and charged for extras after that. And now they’re stuck with a VERY expensive, delayed seat, which occupies way too much space on their aircraft, and as such they have had to make huge compromises like shrinking the first and business class cabins. They will seriously lose out in the long term.

#6301. The Airline That Invented Premium Economy Just Built A 42-Inch Seat Nobody Else Can

Getting passengers in seats is the number one priority of all airlines. How an airline achieves this is usually down to routes as well as the product itself and how it differs from others in the market. Today, the most contested part of the cabin has arguably become premium economy. Global carriers are racing to capture affluent long-haul commuters, and the strategic challenge is no longer just about building a spacious seat, but deploying it where it can inflict the maximum competitive damage. EVA Air is one of the airlines that is leading the way, a pioneer of the premium economy concept, and still retaining its dominance.

The airline's recent progress signals a deeper structural shift in how boutique international airlines challenge massive legacy alliances on ultra-long-haul flight tracks. Instead of funneling travelers through crowded West Coast transit points, the focus has shifted toward capturing high-yield corporate and premium leisure demand directly from prime East Coast markets.

First, the new staple route between Taipei Taoyuan International Airport (TPE) and Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) begins a tale of aggressive expansion of intercontinental capacity. Operating four times per week, this new corridor marks the carrier's tenth North American gateway, pushing its total regional footprint to an unprecedented 98 weekly flights. By entering the US National Capital region, the airline is intentionally establishing a direct pipeline into a market that generates immense corporate, diplomatic, and premium diaspora traffic.

Skipping over traditional multi-stop routings changes the financial landscape for travelers who have spent years navigating arduous connections. In the past, more than 40,000 passengers traveling annually between the Washington metropolitan area and greater Asia had to connect through highly congested West Coast hubs, according to Travel Tourister. The new direct 7,860-mile (12,649 km) sector completely removes that friction, offering an efficient 14-hour eastbound sprint and a 15.5-hour westbound block time, to the delight of these regular travelers.

The economic ramifications of this single-route injection are massive, highlighting the high-yield value of mature transpacific corridors. According to EVA Air, the new service will generate more than $61 million in annual economic impact for the capital region while significantly shifting market-share balances. For an independent carrier operating outside the major transatlantic mega-alliances, getting a firm foothold at Dulles is an excellent way to capture elite corporate accounts that traditionally rely on domestic legacy carriers.

A route is never complete without an accompanying aircraft, and fortunately for EVA Air, the best choice is already in the fleet. The carrier chose to configure its newest batch of Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner airframes in a tightly optimized three-class layout, balancing premium margin and structural density. Total capacity is capped at 278 seats, meticulously divided into 26 Royal Laurel business class suites, 28 Premium Economy spaces, and 224 standard economy seats.

By dedicating just four rows to the premium economy environment in a spacious seven-abreast, 2-3-2 configuration, the airline is breaking firmly with the industry status quo. This cabin density lets the airline offer a generous 42-inch (106.7 cm) seat pitch, giving passengers far more personal space than competitive alternatives. Each seat incorporates an advanced cradle-motion system that slides the lower cushion forward and upward simultaneously, providing an eight-inch (20.3 cm) recline without encroaching on the passenger behind.

The cabin composition maximizes revenue potential per square foot by catering to an affluent middle market that values workspace over basic transit. Each space is loaded with utility, featuring a 15.6-inch (39.6 cm) high-definition touchscreen monitor, built-in personal electronic device holders, and dual power configurations. By choosing a lower seat count over a dense layout, the airline creates a scarce, high-demand asset that lets it maintain strong pricing integrity during both peak and shoulder travel seasons.

One particular carrier is planning to expand its services significantly.

The immediate arrival of a 42-inch (106.7 cm) product standard at Dulles heavily disrupts the traditional long-haul landscape connecting the eastern United States to East Asia. Elite regional competitors have historically maintained a highly uniform product standard on their ultra-long-haul fleets, typically capping their mid-cabin offerings at a conventional 38-inch (96.5 cm) pitch. This four-inch (10.2 cm) discrepancy creates a severe competitive deficit for legacy operators that have long relied on cabin density to maximize raw ticket volume.

Compared with the tight layout choices of alternative alliance carriers, the spatial divergence becomes clear to corporate travelers who pay close attention to every product offering. Competitors operating out of neighboring East Coast hubs often deploy an eight-abreast 2-4-2 alignment on their flagship aircraft, narrowing the cushion width available to individual passengers. Scaling down to a seven-abreast configuration on a widebody frame restores substantial shoulder room, turning a long 15-hour flight track into a manageable workspace.

Put simply, this is precisely how an independent player dictates market expectations from a single international gateway. Travelers experiencing the enhanced spatial layout quickly develop a lower tolerance for restrictive industry-standard cabins on subsequent transpacific journeys. As this route matures into the late summer season, an elite intermediate tier will force surrounding operators to re-evaluate whether their high-density configurations can truly protect their premium market shares.

Launching a direct transpacific service to the East Coast serves a clear structural purpose by shifting traffic away from traditional West Coast connecting gateways. Travelers originating in the mid-Atlantic region had to funnel through immense hubs like Los Angeles or San Francisco to reach East Asia. This extra domestic leg adds hours of travel time, heightens the risk of misplaced baggage, and introduces the fatigue of terminal transfers. Now offering a direct alternative, the carrier skips over these consolidated bottlenecks entirely and establishes a more streamlined transit corridor.

Capturing high-value traffic from the corporate and diplomatic sectors requires direct geographic access to the political heart of the United States. Connecting points like Seattle or Los Angeles add operational friction that premium business travelers actively seek to avoid. The three-class aircraft setup provides dedicated mid-cabin space that aligns with corporate travel rules, which often restrict business class bookings but permit premium travel on long flights, according to a Reddit thread. This means EVA Air now directly competes with legacy alliances by pulling lucrative corporate contracts away from domestic multi-stop routings.

The geographic advantage is particularly striking when analyzing the specific corporate demand from the defense and technology corridors flanking Virginia and Maryland. These fields rely heavily on constant communication with East Asian manufacturing bases, making efficient transpacific transport a vital business requirement, according to the Virginia Economic Development Partnership (VEDP). Avoiding a West Coast transfer saves corporate clients at least three hours each way while ensuring high-yield revenue flows directly to a single carrier instead of being split among domestic codeshare partners.

Operating flights that exceed 15 hours always comes with the steep weight penalties of ultra-long-haul aviation. To sustain a route of this length, an aircraft must carry thousands of gallons of fuel simply to burn it off during the initial hours of flight, which severely restricts the remaining payload capacity available for heavy cargo, according to Aviation Metric. Relying heavily on discounted economy fares cannot offset these operating costs, especially since the maximum size of the business-class cabin is limited by the cabin's dimensions. The route's commercial viability depends heavily on maximizing revenue density in the mid-cabin environment.

The mid-cabin space acts as a financial buffer because it generates premium-tier margins while consuming far less floor space than luxury lie-flat berths. Corporate travelers moving through this cabin category typically pay fares that are twice the cost of a standard economy ticket, yet the footprint per passenger expands by only a fraction. Operating with a highly optimized revenue density like this keeps the route consistently profitable during off-peak travel seasons when leisure demand declines.

The true power of this mid-cabin asset is fully realized when it is integrated into a rapid-transit hub network. Arriving at a hub in the early morning allows travelers to clear transit security and board connecting flights to major East Asian manufacturing and financial centers within a tight window. EVA Air's coordination turns a single ultra-long-haul route into a comprehensive gateway, capturing complex multi-city business itineraries that traditional domestic carriers cannot easily replicate with multi-carrier alliances.

The launch of the Mid-Atlantic corridor is only the initial phase of a broader systematic strategy to standardize this premium configuration across the global network. Introducing a dedicated three-class layout on the twin-engine widebody fleet is, of course, a distinct shift away from treating premium economy as an optional regional product. Ultimately, it positions the mid-cabin experience as a foundational tier that will define future intercontinental operations.

As more factory-fresh airframes arrive from the assembly line, this high-comfort standard will gradually scale into highly competitive West Coast markets and key European trunk routes. Markets like San Francisco, Munich, Milan, and Vienna are scheduled to receive these reconfigured three-class widebodies to ensure product consistency across diverse transpacific and transatlantic flight paths.

EVA Air's fleet harmonization creates an intense competitive challenge for global alliance partners that still operate older configurations with inferior legroom standards. Standardizing an industry-leading pitch across a growing widebody fleet sets a new quality benchmark that leaves rivals with little choice but to invest in costly cabin retrofits or cede lucrative market share. The race is now well and truly on, and it seems that EVA Air is the one to chase.

It has been two years since Singapore Airlines began teasing all-new business- and first-class cabins, and nearly 10 years since the last time the airline unveiled a new generation of flagship products.

But after much anticipation and a flurry of recent announcements — about upgrades and refreshes on everything from the airline’s dining program, inflight meals and serviceware to its KrisWorld entertainment system and amenity kits — we finally got to see what the new Singapore Airlines business- and first-class seats are like. We also got a preview of the new economy and premium economy seats coming to its Boeing 777-9s.

TPG joined a slew of international media for two days of announcements and executive interviews culminating in the big reveal at Marina Bay Sands. The presentation even included a newly composed theme song titled "Made of every world you can dream of," performed by flight crew.

“Today Singapore Airlines unveils the next chapter in our end-to-end travel experience,” began Singapore Airlines CEO Goh Choon Phong in his remarks to the crowd. “This is an important milestone and it is also part of our continuous journey to…invest in a product we know our customer will love.”

The new products represent a multi-year investment of over 2 billion Singaporean dollars ($1.56 billion) in addition to the S$130 million ($102 million) the airline has spent renovating its SilverKris lounges around the world.

“This is our biggest investment in improving the customer travel experience because we’re not just talking about seat development,” Siva Govindasamy, divisional vice president of public affairs, said. "We’re talking about improvements in the customer service journey from end to end.”

The airline surveyed over 5,000 frequent flyers, incorporating their feedback on what they were looking for from the travel experience, what elements of Singapore Airlines’ current seats and service they liked, and what needed to evolve.

“Our development process has been shaped by extensive research and feedback to help us understand how our customers work, dine, relax, sleep and use technology in their journeys,” Lee Lik Hsin, Singapore Airlines’ chief commercial officer, explained to a small media gathering ahead of the event. “This launch represents a significant milestone, but not an end point,” he continued.

Based on what we saw of the new seats and service elements, here are all the fancy, industry-leading features the airline has in store.

Related: Singapore KrisFlyer: Ultimate guide to earning, redeeming and elite status

Perhaps the most exciting announcement of the bunch was the unveiling of Singapore Airlines’ new long-haul first-class seats.

Designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, these fixtures were initially slated for the airline’s upcoming order of Boeing 777-9s. But given the delays on those aircraft deliveries, Singapore is also installing them on its ultra-long-range subfleet of seven Airbus A350-900ULRs starting in the second half of 2027. This will be the first time the airline’s A350s have sported a first-class cabin.

The A350s will have just four of these seats on board in a 1-2-1 configuration at the very front of the plane. The 777-9s will eventually have six of them on board — two running down either side of the cabin and two in the center. They have 89 1/2 inches of pitch, giving them a fairly large footprint (though not as big as the Suites aboard the airline’s Airbus A380s). Singapore Airlines has no plans to update the first-class cabins on its Boeing 777-300s or A380s.

In one of the lighter moments during the pre-reveal press conferences, a journalist asked Singapore’s Hsin how flight crew would address couples who might use the space inappropriately. “We will address it,” Hsin replied without missing a beat, prompting chuckles around the room. “We want every passenger to be able to enjoy the comfort that we have provided without disturbing the comfort and experience for any other customer.”

Back to the seat, though: It incorporates a cocktail tray for inflight aperitifs and wardrobe areas in the aisles where passengers can stow their clothes (after slipping into the airline’s new pajamas, of course ... more on that below). Those with a keen eye will also notice a subtle batik motif on the soft wall panels hearkening to the airline’s famous uniforms and branding.

The chairs are upholstered in Poltrona Frau leather, are 23 inches wide (30 with the armrests lowered) and recline to 80-inch lie-flat beds that flight attendants will make up with 100% cotton linens, a duvet and a selection of pillows, as well as a breathable new mattress topper from German luxury brand Paradies.

Passengers can adjust the various components of the seat including the arm and legrests, the ottoman and lumbar support. They can also change the lighting using the inflight entertainment system controls and create a profile so that their settings carry over to their next flight.

Passengers can dine face-to-face thanks to large, sturdy tray tables. They will also find a wireless charging pad, USB-C ports and a universal AC power port to keep their devices charged. The 777-9 seats will have a USB-A port as well.

The storage areas include a slim personal wardrobe, a leather-lined vanity drawer and a small compartment for a cabin bag beneath the ottoman.

The inflight entertainment system is a 32-inch 4K touchscreen loaded with the airline’s KrisWorld content system. It will include an integrated touch panel display for flight information, destination weather, inflight Wi-Fi connectivity status and lavatory availability.

Passengers will receive Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones to use, but they can also connect to the entertainment system with their own Bluetooth headsets.

Overall, the new first-class seats are a big step forward from the first-class cabins you’ll find aboard the airline’s Boeing 777-300s; they sit somewhere between those and the A380 Suites. Their look feels like an evolution of the Suites' palette and finishes, with welcome technology updates that should keep travelers happy and connected.

Related: The ultimate guide to Singapore Suites

Lest you think first class is the biggest news, the airline also unveiled its all-new business-class seats, designed from the ground up in conjunction with seat manufacturer Recaro and BMW’s DesignWorks.

These seats will appear on the Boeing 777-9 and both the A350-900ULR and the long-haul A350-900; they will not appear on the airline’s medium-haul A350s. If you’re losing track, don’t worry, we have tables below that lay out the details. We also got a few exclusive shots from a mock-up cabin at Singapore Airlines' headquarters the day before the official unveiling, which you can see below. (Just note that they don't have all the finishes and other details the final seats on board will have.)

“We wanted to bring an automotive-inspired seat and our knowledge from experiential design into the cabin,” explained BMW DesignWorks CEO Julia de Bono. Thus, the seats feel like a mix between seats in a luxury sedan and a racecar with mineral gray-toned leather and bright yellow trim, meant to convey balance and stability on the one hand and energy and creativity on the other, according to De Bono.

The seats are laid out in a front-facing 1-2-1 pattern — this was a direct result of customer feedback, with frequent flyers telling airline executives that they wanted to move past an angled orientation, which could feel constraining at times.

Passengers will also receive new padded seat covers with memory foam for cushioning and support.

The tray table placement and stowage — which pops out from under the entertainment screen and is flexible to maneuver — also gives the seat a larger ottoman, alleviating a common complaint about the airline’s current business-class seats.

Like the new first-class seats, these will allow passengers to create a profile via the inflight entertainment system, so their preferred seat and lighting settings are saved from flight to flight.

They have 22-inch 4K touchscreen entertainment systems (20 inches on the 777-9) with Bluetooth pairing capability. Among the storage spaces are a small cubby that slides out from the chair-side seatback and a little cupboard next to the entertainment screen. Passengers will also find wireless charging pads, USB-C ports and universal power plugs.

Related: Which Singapore Airlines business class is better? A380 vs A350

Singapore Airlines worked with FactoryDesign and Collins Aerospace to create updated versions of its economy and premium economy seats specifically for the Boeing 777-9. There are currently no plans to install these aboard the airline’s other jets.

The new premium economy seats have a swanky, contoured look with dark gray leather upholstery and vibrant orange accents. They will see their seat pitch increase from the 38 inches previous versions offer to 40 inches, and they will get an extra inch of recline, rounding it up to 9 instead of 8. They will be 19 inches wide and have adjustable leg and footrests plus adjustable headsets.

Their entertainment screens will be 16 inches wide with 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability. The seats will also feature universal power plugs, USB-C ports and USB-A ports on some aircraft.

As for economy seating, these look a lot like current versions and are squeezed into a tight 3-4-3 layout, with just 17.6 inches of width per seat. Their screens get an upgrade to 13 inches and 4K resolution, with Bluetooth pairing available. They will also have USB-C ports (and A versions on some aircraft) plus universal power plugs.

Related: Worth the upcharge? Flying Singapore Airlines premium economy

So how exactly are all these new seats going to get onto planes? And when will passengers start seeing them? Here’s the plan.

Singapore Airlines currently has 58 Airbus A350s. Seventeen of those are configured for medium-haul and regional routes.

Of the remaining 41, 34 are long-range A350-900s with business class, premium economy and economy on board. These will be kitted out with new business-class seats, with the following adjusted seat counts in each class. The process is expected to start in the second half of 2027 and to last through 2030.

The other seven A350s are the airline’s A350-900ULRs (which stands for ultra-long-range) and are deployed on the airline’s longest routes from Singapore Changi Airport (SIN) to John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) and Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR). These ULR jets will receive a full overhaul, including new first- and business-class seats. The changes will reduce the plane's overall seating capacity to 132, down from 161.

All the seats on this jet will be new, but here’s how it breaks down.

The good news is that the majority of Singapore Airlines' long-haul fleet will have new first- and business-class seats on them once this retrofit is complete and the 777-9s are in service. The bad news is that we don't know exactly how long that will take, and we don't know which routes will see the new seats first.

In the meantime, here are some of the other fun things the airline has cooking up — quite literally.

Related: A review of Singapore Suites first class from Frankfurt to New York

As if new seats weren’t enough, Singapore Airlines is making major updates to its meal service as well.

The airline is already well-known for offering a “Book the Cook” meal preorder service with dozens of dishes available to flyers in Suites, first, business and premium economy. And there are about to be a lot more options.

The airline is touting over 100 new and refreshed dishes, including appetizers, mains and desserts. They will be introduced across all four classes of service under a new category titled “SIA Chefs’ Selection” developed by the airline’s partner guest chefs, including Monica Galetti, Nandu Jubany, Sanjeev Kapoor, Sid Sahrawat, Yoshihiro Murata and Zhu Jun.

Among the new dishes you might spot are poached Maine lobster with Champagne sauce in Suites and first class; Japanese-inspired prawn cocktail in business class; beef short rib in coconut-based sambal percik with nasi kerabu rice in business class; tandoor-roasted paneer in tangy pasanda gravy in all classes; and Irish lamb stew with buttered cabbage and caraway seeds in premium economy.

And take a closer look at what those dishes will be served on in business and first. The airline is introducing an all-new line of chinaware from French luxury brand Christofle, making it the first airline to partner with the long-standing luxury house.

The patterns are inspired by Christofle’s Malmaison Imperiale collection and incorporate an interpretation of Singapore Airline’s floral batik patterns. There will also be new custom-designed Christofle glassware, including tulip-shaped champagne flutes and long-stemmed wine glasses for greater utility.

A new selection of spirits across the board and new wines for business- and first-class passengers is coming, too. First-class and Suites passengers will be treated to an expanded selection of champagnes including Krug Grande Cuvee, Louis Roederer Cristal, Taittinger Comtes de Champagne, Charles Heidsieck Blanc des Millenaires and Bollinger La Grande Année. Those in business class will find Charles Heidsieck Brut Reserve NV and Piper-Heidsieck Vintage.

Among the new spirits to be carried on board, there will be a blended whisky from Japan’s Komoro Distillery created exclusively for Singapore Airlines first class; a Bowmore 19 Year Old pinot noir Cask Finish single-malt Scotch whisky and Roku Botanical Kasane Edition gin in business class; and Whyte & Mackay blended Scotch whisky in premium economy and economy.

Related: Behind the scenes with Singapore Airlines' wine experts as they choose the Champagnes that will be on board soon

For a carrier with such a premium reputation, one thing that surprises some business-class passengers is that Singapore Airlines has not traditionally provided amenities in business class. (First-class passengers do get them, though.) That’s all about to change, starting this week.

In fact, Singapore Airlines is introducing all-new amenity kits available on flights over six hours. Here’s what’s in store for passengers.

When Singapore Airlines launched its second-generation A380 first-class Suites in 2017, it also formed a partnership with French luxury house Lalique to create onboard amenities including pajamas, linens and amenity kits with fragrances and skincare products.

Now, with the introduction of its third-generation suites, the airline is turning to French cosmetics brand Sisley to create all-new men’s and women’s kits for first-class passengers featuring anti-aging Sisleya (for women) and Sisleyum (for men) products.

Passengers will also find Sisley’s Eau de Campagne fragrance, moisturizing body lotion and floral spray mist along with dental kits in the first-class lavatories.

As for pajamas, customers will receive all-new sleeper suits in dark gray cotton with a subtle imprint of the airline’s batik pattern on the plackets and side seams, along with new, better-padded slippers. They will be available in four sizes.

In Singapore Airlines' fancy The Private Room lounge and the First Class SilverKris Lounge at Changi terminals 2 and 3, passengers will also find Hair Rituel by Sisley fortifying densifying shampoo and restructuring conditioner in the shower suites, along with Sisley’s Eau de Campagne bath and shower gel, fragrance and moisturizing body lotion.

Singapore Airlines is also introducing new amenity kits and, for the first time, pajamas for business-class passengers.

The sleeping apparel will be navy blue poly-cotton with a subtle batik print on the tops’ inner collars and the lining of the trousers’ pockets. They will be available in two sizes.

Business-class passengers will also receive new amenity kits from Swedish brand Byredo that include:

The business-class lavatories will have Blanche body lotion and vitamin E and chamomile facial toner.

Don’t worry, the airline hasn’t forgotten about premium economy passengers, who pay a pretty penny for that extra legroom. They will now receive new zip pouches made from recycled materials and decorated with the airline’s recognizable batik motif.

The pouches will contain Australian personal care brand Ink & Water’s white tea-scented lip balm as well as eye masks, socks and dental kits.

Related: Singapore Airlines premium economy review

Even the folks in economy will receive drawstring pouches with a batik motif containing eye masks, socks and a dental kit.

Long flights are tough on kids, so for travelers 12 years and under on flights that are over five hours long, the airline will offer collectible Beary soft toys — essentially airline-branded teddy bears. On all flights, the airline also offers Pixar’s “Toy Story”-themed amenities, which include things like infant bibs, activity pads for kids and drawstring bags.

Related: I make my own amenity kit for long-haul flights: Here’s what’s inside

Singapore Airlines will also update the KrisWorld inflight entertainment systems on its A350s and offer new systems on its forthcoming 777-9s.

The new systems will have 4K resolution and Bluetooth pairing capability, with interface improvements including better search functions, content shortcuts, a mini-player (so passengers can browse content while watching something), better personalization and wellness programming.

First-class passengers will receive Bang & Olufsen noise-canceling Bluetooth headsets for inflight use, while business-class and premium economy flyers will receive active noise-cancellation headsets. Economy passengers will receive wired headphones, but they will be able to pair their own Bluetooth devices with the new systems.

The airline will also progressively roll out new Starlink Wi-Fi service starting in 2027 aboard its Airbus A380s, A350-900 long-haul fleet and its A350-900ULRs. Like the airline’s current Wi-Fi offerings, Starlink service will be free for business- and first-class passengers and passengers in all cabins who are members of KrisFlyer or PPS Club.

“For our customers, every touchpoint — from seats, meals, inflight entertainment, connectivity and amenities, to our lounges and other ground experiences — is part of one similar Singapore Airlines journey," Phong said in his speech at the unveiling event. "By continuing to invest and elevate this end-to-end customer experience, we offer greater comfort and convenience while reinforcing our commitment to earning their trust and loyalty at every single phase of their journey.”

New airline seats represent huge investments of time, money and research, not to mention the costs of updating onboard services and amenities. That makes Singapore Airlines’ current slate of announcements all the more exciting.

Flyers have a lot to look forward to on board the airline’s long-haul A350s and forthcoming 777-9s. While the first-class seats are not as large as the Suites on board the airline’s A380s, they are still roomy with high-end finishes and up-to-date tech that passengers should welcome.

As for premium economy and economy, hopefully the airline will consider bringing its latest seats to the A350 as well in an attempt to standardize the experience across the fleet. Still, for 777-9 passengers, these updates will be a win.

If you're curious to see some of these unveiled elements for yourself, there should be a special display at The Jewel at Changi in the coming weeks, followed by one in the transit area of the airport's Terminal 3 in early 2027.

What do you think of Singapore Airlines’ new seats? Leave a comment with your impressions below!
