#6299. United’s Premium Boeing 787s With New Cabins: Which Routes Do They Fly?

We recently saw United Airlines introduce its long awaited new Boeing 787-9s, featuring all-new cabins, which are being branded as United Elevate. This represents the evolution of the carrier’s long haul experience, including all-new Polaris business class seats.

Of course one common question is which routes actually feature these new planes. So in this post, I’d like to go over that — which planes have the new cabins, and which routes do they fly? The airline is flying these planes on an increasing number of routes out of two hubs, so there are more opportunities to try this product.

Prior to 2026, United already had over 80 Boeing 787 Dreamliners in its fleet, split between the 787-8, 787-9, and 787-10 variants. However, United is now taking delivery of another 71 Boeing 787-9s, which recently started to be delivered (in addition to 56 Boeing 787-10s, which will be delivered as of 2028).

What’s exciting about these planes is that they feature an all-new passenger experience, and are in an ultra premium configuration. The planes feature just 222 seats, compared to the 257 seats you’ll find on all the previous 787-9s.

If you want to actually fly a United Boeing 787-9 with the new United Elevate interiors, what are your best odds of getting on one of these? The good news is that they’re consistently scheduled on certain routes.

As it currently stands, United has 16 of these 787s in its fleet, with several more expected to be delivered in the coming months. United plans to have 33 of these jets by 2028, so the airline is taking delivery of an average of around one of these per month (though the pace has been even faster in the first several months).

When you go to book a ticket, the best way to tell if a flight is operated by the new plane is whether you see “Polaris Studio available” listed under the United Polaris fare options (assuming those seats are for sale). Otherwise there are no obvious indicators, other than looking at the seat map.

We recently saw the IATA winter season kick off, and with that, we’re seeing the plane based out of both Houston (IAH) and San Francisco (SFO).

You’ll currently find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of San Francisco:

You’ll then find the 787 with Elevate interiors scheduled to fly to the following destinations out of Houston:

Let me emphasize that schedules are always subject to change (especially when Boeing delivery delays are a potential factor), and the above is just how things currently stand. I’m also not including flights between San Francisco and Houston, which sometimes see the plane so that it can be rotated between hubs, but obviously that route doesn’t feature the true Polaris soft product.

In recent months, we’ve seen United start to take delivery of its brand new Boeing 787-9s, featuring a more premium layout, plus new cabins. These are exciting planes for passengers, as they feature a much improved onboard experience. They’re also great in terms of upgrade and award availability, given the number of premium seats.

If you want to fly United’s new 787s, you’ll currently find them flying out of Houston and San Francisco. Out of Houston, they’re primarily flying to London, Sao Paulo, Sydney, and Tokyo, while out of San Francisco, they’re primarily flying to London and Singapore. It’s great to see the pace at which United is taking delivery of these planes.

I look forward to trying the new interiors, though I’m hoping to wait until these planes have Starlink installed, since I think that really completes the experience.

What do you make of United’s new Boeing 787-9s, and the routes they’re flying?

#6298. How to Watch the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade

As the turkey thaws and a day of cooking prep begins, an equally integral Thanksgiving tradition is Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade. Last year, 3.5 million spectators lined New York City’s streets to watch the procession of vibrant balloons and whimsical floats bob and weave through Midtown Manhattan to the beats of countless marching bands and celebrity performers. Beyond the city, a record-setting 34.3 million tuned into the NBC and Peacock broadcast, making the Emmy-winning production the year’s most-watched entertainment telecast. This year's promises to be even grander, as 2026 marks the 100th anniversary of the spectacle, which started in 1924 (though it wasn’t held from 1942 to 1944 because parade materials were reserved for wartime efforts).

“As a kid from the Bronx, it is an honor to bring this cherished tradition…to the city of New York every year,” the parade’s executive producer since 2021 Will Coss tells Condé Nast Traveler. The annual highlight for him is seeing the joyful expressions of spectators of all ages as the parade passes them by “showcasing some of the most iconic and recognizable pop culture characters and figures.”

This year marks the 99th anniversary of the Macy's Parade, an annual Thanksgiving tradition.

On the eve of the parade's centennial, the team—composed of painters, carpenters, animators, sculptures, welders, designers, engineers, and electricians—is honoring its past by way of revived classics like Felix the Cat and Underdog balloons. Ardent fans will also find a swath of newcomers that include a Fantasia-inspired Mickey, cowboy Minion, and a Peanuts duo. “The team at Macy’s Studios works year-round to make this historic parade bigger and better for our audiences every year,” Coss says. Here’s everything you need to know about the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade in 2026—all its surprises, delights, and familiar joys.

When Macy’s first debuted its one-million-square foot New York City flagship store at 34th Street between Broadway and Seventh Avenues in 1924, the retailer threw a Christmas parade on Thanksgiving morning to boost holiday sales—with a much longer route starting at 145 Street and Covent Avenue. Balloons joined the lineup in 1927, starting with Felix the Cat, and the festivities were first broadcast nationally in 1947.

These days, the festive parade follows a 2.5-mile path from the Upper East Side to Midtown Manhattan. Starting at the corner of 77th Street and Central Park West, the route heads south to Columbus Circle and then turns east, heading along 59th Street to Sixth Avenue. From there, it goes straight down Sixth Avenue to 34th Street, ending in front of Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

Clifford the Big Red Dog in Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Coss recommends arriving early for a great view. Many spectators start to gather as early as 6 a.m. along the beginning of the route on Central Park West (approach from the west) from 61st to 75th Streets. Other prime spots include the south side of 59th Street between Columbus Circle and Sixth Avenue and the entire stretch of Sixth Avenue between 38th and 59th. Spectators should be aware there is no viewing on Central Park West between 59th and 60th Streets, or anywhere south of 38th Street.

Coss also reminds those bringing children to dress warmly for the chilly weather and to be prepared to entertain young ones for a few hours while waiting to spot the first float. He suggests avoiding strollers, large bags, backpacks, and umbrellas.

In celebration of its centennial, some 100 inflatables will fly. Returning after decades are much-anticipated Felix the Cat (the parade's first character balloon, introduced in 1927) and Blue Hippopotamus (from the 1931 parade), while Hello Kitty and Underdog (who appeared in every parade from 1965 through 1984) will also make cameos. New to the scene are Bluey, Buckaroo Bob the Minion, and Snoopy persona Joe Cool with Woodstock, among others. The procession will also welcome 52 floats, 31 clown crews, nine specialty units (such as trycaloons, or balloons ridden on tricycles), seven marching bands, and five balloonicles (that’s a balloon-vehicle hybrid).

TODAY’s Savannah Guthrie, Hoda Kotb, and Al Roker will host the live broadcast of the 100th Macy’s Parade. Though this year's performance lineup has yet to be announced, the 2025 roster featured 26 celebrity performers, ranging from Colbie Caillat and Christopher Jackson to Foreigner and Taylor Momsen, complete with a performance by KPop Demon Hunters’ HUNTR/X singing voices EJAE, Audrey Nuna, and Rei Ami. As anticipation for the parade's centennial only increases, Coss says this year will “bring new surprises and delights to the iconic holiday tradition and truly celebrate this incredibly special anniversary.”

For some, the majestic Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is an official marker of the transition into the Christmas season in New York City.

Americans can watch the live telecast on both NBC and Peacock on Thursday, November 26, from 8:30 a.m. to noon in all time zones, while Telemundo will air a Spanish-language simulcast hosted by Andrea Meza, Aleyda Ortiz, and Clovis Nienow. For late risers, an encore will air starting at 2 p.m. ET/PT, and the full broadcast will also be on NBC with live audio description on Secondary Audio Program channel (SAP). Behind-the-scenes footage will be shared on social media @macys and #MacysParade via Instagram, TikTok, and Threads.

To rev up for the turkey day excitement, “Countdown to the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade” will air on Wednesday, November 25, on NBC and Peacock. The primetime special will broadcast live from the parade starting line with exclusive previews and behind-the-scenes stories from the balloons and floats.

One of the most underrated—and free—ways to experience the parade is by attending the Thanksgiving Eve balloon inflating event on Wednesday, November 25, a “time-honored tradition and special peek into the parade celebrations,” Coss says. Since 1994, the Macy’s Thanksgiving Parade has invited guests to see the process the balloons undergo to reach their larger-than-life size and scale the afternoon before Thanksgiving. Last year’s took place between 1 p.m. and 6 p.m., with the line opening at noon.

Those interested can enter at West 72nd Street and Columbus Avenue, where they’ll be guided through a security checkpoint and then can roam between West 77th and 81st Streets to view the balloons. Note that prohibited items include bags or backpacks larger than 12-by-6-by-12 inches, lawn chairs, large coolers, alcoholic beverages, chairs, weapons, drones, pets, and umbrellas; participants will be screened before entering the route.

For the latest up-to-date information, visit macys.com/parade for details on the parade and nbc.com/macys-thanksgiving-day-parade for updates on the broadcast.

#6297. How Much Cheaper Is A Turboprop To Own Than A Light Jet In 2026?

How much cheaper is it to buy and run a turboprop compared to a light jet? The answer is, unfortunately, not very clear-cut, but when evaluating private aircraft ownership, prospective buyers quickly find that even though both categories offer access to regional airfields, their financial profiles diverge sharply once operational factors are taken into account.

Choosing between a high-performance single or twin turboprop and a light jet is easily one of private aviation's most contentious decisions. The cost difference matters for corporate flight departments and high-net-worth individuals who want to optimize travel budgets without overpaying for capability they rarely use. After all, cost ultimately drives the decision.

On average, a modern executive turboprop costs 30% to 45% less to own and operate, on an hourly direct-cost basis, than a comparable light jet. Benchmark operational data from SkyCost puts popular single-engine turboprops like the Pilatus PC-12 around $1,100 per flight hour in direct operating expenses, while twin-engine turboprops like the Beechcraft King Air 350i average roughly $1,500 per hour.

By contrast, popular light jets incur noticeably higher variable costs. A Cessna Citation CJ3+ typically comes in at approximately $2,200 per flight hour, whereas an Embraer Phenom 300E runs closer to $2,600 per hour when factoring in fuel, engine reserves, and routine airframe maintenance. It may not seem like a massive increase compared to airline lease costs, but in private aviation, these differences add up significantly over many years of ownership.

The trade-off for this price gap comes down to speed and altitude. Light jets trade their higher hourly run-rate for cruise speeds exceeding 450 knots and upper-tier service ceilings above 40,000 feet (12,192 m), while turboprops trade top-end velocity for dramatic fuel efficiency and field versatility. Each aircraft has a specific use case, so if getting to the destination quickly is paramount, operators will look for the more expensive option.

To get a clearer picture of operating costs across these aircraft types, start by dividing financial commitments into two operational buckets. Looking at variable hourly costs and fixed annual overhead separately can help you compare options more clearly. While the purchase price and cabin amenities capture initial attention, recurring cash burn from fuel consumption, engine overhaul reserves, pilot salaries, and hangar fees ultimately determine total cost of ownership over a multi-year horizon.

The main variable driving the cost split between turboprops and light jets is thermodynamic efficiency. Turbine engines turning propellers burn significantly less Jet-A per hour at lower altitudes than high-bypass turbofans operating during takeoff, climb, and regional cruise. Maintenance power-by-the-hour programs and hull insurance premiums further widen the gap, as high-speed jet airframes need more complex inspections and command higher insurance underwriters' baselines.

Beechcraft King Air 350i (Twin Turboprop)

For instance, an owner flying a PC-12 for 300 hours annually can expect total direct variable expenses to hover near $330,000. Operating a Phenom 300E across that same 300-hour flight profile pushes direct variable expenses past $780,000, or an annual operational variance of nearly half a million dollars before accounting for fixed crew and hangar fees.

The rising demand for high performance single-props with GA flyers.

Corporate flight department managers and aircraft brokers will consistently emphasize matching an airframe to mission profile rather than brand prestige, even though many customers naturally gravitate to a well-known manufacturer. It is important to note that on mission legs under 400 nautical miles (740 km), light jets spend a disproportionate amount of their total flight time climbing to and descending from high cruising altitudes, preventing them from exploiting their speed advantage.

Coverage from Aeroclassifieds highlights that the block time difference on a 350-nautical-mile (648 km) trip between an aircraft like the King Air 350i and a Citation CJ3+ is often less than 15 minutes once ground taxi and air traffic control vectors are factored in. As charter broker pricing summaries from FlightStratix indicate, paying a 40% to 60% hourly premium for a light jet on short regional hops yields negligible door-to-door time savings while generating substantially higher fuel burn.

Consequently, regional charter operators and fleet managers view turboprops as unmatched tools for short-field cargo, medevac, and regional passenger transfers. Industry consensus confirms that while light jets dominate the longer stage lengths, turboprops offer superior financial retention and asset utilization for short-haul operational profiles that are far more enticing to prospective buyers.

When weighing ownership costs against aircraft performance, stage length dramatically changes the economic breakdown. For missions extending beyond 800 nautical miles (1,481 km), the speed differential of a light jet begins to outweigh the raw hourly savings of a turboprop. For that reason, the increased operational cost of light jets is far less of an issue, because it fills the operational needs far more suitably.

A Phenom 300E cruising at 464 knots completes an 800-nautical-mile journey in roughly under two hours, whereas a turboprop cruising at 290 knots requires nearly two hours and 45 minutes. Because the turboprop remains in the air for an additional 45 minutes, its total fuel burn and maintenance accumulation for that specific trip increase, narrowing the absolute cost delta per mission while consuming significantly more productive travel time. This will stand out clearly to potential buyers deciding between the two types.

Furthermore, light jets offer superior cabin pressurization differentials and fly well above regional weather layers at FL410 to FL450, offering a smoother flight experience, as noted in Simple Flying analysis. For buyers regularly flying mountain passes or transcontinental sectors with tight schedules, the extra expenditure of light jet ownership holds tangible operational value that a turboprop is not built to match.

Private jet charter rates range from $2,000 to more than $20,000 per hour, but taxes, fees, discounts, and passenger count determine the true costs.

Despite their clear financial advantages, turboprops carry specific operational caveats prospective buyers need to calculate; otherwise, they may risk buying an aircraft that doesn't fit their needs. High-altitude weather avoidance is a notable limitation because turboprops typically cruise between 25,000 feet (7,620 m) and 30,000 feet (9,144 m), placing them directly in regional turbulence and icing layers that light jets comfortably overfly, as noted by Monroe Aerospace.

Additionally, some single-engine turboprops face specific insurance and operational restrictions when conducting commercial night or overwater operations in certain international jurisdictions. Twin-engine turboprops like the King Air 350i mitigate single-engine redundancy concerns but consume significantly more fuel, narrowing their hourly cost advantage over small entry-level light jets like the Citation M2.

Lower cruise ceilings place aircraft in weather and turbulence

Advanced de-icing boots and tactical radar routing

Passenger hesitation over single-engine oceanic routes

Opt for twin-engine platforms or dual-generator redundancy

Propeller overhaul cycles add recurring airframe expenses

Enroll in comprehensive prop and engine coverage programs

Buyers will also need to account for propeller overhaul schedules. While turboprop engines, such as the ubiquitous Pratt & Whitney PT6, are renowned for extreme reliability, propeller blade inspections and governor overhauls are recurring maintenance line items absent from jet turbofans.

Ultimately, choosing between a turboprop and a light jet comes down to an honest assessment of annual flight distance and mission length. For operators whose typical routes fall under 500 nautical miles (926 km), a turboprop delivers most of a light jet's practical utility at a noticeably lower share of total operating cost.

For corporate flight departments seeking maximum runway availability, including access to grass strips, unpaved runways, and short mountain airfields, platforms like the Pilatus PC-12 or King Air 350i are truly unbeatable economic tools. However, if routine missions need rapid point-to-point transit over 800 nautical miles (1,481 km) or require flying above severe weather, the higher acquisition and hourly costs of a light jet are a justified investment.

As private aviation operating costs evolve throughout 2026, turboprops continue to solidify their position as the industry's most cost-effective business tools. Evaluating true annual flight hours against stage-length metrics helps ensure buyers select an airframe that balances operational comfort with disciplined financial performance, rather than ending up wishing they had chosen differently.

#6295. 8 Dreamy Hotels Our NYC Editors Are Booking This Winter

If there’s one thing the editors at Condé Nast Traveler love, it’s weekendmaxxing. We’re all about scouting the very best hotels upstate, or catching a quick flight to Miami, all before returning back to our New York City office by Monday. The art of the weekend trip becomes especially important in the wintertime, when the city closes its blinds and hibernates until spring. This is when an off-season jaunt to the Rockaways, or a hideaway in a Berkshires lodge, becomes all the more appealing. Essentially, we love a trip where you can get cozy somewhere else—because sometimes all you need is a simple change of scenery to tackle the winter blues.

From wellness sanctuaries nestled in the Catskills to country retreats in New England, these are the hotels our editors are eyeing for when the weather turns brisk, all within a few hours of NYC or a short flight away.

Where are you staying? Mayflower Inn & Spa, Washington, Connecticut

What drew you to this hotel? I visited Mayflower Inn back in spring 2024 with one of my best friends while she was pregnant with her second baby, and I’ve been dying to go back ever since. I don’t know if I’ve ever felt more relaxed than I did while there—we spent hours in the spa, chatted by the firepits, stuffed ourselves with farm-fresh meals, and feasted our eyes on some incredible interior design.

What are you eating? I won’t be leaving the hotel for food, that’s for sure. I’m always impressed by the F&B at Auberge properties, and the Mayflower Inn was no exception. The Garden Room offers creative but approachable seasonal cuisine from breakfast through dinner (don’t skip the burger), and the Tap Room is where you’ll find a tavern-style food menu plus a mixologist slinging delicious cocktails and mocktails.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The Mayflower Inn is located in Washington, Connecticut, a small town in Litchfield County, a region beloved by many of my colleagues. Next time I visit the hotel, I’ll have to make a few stops along the way to see what all the fuss is about.

Where are you staying? Urban Cowboy Lodge, Big Indian, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Urban Cowboy Lodge has been on my weekend getaway wish list for years, and there’s something about it in winter that feels particularly charming—maybe it’s the delightful snow-filled view from the bathtub (pictured above) that drew me in. I’m imagining myself curled up with a good book by the lounge’s fireplace, draped in a Pendleton blanket, then dipping into the aforementioned copper clawfoot bathtubs. At just about two-and-a-half hours north of Manhattan, it’s a not-too-far excursion I’m saving for when I really need a break from winter in the city.

What are you eating? Phoenicia Diner, of course. I’m also keen to try out some of the many craft beers at Ralph’s Bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I’m not a skier, so in the winter, heading to the Catskills comes with more of a stay-indoors-and-get-cozy vibe for me. Besides a pit stop at Phoenicia Diner, I imagine the furthest I’ll trek is over to the sauna and bowling alley.

Where are you staying? The Rockaway Hotel & Spa, Rockaway Park, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Aside from the ocean views—poetically perfect for New York in the winter—The Rockaway is home to one of my favorite wellness scenes in the city. The space transforms its outdoor pool area (which, in the summer months, is home to outdoor concerts and DJ-led pool parties) into the cozy Winter Pool House. The space gets decked out with outdoor cedar barrel saunas and the softest plush robes to wear while you transition to the heated outdoor pool. The warm water mixed with the ice-cold breeze coming off the nearby coastline is glorious.

What are you eating? I’ll be heading to Margie’s—the mood-lit hotel lobby restaurant—and ordering a juicy cheeseburger and a frosty gin martini. What better way to warm your soul?

What do you hope to get up to in the area? The beauty of visiting this hotel in winter? No summer beach crowds. I’ll likely bundle up, head to the beach for some meditation, and head right back to my cozy room at The Rockaway to soak up the views even more.

Where are you staying? Wildflower Farms, Auberge Collection, Gardiner, New York

What drew you to this hotel? I’ve had Wildflower Farms on my wish list for the past few years. Every photo I see of the property on Instagram looks so dreamy. It feels like a true escape from the city—quiet, cozy, and restful. Located in New York’s Hudson Valley, it’s a quick 90-minute drive from NYC, making it a convenient pick for couples or families seeking an easy getaway.

What are you eating? I’m most eager to have coffee and pastries around the fire at the Great Porch, Wildflower’s open-air communal space with sprawling views of the Shawangunk Ridge. And of course, I’ll be dining at the resort’s on-site restaurant, Clay, where the rustic American menu is full of seasonal ingredients from local farms.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? I usually try to pack as many activities and must-try coffee shops and restaurants as possible into my trip itinerary, but Wildflower Farms encourages you to slow down. You’ll find me at Thistle, the resort’s on-site spa where hand-harvested, small-batch oils and scrubs are used during tailored treatments.

Where are you staying? Inness, Accord, New York

What drew you to this hotel? Inness is resplendent in the summer, so I’ve always been keen to see a different side of it come hunker-down weather. Its cabins are certainly primed for rest, thanks to the fireplaces, but there’s also the outdoor pit with prime-time views of the Catskill Mountains decked in snow. I also love the central farmhouse, where cozy seats call out for a great book and a hot cocoa. And if you can drag yourself out, which you should, there are loads of hikes and walks, including those along the Ashokan Reservoir, which is one of my favorite spots.

What are you eating? Stacks of pancakes; comfort-food entrées like risottos; a round of Dorato Negronis at the bar.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Spending the afternoons shopping and dining in some of my favorite nearby towns, like Kingston and Woodstock.

Where are you staying? Four Seasons Hotel at The Surf Club, Surfside, Florida

What drew you to this hotel? When one of my best friends announced she was celebrating her 30th birthday in Miami, a city I’ve shockingly never been to, the first place I thought of was the Four Seasons Hotel at the Surf Club; I remember reading about its incredible celebrity guest history, which includes everyone from Frank Sinatra to Elizabeth Taylor.

What are you eating? Perhaps we’d start with a toast at the on-site Champagne Bar, then move on over to dinner at Lido for seafood-inspired pastas.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Laze around by the pool, enjoy the quieter beaches of Surfside, and maybe stroll through the Rubell Museum in Allapattah.

Where are you staying? Tourists, North Adams, Massachusetts

What drew you to this hotel? I love heading north of the city in the colder months—leaning in and getting even colder and cozier. And the words “reimagined motor lodge” are another form of catnip for me. I love the sense of nostalgia paired with very plush, updated interiors, ideal for hiding out for a wintery weekend.

What are you eating? I’d carve out time for the hotel’s restaurant, the Airport Room, ideally timed to one of the chef pop-ups they do—though given the three-and-a-half-hour drive from New York City, I’d probably also plot out an en route lunch in Kingston as well.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Wintery hikes on the nearby trails, lots of reading by the fireplace, and maybe some of the arts and crafts activities—why not.

Where are you staying? Eastwind, Windham, New York

What drew you to this hotel? When I first caught sight of Eastwind, I was really into the property’s sprawl—there are different types of accommodations (cabins, hotel-style rooms), and everything is wound together via a small trail system lined with fairy lights, from the beer garden to the main house. It feels like a really great spot to get away from the noise of New York City.

What are you eating? The on-site restaurant, Dandie’s, serves up barbecue in a cozy, window-lined space—get some house-made gelato for dessert. And definitely make a detour for brunch at Phoenicia Diner on your way back to the city.

What do you hope to get up to in the area? Stop by Harriman State Park for a hike to stretch your legs on the way north. Once you’re there, you’ve got skiing options (Windham Mountain Club), more hiking trails (The Windham Path), and indoor activities (Helsinki Hudson for music lovers; Olana Historic Estate for museum enthusiasts).

As the most discerning, up-to-the-minute voice in all things travel, Condé Nast Traveler is the global citizen’s bible and muse, offering both inspiration and vital intel. We understand that time is the greatest luxury, which is why Condé Nast Traveler mines its network of experts and influencers so that you never waste a meal, a drink, or a hotel stay wherever you are in the world.

#6294. American Airlines business class to Prague for just 55,000 points: Here's how you can do it, too

It's not often that you can fly from the U.S. to Europe in business class for just 55,000 points, but sometimes, deals are out there — especially if you use American Airlines AAdvantage miles or Atmos Rewards points.

I found a great award using Atmos Rewards Points on American Airlines' newly resumed nonstop flight from Philadelphia to Prague. As mentioned, I paid just 55,000 points (and $5.60 in taxes and fees).

I'll get into some detail on how to find these kinds of deals, but first, let's talk a bit more about this flight.

I wanted the chance to check American's European service and compare the business-class products on the older 787-8s (like the one I flew to Prague) and the new premium-heavy 787-9P planes I've flown to London.

American Airlines relaunched its Prague service in May of this year. It had previously served the route for a few years, in 2018 and 2019, before abandoning it during the coronavirus pandemic.

AA now operates the route seasonally during the busy summer period, from May to October, between Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) and Václav Havel Airport Prague (PRG). The airline has already said the route will return for summer 2027.

Another good sign for the route: AA is adding more European destinations from Philadelphia next summer, including Vienna and Porto, Portugal. American Airlines calls Prague part of "the airline's Central European network."

I kicked off my journey with a few days in Philadelphia before heading to the airport.

A post shared by Clint Page Henderson (@clintpage1)

American Airlines' Flagship Lounge at Philadelphia opened in May of last year, after years of delays. It is a lovely space to spend a few hours before your flight, though it can get crowded at times. I could access it because I was flying long-haul business class.

A great American Airlines agent named Thomas Doersam, who has been with AA for 38 years, gave me a quick tour of the Flagship and the adjacent Admirals Club.

The Flagship lounge (American's fifth) is near Gate A15, where AA's long-haul flights depart. Eligible passengers flying long-haul business class can use the Flagship Lounge, which includes those in business class on these flights.

Others have access to the Admiral's Club just across the way.

It has been lovely to see American Airlines invest so much in its lounge product. In fact, a sixth Flagship lounge was announced for Charlotte, along with a massive new Admiral's Club that will clock in at more than 40,000 square feet.

I had seat 1L on this 11-year-old Boeing 787 Dreamliner, with the ship number N806AA. This is a legacy interior that will eventually be phased out.

TPG reported that these planes will receive new Flagship business-class suites and a full cabin refresh, though AA didn't say when that would start.

I was on the smallest Dreamliner variant, and the business-class cabin had just 20 seats in a 1-2-1 configuration. All the seats had aisle access.

These lie-flat seats were 21 inches wide and featured American's version of the Safran Concept D seat (formerly known as Zodiac).

I found them to be fairly comfortable, if a bit narrow, during the overnight journey.

Some flyers complain about these seats since some are rear-facing. The seats are attached to each other, and some people say they feel it when the person seated next to them moves. (Some flyers even refer to them as "rocking chairs.") It never bothered me on my previous trips in these seats, and it didn't this time either, even though I was in the first row.

There were also 28 premium economy seats on this plane — a comfortable and potentially more affordable option.

There were also 186 economy seats, including 48 Main Cabin Extra seats.

Inflight entertainment was provided by a 15-inch screen that could pop out with the push of a button. There were plenty of shows and movies to choose from.

Still, these screens are showing their age, especially now that more innovative 4K screens are rolling out across many fleets (including American's).

Inflight Wi-Fi was provided by Panasonic and cost $35 for the full flight. It was just OK, and I was glad I wasn't relying on it for important work. American Airlines will begin rolling out Starlink Wi-Fi in 2027, but in the meantime, representatives say there are plans to improve Wi-Fi speeds on its 787s, too. I expect the overall tech picture to improve dramatically over the next few years.

The airlines have had some pretty major connection problems recently.

Remember, these seats are a decade old and show a bit of wear and tear. Still, it's a comfortable cabin, and because there are so few business-class seats, it does feel a bit special.

My seat had plenty of other bells and whistles that I won't go into too much detail here, but I appreciated the overhead air vents and some of the nooks and crannies for storing items.

I also loved American's newer bedding. The zipper bag held a large blanket and pillow; mattress pads were also available at each seat. While it may not look as fancy as United's Saks bedding, I found it super comfortable.

Amenity kits were made in honor of the World Cup, featuring a clear design filled with standard amenities.

You can read more details about the hard product on these planes in the reviews linked above, but I think, in general, I'm a bigger fan than most when it comes to the seats on these Dreamliners.

As I mentioned, I don't mind the older 787s, but there's no question: American's new 787Ps are a fresher product.

TPG's Eric Rosen and I reviewed the new product last year, and we were both pretty impressed. AA unveiled its all-new Flagship Suite business class in May, and Eric and I were eager to experience the new planes and try out the Flagship Suite Preferred and Flagship Suite business-class seats. He took a flight from London to Chicago, and I was flying from Chicago to London.

Unlike the 787-8s, which have just 20 business-class seats, the new 787Ps have a whopping 51 Flagship Suites.

It will be interesting to see whether AA expands the business-class and premium-class cabins during the retrofit of these planes.

You can really see the differences in the photos below.

Aside from the size of the business-class cabin, the biggest difference is the sliding doors on the 787Ps.

There are eight Flagship Suite Preferred seats on the 787Ps — an upgraded version of the new suites with additional space.

Finally, the new 787Ps have updated designs, more storage, a lounger mode on the seat controls, wireless charging and dramatically better 17.3-inch IFE screens with both Bluetooth and touchscreen capability.

While I love the new planes, I wouldn't choose a more expensive redemption just to fly them.

I had a great crew on my flight to Prague, with friendly service and generally good food and beverage.

Not only did we get a predeparture beverage, but service was prompt, friendly and efficient.

Dinner started with warmed nuts and a beverage of your choice. Appetizers included a small romaine salad, along with citrus-poached shrimp and ceviche-style fish. For a main course, I finally tried American Airlines' new "sliders and fries." It was only available as a pre-order, but I'm so glad I took the time to select it because it was delicious.

Dessert was the classic sundae which I ordered with extra whipped cream. How can you resist?

Breakfast was yogurt with granola and fruit that AA calls a "fresh fruit bowl" — perfectly fine for an airplane breakfast. The best part was the multiple cappuccinos I drank. (American brought back espresso drinks in business class in 2025, and I've made full use of the perk.)

I even received a thank-you note from my flight attendant, Daniel — a rare and lovely touch that I don't often find with U.S. airlines.

As I mentioned, I scored my business-class seat for just 55,000 Atmos Rewards points and $5.60 in taxes and fees. Remember, you can book American Airlines flights using Alaska points, and it can often be an even better deal.

Related: Why American Airlines AAdvantage has become my most valuable rewards currency

Often, when a new route is launched or resumed, you'll see airlines make award tickets more available than usual. That's just what happened here, when the airline made business-class redemptions on both Prague and its newly resumed Budapest route widely available, even on partners like Alaska.

When a new route starts or an old one resumes, check award availability as soon as the seats go on sale.

To start, flexibility is key. If you can be flexible on dates and destinations, the world literally opens up. Let the deal guide where you go.

Try booking as soon as schedules open up. For carriers like Japan Airlines, you'll find the best availability 11 months in advance, as that's when seats open to partner airlines.

Award search tools have also become a huge part of my process. Seats.aero, ExpertFlyer (owned by TPG parent company, Red Ventures) and Roame.travel are my favorites. I also love the award tool Points Path, which sits on my browser, so I see award availability when I search on Google Flights.

American Airlines also has a great tool that I use to find deals. I use the airline's award search calendar to find business-class seats for months at a time. Here's an example of that for flights from New York City to Rome, Paris and Amsterdam for next year.

I wouldn't book any of these because of the high taxes and fees for partner awards, but it at least gives an idea of what's out there.

My last suggestion: Keep checking flights in case the price drops.

Sometimes, it can make sense to lock in a coach redemption and then keep checking to see if business class opens up at a reasonable rate.

If you are willing to be brave, more availability often opens up at the last minute, and you can find some great deals.

#6293. Amex Platinum Card Review: Benefits & Credits That Easily Justify The Fee

While premium cards are incredibly popular nowadays, this is really a market that Amex started, with the American Express Platinum Card®. It takes some effort to maximize the card’s perks, but if you’re willing to put in the time, the value is potentially incredible.

This is my in-depth Amex Platinum Card review, so let me talk about the card’s value proposition, and the perks that make the Amex Platinum worthwhile. This is a card you should get for the rich benefits that it offers, including the lounge access, credits, and elite status, and not necessarily a card you should spend a lot of money on under normal circumstances, since there are more rewarding cards for that.

Link: Learn more about the American Express Platinum Card®

Before I get into my full Amex Platinum Card review, I want to go over the card’s key details at a glance. The card has such a long list of statement credits that it’s impossible to cover those briefly, so keep reading below to see those, as they could be worth up to thousands of dollars annually. To keep the list to non-statement credit details, here’s what you can expect:

I also put together my pros and cons of the Amex Platinum Card:

The Amex Platinum Card potentially has a huge welcome offer, though the card also has a high annual fee. So let’s cover all those details first, including card eligibility, since these are major factors cardmembers consider when applying for a card.

The Amex Platinum Card currently has the following lucrative welcome bonus offer: You may be eligible for as high as 175,000 Membership Rewards® Points after spending $12,000 in eligible purchases on your new Card in your first 6 months of Membership. Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer.

Welcome offers vary and you may not be eligible for an offer, so you’ll want to start the application, and then you’ll see what kind of an offer is available to you.

Based on my latest miles & points valuations, Membership Rewards points are worth 1.7 cents each, so depending on the offer you’re eligible for, this could be worth almost $3,000 in value. That’s pretty stellar, especially for a card that offers so much ongoing value after your first year.

The welcome bonus on the Amex Platinum Card isn’t available to those who currently have the card, or those who have had the card in the past (so the card has a “once in a lifetime” rule). If you’ve had the card in the past you’re still eligible to be approved, you just won’t get the bonus.

Note that this is a hybrid card and not a credit card, meaning that having this card won’t count toward Amex’s limit of five credit cards per person. Make sure you consider all of Amex’s standard application restrictions before applying.

Eligibility for this card is otherwise unrelated to having any other type of card that’s not an Amex Platinum, so lots of people should be eligible for the offer.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee. Even among premium cards, this is among the highest annual fees out there, though for many people, the perks will more than offset the fee.

If you want to add authorized users to the card, you’ll pay $195 each (Rates & Fees). Fortunately there are some solid perks for authorized users, including lounge access, so some people might find that adding them is worthwhile.

As you’d expect of a premium travel card, the Amex Platinum has no foreign transaction fees (Rates & Fees). This means you can use it abroad without racking up fees, though it’s not usually the best card for maximizing everyday spending on categories like dining.

Personally, I think the Amex Platinum Card is worth having for the benefits it offers, though it’s not a card that I think is worth spending much money on, with limited exceptions.

Some other Amex cards offer big bonus categories. For example, the American Express® Gold Card (learn more) offers 4x Membership Rewards points at restaurants worldwide (on up to $50,000 in purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points) and at U.S. supermarkets (on up to $25,000 of spending per calendar year, and then 1x points), which is extremely lucrative.

Unfortunately, the Amex Platinum Card isn’t as generous in that regard. However, there are still some useful bonus categories…

The best bonus category on the Amex Platinum Card is 5x points on airfare purchased directly from airlines or through American Express Travel® (on up to $500,000 of flight purchases per calendar year, and then 1x points). This is spectacular, and it makes it the best card for airfare purchases, in my opinion.

Officially booking through online travel agencies (except amextravel.com) wouldn’t earn you bonus points, though in practice it may still sometimes code for 5x points. That’s because often online travel agencies still have the airline bill you directly when you book flights through them.

I value Membership Rewards points at 1.7 cents each, so to me, that’s the equivalent of an 8.5% return on airfare spending, which is incredible.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers 5x Membership Rewards points on prepaid hotels that are booked through Amex Travel. As a general rule of thumb, this isn’t worth it. That’s because you’re usually not earning loyalty points with your preferred hotel program when you book through Amex Travel, so that’s quite an opportunity cost.

The exception is Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, where prepaid reservations earn 5x points. That can be a good deal because of the perks you get, and also because you still earn points with your preferred hotel loyalty program. You can also combine this with the card’s annual hotel credit to really maximize value. I’ll talk more about that in a bit.

The above are the only bonus categories — otherwise, the Amex Platinum Card offers 1x points per dollar spent, which isn’t especially good. There are other cards offering 1.5x-2x points per dollar spent, so I would much rather put my spending on those cards, or on another card that’s best for everyday spending.

The Amex Platinum Card earns Membership Rewards points. This is one of the major transferable points currencies, and is a favorite points currency for many. While I love Membership Rewards, I’d say that not everyone should be earning these points.

The best way to redeem your Amex points is to transfer them to one of the Membership Rewards airline or hotel partners. Points can be transferred to the below airline partners and hotel partners.

The reason this represents such a good option is that you can get outsized value toward premium airfare, especially for travel in first and business class. These tickets are often super expensive if paying cash, while they can be a good deal with points.

For example, I frequently transfer my Amex Membership Rewards points to Air France-KLM, and then redeem 60,000 points for business class across the Atlantic. Best of all, there are sometimes transfer bonuses of up to 25-30%, which lowers my real “out of pocket” in terms of Amex points even further.

I’d note that while you can redeem Membership Rewards points toward the cost of merchandise or gift cards, or to pay off your statement, these aren’t good uses of your points. You’ll typically get less than one cent of value per point, so that’s not how I’d redeem them.

I’d recommend earning Membership Rewards points if your primary interest is transferring points to partner programs.

The Amex Platinum Card really shines when it comes to its credits, as the card potentially offers thousands of dollars in annual credits. As you can imagine, for some people this alone will more than justify the annual fee. The catch is that there are some hurdles to using all of these, so don’t consider most of these credits to be worth face value.

However, I’d argue that it’s quite easy to recoup your entire annual fee on these credits alone. So let’s take a look at what you need to know about these credits, and how you can maximize them. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $600 per year in hotel credits. This is a semi-annual credit, so you get a $300 credit in January through June, and a $300 credit in July through December.

This is actually a pretty easy perk to use — just book a prepaid hotel through Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® (no minimum stay) or The Hotel Collection (two night minimum stay) through American Express Travel®, and you can receive up to a $300 credit semi-annually. Effective January 1, 2027, Fine Hotels + Resorts® bookings will require a minimum two-night stay to be eligible for the Hotel Credit.

If you ask me, this perk alone can help recoup most of the card’s annual fee. So a major point in deciding whether this card makes sense is crunching the numbers as to whether you can get full value from this.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $400 per year in Resy credits, and enrollment is required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $100 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward dining at eligible U.S. Resy restaurants.

There are no hoops you have to jump through, so as long as you dine at an eligible Resy restaurant and pay with your card, you can receive the statement credit. Personally, I’d consider this benefit to be worth close to face value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in digital entertainment credits, with enrollment being required. This comes in the form of a $25 monthly statement credit on eligible purchases or subscriptions with any of the following:

I’d consider this to be quite valuable, since there’s an impressive variety of partners with which you can maximize this perk.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Lululemon credits, with enrollment being required. This is a quarterly credit, so the idea is that you receive up to $75 worth of statement credits each calendar quarter toward purchases at Lululemon stores in the U.S. If you’re in the market for some athleisure wear, this is a great option.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $300 per year in Equinox credits, and enrollment is required. This comes in the form of up to $300 in statement credits each year on a digital or club membership at Equinox. If you’d otherwise pay for an Equinox membership, this is a great perk, while otherwise, it’s probably of limited value.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a $300 credit when purchasing a SoulCycle bike. This credit can be used toward the purchase of a SoulCycle at-home bike, and it can be used for the purchase of up to 15 bikes per year.

You need to make the entire purchase of a bike in one transaction on your Amex Platinum Card in order to qualify for these savings. Suffice to say that this will be of limited value to most cardmembers.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $219 per year in CLEAR credits. When using your card to pay for a CLEAR membership, you’ll receive statement credits of up to $219 per calendar year. For those not familiar with CLEAR, this company can save you time at security, by allowing you to use your biometric data to skip the ID check.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in airline fee credits, which can be used toward airline incidentals and fees. The credit is offered every calendar year, so it follows a strict January 1 through December 31 calendar.

Every year you can designate on which airline you want to receive the credit, of the following:

You can change your airline selection in January of each year. If you don’t change your selection, then you automatically keep the same airline choice as the previous year.

Unfortunately, you can’t use your credit toward the following:

Airline tickets, upgrades, mileage points purchases, mileage points transfer fees, gift cards, duty free purchases, and award tickets are not deemed to be incidental fees.

This is particularly useful for airline ticket change fees (of which there are few nowadays), baggage fees, and other costs you may incur with an airline. Personally, this is something I have no trouble maxing out.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Oura Ring credits. This is valid if you use your card to purchase an Oura Ring through ouraring.com, and enrollment is required. I’d say this is very niche, but if you’re in the market for this product, it has the potential to be valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $200 per year in Uber credits. The way this is broken up, you get a $15 credit per month, and then in December, you get a total of $35 in credits. You can use this either for rides with Uber in the US, or for food with Uber Eats in the US.

To activate this benefit, you need to enter your Amex Platinum Card card number on your Uber account, and then you should see the benefit unlocked. You’ll see an amount added to your Uber Cash balance every month, and the discount will automatically be applied to the first eligible ride or food delivery.

An Amex Card must be selected as the payment method for your Uber or Uber Eats transaction to redeem the Amex Uber Cash benefit

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $120 in statement credits each calendar year after purchasing an auto-renewing Uber One membership with the card. This is separate from the card’s $200 annual Uber Cash benefit.

An Uber One membership offers all kinds of benefits for rides with Uber and deliveries with Uber Eats, so if you use the platform with any frequency, this is pretty valuable.

The Amex Platinum Card offers up to $12.95 per month in credits toward a Walmart+ membership, which covers the full membership cost. Enrollment is required. (Up to $12.95 plus applicable local sales tax. Plus Ups not eligible.) With Walmart+, you can receive free deliveries on groceries or get savings at gas stations or on video streaming.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Global Entry or TSA PreCheck statement credit every four years. Simply charge the membership fee to your card, and it will be automatically reimbursed. It’s worth getting Global Entry, which has a $120 application fee compared to PreCheck’s $85, because it includes TSA PreCheck membership too.

It doesn’t matter who the fee is being paid for, as long as you charge it to your eligible card.

The Amex Platinum Card offers one of the most comprehensive lounge access benefits of any card. This is called the Global Lounge Collection, and it offers access to over 1,550 airport lounges across 140 countries for eligible cardmembers. This includes proprietary Amex lounges, as well as access to lounges run by other airlines and companies.

Before I go through the details, let me mention that Lufthansa lounge access has been cut as of October 1, 2026, which is why I’m not including it in the list, though that used to be a benefit.

Amex is well known for its Centurion Lounges, and the Amex Platinum Card can get you into these lounges. These are significantly better than what you’ll find in most U.S. airline lounges, with a solid selection of hot food and cocktails.

Currently, U.S. locations include Atlanta, Charlotte, Dallas, Denver, Houston, Las Vegas, Los Angeles, Miami, New York JFK, New York LaGuardia, Philadelphia, Phoenix, San Francisco, Seattle, and Washington, with more to come. There are also Centurion Lounges in Amsterdam, Hong Kong, London, and Tokyo, among other international destinations.

You can access these lounges up to three hours before your flight’s departure (if you’re connecting, then the three-hour limit doesn’t apply). Please note that you’re only eligible to bring in guests on a complimentary basis if you spend at least $75,000 per calendar year on the card.

The Amex Platinum Card also offers access to the Delta Sky Club, with some limitations. Card members can receive access within three hours of a departing or arriving flight, and must present their card, a boarding pass showing a confirmed reservation for an eligible Delta flight, and a government-issued ID.

Eligible cards issued in the United States receive 10 visits to the Delta Sky Club each year, to be used from February 1 until January 31 of the next calendar year, with all visits within a 24-hour period counting as a single visit. It’s also possible to earn an unlimited number of visits by spending $75,000 in eligible purchases on a card account in a calendar year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers a Priority Pass™ membership, which gives you access to lounges around the world. You can bring up to two guests into these lounges. While these aren’t the most exciting and high quality lounges, there’s no denying that this gives you access to a comprehensive collection of lounges.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to Plaza Premium Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card, and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring one guest with you at no additional cost. This is hugely valuable, as Plaza Premium has dozens of lounges around the world, which are among the highest quality contract lounges you’ll find.

The Amex Platinum Card offers access to the growing network of Escape Lounges. Just present your Amex Platinum Card and you’ll be admitted, and you can even bring in guests.

Beyond the annual credits that potentially more than justify the annual fee, as well as an incredible lounge access program, the Amex Platinum Card also offers status with three hotel loyalty programs, status with three rental car loyalty programs, access to a program that gets you valuable hotel perks, and discounts on many premium cabin airline tickets. (Enrollment is required for select benefits)

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Hilton Gold elite status for as long as they have the card. This status is useful, and offers the following perks:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive complimentary Marriott Gold status for as long as they have the card, which offers the following perks, among other things:

Those with the Amex Platinum Card receive Leaders Club Sterling status from Leading Hotels of the World. Leading Hotels of the World is a collection of independent, luxury properties, so this offers perks at some properties that don’t otherwise participate in major global hotel groups.

This status typically requires $5,000 in annual spending at these hotels and offers perks such as five pre-arrival upgrades per year.

The Amex Platinum Card offers Hertz President’s Circle elite status, which is Hertz’s top-tier status. Your status is valid as long as you remain a cardmember; you just need to enroll. This should take the pain out of renting cars and offers the following perks:

The Amex Platinum Card offers National Emerald Club Executive status. You have to enroll to take advantage of this, and it’s valid for as long as you have your card. National is my favorite rental car company, and Executive status lets you pick out your car from the lot, and skip the counter altogether.

The Amex Platinum also offers Avis Preferred Plus status. Once you enroll, you’ll get this mid-tier status level with the rental car company and qualify for complimentary upgrades when available, a 25% points bonus, and a dedicated reservation and customer service line. You also get access to a discount code that can save you up to 25% off qualifying rentals.

With the Platinum Member Airfares program (formerly known as the International Airline Program), you can save on the cost of international first class, business class, and premium economy airfare, on around two dozen airlines. This typically provides discounts even on already discounted tickets, so is a spectacular value.

If you book paid international premium cabin travel with any frequency, this could cover the card’s annual fee over and over.

With the Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts® program, you can receive extra perks for stays at over 1,900 luxury hotels around the world. These benefits include the following:

Best of all, the rate is typically in line with the best available rate. Having the Amex Platinum Card gets you access to this, and if you prepay your reservation, you even earn 5x points. You can even stack this with the card’s up to $600 annual hotel credit.

The Amex Platinum Card offers several travel insurance benefits that can add extra peace of mind. You’ll want to consult the card’s benefits guide for the exact terms and any caps and exclusions, but here’s a quick overview:

Up to $500 per Covered Trip that is delayed for more than 6 hours; and 2 claims per Eligible Card per 12 consecutive month period. Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. The card also offers an extended warranty protection benefit as well as purchase, return, and cell phone protection.

Extended warranty and purchase protection: Eligibility and Benefit level varies by Card. Terms, Conditions, and Limitations Apply. Please visit americanexpress.com/benefitsguide for more details. Underwritten by AMEX Assurance Company.

What benefits do authorized users on the Amex Platinum Card get? They receive most of the same perks as primary cardmembers.

This includes all the lounge access perks, access to Amex Fine Hotels + Resorts®, Hilton and Marriott Gold status, Leading Hotels of the World Sterling status, access to the Amex International Airline Program, additional Global Entry/TSA PreCheck credits, and more.

The main thing that authorized users aren’t getting is incremental credits, so they’re not receiving extra airline fee credits, digital entertainment credits, Uber credits, etc.

Of course there’s never going to be any “one size fits all” answer as to whether a card makes sense, since we all value perks differently. However, speaking only for myself, I’d argue that the Amex Platinum Card is rather easy to justify.

To start, let’s just take a look at the credits. Personally, I’m able to get full value out of the $600 annual hotel credit, $400 annual Resy credit, $300 annual digital entertainment credit, $200 annual airline fee credit, and $200 annual Uber credit. That’s $1,700 in value right there, and it actually doesn’t take much effort for me to maximize that.

That also says nothing of all the other perks offered by the card, from the bonus points on airfare, to the lounge access, and more. So yeah, I’m really finding this card to be pretty great. Let me emphasize that in 2027 the hotel credit will be harder to maximize, so I’ll need to assess how much value I get out of that. But even if you drop that benefit entirely, I’m still getting $1,100 in value from the other credits.

Everyone has to crunch the numbers for themselves, but I think the math works out very nicely on this product. But that’s not the case for everyone. So who should skip the Amex Platinum Card?

If it won’t be easy for you to get full value out of the card’s many travel and statement credits — or even if you just don’t want to be troubled with keeping track of so many credits to prevent leaving value on the table — the Amex Platinum may not be the card for you. Credit card fatigue is a real problem!

It’s also not a great card for everyday spending, since it doesn’t earn bonus rewards on categories like dining. I’ve written a more detailed post specifically addressing the question of whether the Amex Platinum is worth it, so I recommend checking that out.

This also brings me to the next section, which is the best Amex Platinum alternatives.

There are several premium cards to choose from nowadays, so it always makes sense to look at what the competition is offering. Let’s look at a few popular alternatives to the Amex Platinum.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve® (learn more) is the other premium card heavy hitter, with a slightly lower annual fee of $795. I have a full post comparing the Amex Platinum and Chase Sapphire Reserve — my verdict is that both cards are worth having, but if you can only pick one, the Sapphire Reserve is better for lazy optimizers while the Amex Platinum is better for those willing to put some real work into optimizing all the card’s benefits.

Here’s an overview of the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s standout features. It’s no slouch when it comes to perks, but its list of benefits and statement credits is considerably shorter than the Amex Platinum Card’s. Specifically:

If you take full advantage of the Amex Platinum’s main statement credits for travel and dining, it has the potential to offer more value than the Chase Sapphire Reserve. But the Chase Sapphire Reserve’s earning rates are better for maximizing everyday purchases, and you might prefer having fewer “coupon book” style benefits to keep track of.

In my opinion, the Amex Gold Card (learn more) is one of the most rewarding cards out there. At $325 (Rates & Fees), its annual fee is significantly lower than the Amex Platinum Card’s, and while it doesn’t have as many benefits, it’s a better choice for everyday spending, especially if you eat out frequently.

Here are the highlights of the Amex Gold:

The Amex Gold Card can’t beat the Platinum when it comes to travel perks, but if your main goal is earning as many Amex points as possible on your spending, it could be a more useful everyday pick.

The Capital One Venture X Rewards Credit Card (learn more) is another premium card with an annual fee that’s one step down from the Amex Platinum — in this case, it’s $395. I find this card to offer strong value, and it’s much simpler than the Amex Platinum Card:

The travel credit and anniversary bonus miles help justify the annual fee, and while 2x miles isn’t the highest everyday spending rate, it’s a better base than 1x points with the Amex Platinum. It’s also worth comparing Amex points with Capital One miles to see which currency you prefer before making a final decision.

The Amex Platinum Card has a $895 annual fee and a much longer list of credits than it used to. This isn’t a card that you should get for the return on spending it offers, but instead, it’s a card to get for all of the perks and credits that it offers.

While the $895 annual fee is obviously steep, personally I’m able to get outsized value thanks to all the credits offered, which offer significant value. And that says nothing of the bonus points on airfare, the lounge access, and more.

So even if you haven’t been able to make the math on this card work in the past, it might be time to give it another look.

#6292. Insanely Modern: Inside The Boeing 777X's Secret Upper Deck

Arnold O. A. Pinto | Shutterstock, Simple Flying

The Boeing 777X is one of the most high-profile aircraft development programs of the past decade. The aircraft's design is incredibly innovative, featuring folding wingtips, a wider cabin, larger windows, and a quieter, more refined long-haul experience. One of the aircraft's most fascinating features is something that most passengers may never even notice.

There is a hidden space above the main cabin that gives the aircraft a kind of secret upper deck. It is not a Boeing 747-style second floor made for travelers, and it is not any kind of flashy onboard lounge. Instead, it is a tightly engineered overhead rest area built into the crown of the jet, ultimately designed to keep pilots rested, connected, and ready on the world's longest flights.

That ultimately makes the aircraft more than just an aviation curiosity. In many ways, this concealed upstairs compartment captures what the 777X is really about. The jet combines visible passenger comforts with unseen operational upgrades that matter just as much.

Boeing has marketed the 777X as a next-generation flagship with a more spacious interior and improved cabin environment, but the plane's hidden upper spaces show just how much modern airline design now revolves around overall endurance, efficiency, and crew performance as well. For ultra-long-haul operators, the 777X's secret upper deck may be one of its smartest innovations.

Before we start diving into the specifics of the crew rest area, it is important to analyze the jet at a high level. The 777X is Boeing's next-generation evolution of the long-running 777 family, as it is a very large twin-engine widebody aimed at airlines that want flagship long-haul capacity, strong economics, and a more modern onboard product without stepping up to a four-engine aircraft.

The family centers on the Boeing 777-9, the largest passenger aircraft Boeing will put into service over the next decade. Complementing this larger model is the 777-8, an aircraft which trades some capacity for ultra-long range, something which is very appealing to operators of all kinds.

Boeing is pitching the jet as delivering lower overall fuel burn and emissions than the aircraft it replaces, bringing with it lower operating costs than competing aircraft in its segment. Boeing has also been quick to market the aircraft's quieter overall noise footprint for airports and communities.

Technically, the headline features are its new General Electric GE9X engines, a new composite wing with folding wingtips, and a cabin package that builds on Boeing 787-style improvements such as larger windows, better humidity, and a wider-feeling interior. In practical terms, that means the Boeing 777X is meant to give airlines more seats, longer range, and premium-cabin flexibility, all of which carriers are actively seeking.

This allows the jet to offer better per-seat economics on dense intercontinental routes. Boeing's latest simulator qualification milestone also shows the program is still moving toward eventual airline entry into service, even after a long and closely watched development path.

The Boeing 777X's crew rest area is best understood as a carefully concealed upper-deck module that is quietly built into the crown of the fuselage. It is important to note immediately that this is not a second passenger floor, as the Boeing 747 has one. On the 777, Boeing has long used this overhead volume to its advantage, capitalizing on the space between the cabin ceiling and the aircraft's outer skin to create private rest quarters for off-duty crew.

That basic idea carries into the era of the ultra-large, ultra-efficient, and ultra-capable Boeing 777X. The manufacturer's 777-9 minimum equipment documentation explicitly references both an overhead flight crew rest and an overhead flight attendant rest, confirming that dedicated overhead crew-rest installations are part of the aircraft's fundamental architecture.

In practice, that means that the jet can provide separate spaces entirely for pilots and cabin crew. This ultimately keeps the flight crew close to the cockpit while moving flight attendants into a secluded compartment away from the principal passenger cabin.

Analysts have evaluated the Boeing 777X's proposed crew-rest areas extensively. They have been designated as enclosed Class One crew-rest facilities because they are equipped with horizontal bunks and amenities such as lighting, ventilation, power, and communication. The result is ultimately a hidden, highly functional secret upper deck that most passengers will never actually see, but which plays a major role in how the aircraft is equipped for ultra-long-haul flying.

Novelty, on its own, is not what makes the 777X's crew rest area particularly interesting, given that crew rests on widebodies have existed for decades. However, it says a lot about modern long-haul aircraft design. On missions that can stretch well beyond 14 hours, airlines need augmented crews, and augmented crews need genuine sleep space rather than improvised rest in passenger seats.

Boeing said that this approach on the 777 could preserve revenue seats and cargo positions, and supplier Collins Aerospace seems equally confident in the capabilities of this upstairs rest concept. Cabin crew will also be excited by this concept, as it will increase comfort while preserving cabin real estate.

This is a fundamental reason why the Boeing 777X's hidden rest area is so significant. It blends human-factors thinking with airline economics. It will help ensure that crews stay alert, compliant, and operationally ready, while allowing airlines to market the visible parts of the cabin to paying passengers in a much more aggressive manner. In other words, the secret upper deck is not a gimmick but rather a quiet, modern efficiency tool.

Beyond hidden crew-rest spaces, the aircraft is packed with dozens of innovations that show how Boeing is trying to modernize the large long-haul twinjet. The most eye-catching piece of this jet is its folding wingtip system, which allows the aircraft to capitalize on the aerodynamic advantages of giving the 777X an incredibly long wing, while also fitting into most gates on the ground.

Boeing has also highlighted the wing's advanced aerodynamics and laminar-flow nacelles, both of which serve to cut drag and improve aerodynamics. Power comes from the huge General Electric GE9X, the latest engine developed for the program, something which gives the Boeing 777X more thrust and better efficiency than earlier 777 variants.

Inside, the aircraft borrows heavily from the 787 playbook, with larger windows, immersive LED lighting, bigger overhead bins, a quieter cabin, lower cabin altitude, improved humidity and cleaner air. Boeing is also promoting smooth ride technology to help reduce the sensation of turbulence.

On the operational side, the Boeing 777X includes main-gear aft axle steering to improve maneuverability and reduce tire scrubbing when turning into tight gates. When put together, these features make the Boeing 777X more than just a stretched update of the current 777. It is designed as a flagship that combines better passenger comfort, improved airport compatibility, and lower operating costs in one very large package.

The Boeing 777X's customer list is a mix of long-established Boeing 777 operators and newer buyers using the jet for both passenger and cargo growth. On the passenger side, the best-known customers include Emirates, Qatar Airways, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines, All Nippon Airways, Cathay Pacific, Etihad Airways, and British Airways' parent company, the International Airlines Group (IAG).

Since then, the roster has expanded further, with Air India, Ethiopian Airlines, Korean Air, and China Airlines all placing orders, underscoring the program's continued appeal across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa. Boeing said in 2025 that customers worldwide had ordered more than 550 Boeing 777X-family aircraft, underscoring the program's importance at the upper end of the long-haul market. This figure has now risen to almost 700.

Cargo operations are also a major part of the story. The Boeing 777X family now includes the 777-8 Freighter, and Boeing has landed orders from Qatar Airways, Lufthansa Group, Cargolux, Silk Way West Airlines, and China Airlines for that model. That means that some customers are buying the 777X purely as a passenger flagship, while others are backing it as a next-generation freighter platform as well.

At the end of the day, the Boeing 777X is set to be a capable widebody twinjet. The plane, however, remains the subject of endless discussion among industry analysts, many of whom are unsure whether it will be the cure to Boeing's woes or the cause of its financial downfall.

Customers are really being held out in the cold, awaiting the jet's certification, which remains uncertain. However, some remain excited about the aircraft's delivery. Ultimately, the jet will offer a best-in-class combination of range and passenger payload, making it a staple of long-haul fleets worldwide.

Another significant factor in why the aircraft will have a substantial impact on the market is the plane's impressive overall operating efficiency. In a world where jet fuel prices only continue to rise, the importance of a capable, fuel-efficient widebody cannot be understated in any way, especially on high-frequency routes.

Why is this being repeated every other week

"This figure has now risen to almost 700"

The latest published net backlog for the 777 family now stands at 602, including 5 -300ER, which will never be delivered to PIA but meet the ASC606 criteria, and 38 777F

Which means the net orders for the 777X family now stands at 559, a far cry from "almost 700"
