#6270. World of Hyatt Card Limited Time Bonus Offer: Earn Four Free Night Awards

We’ve just seen a new limited time welcome offer rolled out on the World of Hyatt Credit Card, making it the ideal time to apply. I’d consider this to be one of the most lucrative hotel credit cards out there — it’s a product you don’t get just for the bonus, but instead, for the long term value that it offers.

Let’s take a look at the details of the card bonus and eligibility requirements, as well as the long term value.

Link: Learn more about the World of Hyatt Credit Card bonus offer

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome bonus that consists of four Category 1-4 free night awards after spending $5,000 within the first three months.

World of Hyatt Category 4 properties retail for up to 25,000 points per night, so the absolute maximum value of this offer is 100,000 points. However, I of course wouldn’t value it that highly. That’s because these free night awards expire 12 months after they’re issued, and you also can’t top off these awards to redeem at more expensive properties. So actually maxing out the value of these isn’t easy.

One thing I should mention is that while I don’t love the lack of flexibility of this welcome offer, it’s significantly better than the standard bonus, which tends to be lackluster. Obviously Chase and Hyatt know that this is a card people will get for the long term value, rather than just for the bonus.

For what it’s worth, based on my latest miles & points valuations, I consider World of Hyatt points to be worth 1.4 cents each.

If you’re interested in applying for the World of Hyatt Credit Card, the eligibility rules for the bonus are pretty straightforward. This product is available to you if you don’t have this exact card, and haven’t received a new cardmember bonus on this card in the past 24 months.

So that means you could potentially earn the bonus if you’ve had the card in the past. Furthermore, eligibility is unrelated to whether you have the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card (learn more).

On top of that, Chase’s general application rules apply, including that you can typically be approved for at most two Chase cards every 30 days, and the Chase 5/24 rule is also worth considering (you may not be approved if you’ve opened five or more new card accounts in the past 24 months).

There’s not a consistent credit score you need to be approved for this card, though I’d hope to have a score in the “good” to “excellent” range, ideally 700+ points. However, people with lower scores have been approved, and people with higher scores have been rejected.

The World of Hyatt Card is one that offers a lot of long term value, so only think of the welcome bonus as being part of the bigger picture. The World of Hyatt Card has a $95 annual fee, and offers the following perks, among other things:

This is a card I’ve had for years, and one that I spend at least $15,000 on annually, so that I earn the second free night award, plus six additional elite nights. If you stay at Hyatts with any frequency, having this card should be a no-brainer. For more details, read my full World of Hyatt Card review.

If you’re looking for a Hyatt co-branded credit card but want a business card instead, then the World of Hyatt Business Credit Card is for you. The card is currently offering a bonus of 70,000 points after spending $7,000 within the first three months.

At my valuation of 1.4 cents per point, that’s roughly $980 in value, which more than offsets the $199 annual fee in year one.

Eligibility is straightforward, as you can’t currently hold this specific card, and you can’t have received a welcome bonus on it within the past 24 months. Having the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card doesn’t affect your eligibility, as you can hold both cards and earn bonuses on each. Standard Chase application rules apply.

For more details, read my World of Hyatt Business Card review, as well as my World of Hyatt personal vs. business card comparison.

The World of Hyatt Credit Card is currently offering a limited time welcome offer that can earn you four Category 1-4 free night awards upon completing minimum spending. Category 4 properties go for up to 25,000 points per night, so this is potentially quite a substantial welcome bonus.

However, the bonus isn’t the main reason you get this card. Instead, it’s about the long term value proposition, including elite nights toward status, an anniversary free night award, etc. Furthermore, it’s a card that’s worth spending $15,000 on per year, if you can swing it, so you can earn a second free night award and six more elite nights toward status.

If this card has been on your radar, this is a good time to apply…

#6269. NTSB: Missed Inspections Let Storm-Damaged Southwest 737 MAX Fly 44 Times Before Dutch Roll Accident

A Southwest Airlines Boeing 737 MAX flew 44 times with undetected storm damage to its tail after missing a post-storm inspection, then later passing a flawed maintenance test. On May 25, 2024, the aircraft experienced a Dutch roll event — classified as an accident due to the substantial damage to the plane — prompting an investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB).

In its final report, the NTSB found that severe winds damaged the plane while it was parked in New Orleans nine days earlier. The damage affected the standby rudder power control unit's (PCU) mounting structure and its connection to the vertical stabilizer, resulting in improper rudder operation. However, a series of maintenance oversights allowed the damage to go undetected for nine days and 44 flights.

The aircraft involved was a Boeing 737 MAX 8 (registration N8825Q), which had been in service for less than 18 months when the following events occurred. On May 16, 2024, it was parked overnight at Louis Armstrong New Orleans International Airport (MSY) when strong winds damaged the vertical stabilizer structure around the standby rudder PCU. However, the aircraft showed no obvious external damage, and no inspection was conducted.

N8825Q then left New Orleans the following morning and completed 44 flights over the next nine days. Then, on May 25, while operating Southwest flight 746 from Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) to Oakland International Airport (OAK), the crew experienced "a small amount of Dutch roll" at 34,000 feet, which lasted a few seconds and occurred again at 32,000 feet.

A Dutch roll is defined by the NTSB as "a coupled oscillation in an airplane’s yaw and roll axes." The phenomenon causes an aircraft's nose and wings to oscillate in opposing movements, potentially making it difficult to control. The 737 MAX continued and landed safely in Oakland, but inspections found damage to the standby PCU's mounting bracket and surrounding vertical stabilizer structure.

Investigators also found that a scheduled maintenance test in Houston two days earlier had been incorrectly signed off, despite evidence that the rudder was not moving correctly. The NTSB stated the probable cause as:

"Damage to the standby rudder power control unit connection to the vertical fin due to an extreme high wind event while the airplane was parked, which remained undetected and resulted in anomalous operation of the standby rudder power control unit."

Boeing's maintenance manual for the 737 included inspections for aircraft exposed to extreme winds, but it did not specify a wind speed threshold. Southwest also had no procedure for alerting maintenance control when parked aircraft experienced extreme winds. As a result, no inspection was carried out immediately after the storm.

Following the storm damage, the aircraft completed 38 flights before it underwent a scheduled overnight maintenance check in Houston on May 23, just two days before the Dutch roll event. This included a test requiring a mechanic to observe the aircraft's tail and visually confirm that the rudder moved correctly in both directions.

However, hangar footage of that test showed the rudder moving to the right but not to the left, with nobody positioned at the rear to observe it. Despite this, Southwest's maintenance records showed the test as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The following day, the crew of the aircraft's fourth flight after the Houston check disconnected the yaw damper after it appeared to overcorrect during turbulence.

The yaw damper was deferred under the minimum equipment list (MEL), and the jet flew one more sector to Phoenix, where the system passed a functional test and was returned to service. Flight 746 was the aircraft's sixth flight since the Houston check and its 44th since the storm in New Orleans.

The term may sound delicious, but these safety-related occurrences are anything but tasty.

Following the accident, Boeing revised its 737 maintenance manual in May 2025, requiring an extreme high-wind inspection when ground winds reach 65 knots (75 mph). This is close to but still below the 73-knot (84 mph) gusts recorded at New Orleans on the night N8825Q was damaged. Meanwhile, Airbus sets a higher threshold for most of its aircraft, requiring an inspection when ground winds exceed 80 knots (92 mph).

Southwest also introduced new inspection procedures and conducted checks across its entire MAX fleet. Between June 17 and 20, 2024, the airline inspected all 231 737 MAX aircraft in its fleet at the time, finding no similar damage. It now monitors weather reports for winds above 65 knots, triggering an inspection program.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

The article repeatedly refers to the dutch roll event as an 'accident' but there was no accident. It also states 'the pilots regained control' but they never lost aircraft control.

Any STUCTURAL damage affecting aircraft flight control systems crosses the boundary between an "incident" and an "accident". The bracket supporting the PCU actuator was bent/broken beyond serviceable limits. The bracket is structural and the PCU is flight control; ergo, AIRCRAFT ACCIDENT. My username is CFII, but I'm also an A&P and ATP, and have encountered that boundary before.

#6267. How To Combine Hilton Honors Points Between Accounts For Free

Every hotel loyalty program has a different policy when it comes to being able to combine points among members. Arguably Hilton Honors has among the most generous policies of any program when it comes to letting members combine points, so I’d like to take a closer look at that in this post.

For what it’s worth, separately I’ve covered the policies of Marriott Bonvoy and World of Hyatt when it comes to combining points.

Hilton Honors offers a generous feature to allow members to combine and share points with others at no cost. First let’s go over the basics:

Technically Hilton Honors has two features by which you can combine points for free, and this can cause quite a bit of confusion. These two options are as follows:

The reality is that these two options are more similar than they may sound. The same limits exist on points transfers regardless of which method you choose:

The end result is the same, though, which is that points are being consolidated in one account. Given the similar restrictions on transfers, personally I think it’s easier to just use the points transfer feature over the points pooling feature, which just adds an unnecessary step.

Before we talk about how combining Hilton points works, why should you even care about this feature? There are a few reasons this could make a difference:

Long story short, being able to combine points just gives you a lot more flexibility.

The process of combining Hilton Honors points differs based on whether you’re just looking to make a simple transfer, or are looking to create a points pool with up to 11 accounts.

This is the most basic function, and also what I recommend. Visit the Hilton Honors points transfer page to start the process of transferring points from one Hilton Honors account to another.

You’ll be prompted to log into your Hilton Honors account, and then will be asked to enter the number of points you want to transfer (between 1,000 and 500,000), along with the name, email address, and Hilton Honors number of the person you want to transfer points to.

This is still facilitated by points.com (as points purchases usually are), except in this case you’re not paying anything. While the points are supposed to be available for redemption immediately, they may only show in your online account activity 24 hours after the transaction was processed.

This is the function to be aware of if you want to have up to 11 people combine points into one account. Visit the Hilton Honors points pooling page to start the process of creating a pooling account with multiple Hilton Honors members.

While the points transfer feature only requires the participation of the member who is transferring points, the process of pooling points requires participation of all members involved. One person can start sending invitations to pool points, which requires entering the names and email addresses of the people you want to invite.

That person will receive an email invitation to join your points pool, at which point they can transfer points to you.

The person will have to log into their Hilton Honors account, and then they’ll be brought to the same page for combining points as above.

If the member does choose to pool/transfer points, the person who invited them will be informed.

The reality is that this process is more or less the same as just combining points, with the difference being that someone is prompted to transfer points, rather than just doing so straight out of their account with no prompting.

Not only does Hilton Honors offer an excellent rate of return (in points) on hotel stays, but there are lots of other great ways to earn Hilton Honors points.

For one, there are four excellent co-branded Hilton Amex credit cards in the United States, including the following:

On top of that, Hilton Honors often sells points at a discount. In many cases there’s a 100% bonus on purchased points (or even more), which allows you to purchase points for just 0.5 cents each (or in some case even less). This can be a good deal, particularly for high-end redemptions (though Hilton Honors devaluations in recent times make these redemptions less exciting than in the past).

It’s always nice to easily be able to move points between loyalty program accounts in order to maximize them. As far as hotel loyalty programs go, Hilton Honors has what’s arguably the best option for combining points.

You can combine points at no cost, with some reasonable limits in place. You can either use the standard points transfer option, or you can go through the process of pooling points; personally I find the former option to be easier.

Have you ever used Hilton Honors’ points pooling feature? If so, what was your experience like?

#6266. Lol: Beond Airlines & Air Cairo Plan All-Business Class Carrier In Egypt

Guys, sometimes I wonder if I’m losing my mind, or if others are. All-business class carrier Beond Airlines has just announced that it’s partnering with all-economy class carrier Air Cairo to launch an all-business class airline flying to and from Egypt.

No disrespect to Egypt, but of all the business ideas in the world, is this really the one that makes the most sense? Maybe next we’ll see Beond partner with Ryanair to offer all-business class service between Leeds and Agadir?

Beond Airlines and Air Cairo have announced a partnership to bring Beond’s all-business class travel experience to Egypt. The two airlines signed a memorandum of understanding for the concept.

For the summer of 2027, Air Cairo will operate Beond-branded flights with all-business class configurations, connecting Egypt with Europe and the Gulf region. This is clearly targeted at inbound tourism to Egypt, so “travellers reach Egypt’s coast, its history and its cities rested and at ease.”

Routes and schedules will be announced in the coming months, with bookings expected to open in the first half of 2027. Just so we’re on the same page here, Air Cairo operates a fleet of planes exclusively in an all-economy configuration, so the airline hasn’t seen merit to offering even a small business class cabin. But now they’ve decided “hey, what we really need is a plane that exclusively has business class?”

Here’s what Beond CEO Tero Taskila had to say about this concept:

“Egypt has some of the most remarkable places on earth, and many travellers who want to reach them in comfort. Air Cairo knows this market better than anyone. Together we can start the holiday from home, not at the hotel. Our cabin gives us the luxurious surroundings. Our people give us the experience. Both have to match the places we fly to.”

Meanwhile here’s what Egypt’s Minister of Tourism and Antiquities, Sherif Fathy, had to say about this:

“Encouraging this partnership is an integral part of the Ministry’s strategy to promote Egypt’s unparalleled tourism diversity and expand its range of distinctive tourism products and experiences. We highly value the role of Air Cairo as one of the key supporters of the tourism industry, whose efforts contribute to enhancing connectivity, supporting tourism growth, and strengthening Egypt’s position as a leading global tourism destination. Such partnerships reflect our commitment to fostering closer cooperation with our partners in the aviation sector to achieve sustainable growth and further enhance the competitiveness of the Egyptian tourism destination.”

Beond Airlines was initially formed as an airline intended to transport people to and from the Maldives. I’ve flown the airline, and the onboard experience was actually quite lovely (with two caveats — the lack of Wi-Fi, plus the limited range of the planes requiring a refueling stop, which limits the ability to get rest).

This airline obviously has funding, and the company’s CEO is a really nice guy who has a fair bit of experience. But nothing about the past few years gives me any faith in the future of the company.

When Beond Airlines launched in 2023, management claimed the airline would have 32 planes and serve 60 destinations within five years, which would be by 2028. Currently, the airline still has two planes, with no additional firm orders, at least as far as I know.

It has just been announcement after announcement from Beond, with little substance to anything:

I have no clue what’s going on here anymore, though I’d assume it’s one of two things:

But I have to say, of everything we’ve seen from Beond, I find this to possibly be the most bizarre development yet. Egypt is generally a budget vacation destination, and not a premium vacation destination. So if an all-business class experience to the Maldives didn’t prove successful, I can’t imagine that Egypt is the key to unlocking prosperity for the airline.

Beond Airlines and Air Cairo are partnering to launch an all-business class airline that will serve Egypt. Egypt is generally a budget travel destination, and there’s an irony to an all-economy airline getting involved in an all-business class operation.

What can anyone really say at this point, though? Beond is all over the place in terms of its strategy. Initially it was going to fly to dozens of destinations out of the Maldives. Then it promised to set up subsidiaries all over the place, including partnering with an airline that liquidated just weeks later. Then the airline suspended commercial operations altogether. And now the airline is planning all-business class service in Egypt.

What do you make of Beond’s latest Egypt play?

#6265. 10 US Airport Projects Replacing Regional Gates With Mainline Jet Capacity

Ethan is an aviation professional with a degree in Aviation Management with Flight from the Florida Institute of Technology. He previously wrote aviation and tourism features for Florida Tech’s student newspaper, The Crimson, where he developed a clear, reader‑focused reporting style. Aviation journalism has remained a consistent priority throughout his career.

He currently holds a Restricted ATP and Commercial Multi‑Engine Pilot certificate and works in aviation supply chain and aircraft component repair. Alongside his industry role, he is pursuing his Certified Flight Instructor rating and actively building flight experience.

A lifelong aviation enthusiast, Ethan spent countless hours at Raleigh–Durham International Airport’s observation deck studying air traffic and practicing amateur photography and videography.

The modern aviation industry is facing a trend that can affect nearly any airline at any commercial airport. Larger aircraft are becoming increasingly dominant at airports across the United States, from congested hubs such as Newark Liberty International Airport to smaller regional gateways.

At the same time, airlines continue to retire aging 50-seat regional jets, while manufacturers Airbus and Boeing maintain substantial backlogs for their narrowbody aircraft families. Long gone are the days of airport master plans that include regional jet-specific satellite concourses catering to a limited aircraft size class.

This list includes airports of a wide range of sizes. These are based on a local decision to scale down regional jet-specific terminal buildings, which helps set airports up to better handle larger equipment. The U.S. Government Accountability Office reports that several reasons are behind the trend: Low-Cost Carriers (LCC), pilot shortages, ATC shortages, airport congestion, and an overall desire for carriers to increase efficiency all contribute to physical airport development now catering to larger jet aircraft, such as the Boeing 737.

Pittsburgh International Airport (PIT) was once a major East Coast hub for USAir, and was configured as such. With a traditional hub and spoke operation, the airport's famous "X" shaped terminal opened in 1992 with its first arrival from San Diego International Airport(SAN), as reported by Blue Sky News. The airport once boasted transatlantic flights that fed into an impressive regional East Coast network.

The terminal also included a commuter section in its original design. Flights operated by USAir Express were the mainstay of the building, also known as Concourse E. However, USAir, having been rebranded to US Airways abruptly ended its lease agreement at PIT, beginning the hub closure process in 2004. This decision soon after rendered Pittsburgh's Concourse E obsolete.

US Airways' decision to end its hub and spoke system in Pittsburgh began a fundamental market shift at the airport. As at many former hubs in the Rust Belt region, like Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) and Cincinnati/Northern Kentucky International (CVG), low-cost carriers (LCCs) entered these markets to capture demand left behind by the de-hubbing of legacy carriers. Thus, PIT's Concourse E was demolished as part of The Transformed PIT, per their website, shifting to accommodate more frequent Airbus A320 and 737 aircraft from carriers such as Frontier Airlines and Allegiant Air.

Historically a regional aircraft-only operation, Northwest Arkansas National Airport (XNA) is no stranger to larger equipment. With a significant increase in service from Allegiant, XNA is now augmented with A320 and 737 service from each of the big three of United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, and American Airlines.

XNA, through its various airline partners, offers mainline service to hubs such as Denver International Airport (DEN), Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport (ATL), and Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) respectively. This shift in traffic is supported by a new terminal construction project, as outlined on the XNA website. Construction is currently in progress on the new addition, while the design development only began in 2025.

While Envoy Air is still the market leader for XNA at nearly 30 percent, the increase in passenger demand has led to mainline and LCC organizations alike to ramp up their Northwest Arkansas schedules; American's mainline services account for 12.1 percent of the market share on its own, according to the Bureau of Transportation Statistics. Allegiant recently cracked the top five in XNA's market share at 10 percent. Allegiant operates an entire mainline fleet of A320 and 737 family jets, avoiding regional jets altogether. This signals to XNA a need airside for more spacious gates.

These airports are making heavy investments in their infrastructure over the next few years.

Wilmington International Airport (ILM) historically served mainly the regional subsidiaries of US legacy carriers such as Piedmont Airlines and Delta. However, this booming coastal community is experiencing increasing commercial aviation demand due to consistent population growth, as reported by the US Census Bureau. ILM reports a record 907,753 enplanements in 2025, according to its website.

The last several years have brought airlines such as Sun Country Airlines, Avelo Airlines, and JetBluein addition to mainline Delta service to Atlanta and American's service to Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT), sometimes onboard an Airbus A321.

Beginning in 2018, the airport began a $69 million terminal expansion project that will create additional gate space and terminal square footage. Local news agency WECT reported in August that the original 2018 project has been expanded to include an extended departures/arrivals curb, a commercial drop-off curb, a pedestrian tunnel, and additional parking facilities, accommodating increasing demand and the growing size of its regular airline equipment.

Few major US airports depended on regional jets as much as Charlotte during the US Airways era. Hundreds of daily departures flowed through concourses designed to handle large volumes of short-haul regional traffic, making CLT one of the country's busiest connecting airports for smaller aircraft.

That operating model is gradually changing. American has increasingly upgauged many routes from 50-seat regional jets to larger regional aircraft like the Embraer E170 and mainline Airbus and Boeing jets. In response, Charlotte has invested heavily in concourse expansions and gate projects that support higher-capacity aircraft and growing passenger volumes, as a part of the CLT Master Plan 2050, per its website.

The airport's recent and ongoing gate expansion efforts, including projects on Concourse A and other terminal facilities, illustrate how former regional-jet strongholds are adapting for a future centered on larger aircraft. Rather than simply adding gates, Charlotte is creating infrastructure better suited to today's fleet mix and the continued shift toward higher-capacity operations.

The 16-foot statue can be a surprising sight to some travelers new to the airport.

In a collaboration between The Metropolitan Airports Commission (MAC) and Delta, Minneapolis-St. Paul International Airport (MSP) has recently completed a monumental Terminal 1 modernization project. The renovation of six of the seven concourses in the Charles Lindbergh Terminal 1 from 2023-2025, according to the MAC. Concourse E at MSP was deliberately excluded; it is home to several airlines including American, Air Canada, formerly Continental Airlines and Spirit Airlines.

Concourse A and B famously serve regional traffic, primarily under Delta Connection's regional subsidiaries of Endeavor Air and Skywest. Formerly frequented by Saab 340 and Bombardier CRJ-200regional jets, these gates are now commonly used by slightly larger Embraer E175s and Bombardier CRJ-900s.

The Star Tribune has reported on additional planned improvements for MSP. Concourse A is slated to feature somewhat of a reduction of its 14 gates, lowering the total number to accommodate a smaller number of larger aircraft than its current CRJ-900 mainstay. Concourse B is slated for complete demolition by 2040 to support this vision as well. Although a rise in LCC traffic is not of immediate concern for this section of the airport, a notable exception is Denver Air Connection, which occasionally parks its Dornier 328s at the B gates. LCCs such as Frontier and Allegiant are localized to Terminal 1's Concourse E or Terminal 2.

For years, many regional passengers at Washington Dulles International Airport (IAD) boarded from the airport's outdoor A-gate facilities, as outlined by IAD's official website. Originally set up to support high volumes of regional jet operations, the airport is now moving in the opposite direction, replacing that infrastructure with modern concourse facilities designed for higher passenger volumes and a wider range of aircraft.

A key component of Dulles' Global Gateway program is redeveloping the eastern portion of Concourse A, where the outdoor regional boarding positions are being converted into enclosed, international-capable gates. The airport says these upgrades will provide more modern facilities while supporting growing international and domestic demand.

The planned Tier-2 Concourse will replace the existing regional facility with a 14-gate structure that can accommodate a broader range of aircraft, including larger narrowbodies and international services. Dulles mirrors MSP in that the broader trend toward more mainline aircraft traffic is not exclusive to LCC carriers filling in available market share; legacy airlines are affected all the same.

Construction could begin as early as Spring 2027.

Bemidji Regional Airport (BJI) does not currently have any capacity improvement plans in place, nor does it have the staggering demand to do so. Rather, the airport underwent a previous renovation and gate expansion that has stood the test of time and was one of the earliest examples of an airport development project prioritizing larger aircraft.

Completed in 2012, BJI's passenger facilities doubled in size, according to its website. The airport's first jet bridge, manufactured by ThyssenKrupp, was installed to handle multiple flights at once. The gate was rated to accommodate aircraft sizes up to and including Boeing 737-900 and A320 jets comfortably and efficiently.

The project reaped benefits for the community with Sun Country Airlines launching periodic charter service to Laughlin/Bullhead International Airport (IFP) on a 737. Aside from that, SkyWest operates a twice-daily service to MSP under the Delta Connection Brand. Formerly served by Northwest Airlines' Northwest Airlink prior to its merger with Delta, the service has evolved from the 34-seat Saab 340 to now being operated by a 69-seat Bombardier CRJ700.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

After some delays, United Airlines is one step closer to launching service on its posh new domestic plane.

The airline on Thursday evening announced it recently took delivery of its first Airbus A321neo “Coastliner” plane.

It’s a premium-heavy aircraft that will feature United’s new Polaris business-class suites and a true premium economy cabin.

And it will soon be a fixture on the carrier’s top transcontinental routes.

United shared a sneak peek of the new jet on social media Thursday evening —  well ... the outside of it, at least.

As expected, the exterior sports a special wrap featuring the “Coastliner” decal.

That’s because United plans to exclusively use this plane on its most premium coast-to-coast flights.

Once in service, you’ll see it on routes from Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) and San Francisco International Airport (SFO).

It will likely also figure into the carrier’s plans at John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK), once United makes its long-awaited return to JFK.

While United had hoped to launch service on the Coastliner this past summer, delays at Airbus pushed the debut back a few months.

The jet is now slated to make its inaugural flight in early 2027, United said this week.

It will certainly be an upgrade to the airline’s prime transcontinental service.

Passengers flying in those suites will get access to United’s Polaris Lounge facilities.

There are also 12 Premium Plus recliners across three rows in a two-by-two configuration.

Plus, in economy there’s a walk-up snack bar.

The whole interior is very similar to the Airbus A321XLR that United debuted late this summer. That longer-range jet is slated to start flying to Europe in the coming months.

United’s looming introduction of the Coastliner comes as a growing number of U.S. carriers are upgrading their top transcontinental products.

This fall, Alaska Airlines revealed it will add lie-flat suites and premium economy to a future subfleet of Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets.

American Airlines last year launched coast-to-coast service with the A321XLR, which sports its latest-generation Flagship Suites up front.

Delta Air Lines, meanwhile, rolled out a version of the Airbus A321neo that doesn't have lie-flat seats (at least not yet) but does have a whopping 44 domestic first-class recliners.

Plus, JetBlue recently announced that passengers flying in its lie-flat Mint cabins would be entitled to enter its new airport lounges in New York City and Boston, even when flying domestically.

United has 50 of these Coastliners (along with 50 of the XLR jets) on order for the coming years.

So this aircraft will be a big part of the carrier’s most lucrative domestic service for years to come.

#6263. Singapore Airlines Unveils New Suites With Double Beds—Rollout Slips Again, And Many Planes Miss Out

First class is coming to the ultra-long-range Airbus A350s that operate the world’s longest flights. Business class gets doors, a different sleeping position, and more foot space. We’re not going to see the first aircraft with the new cabins until the second half of 2027, and several fleets won’t ever get these seats at all.

I flew to Singapore in November 2017 for the unveiling of their last new A380 business class and Suites. Nine years later, plenty of their aircraft still have an older product. And even the 380 itself didn’t finish installation until late 2023. Long haul A350 and Boeing 777 seats date to 2013. I flew to Seattle for delivery of the first 777 that had them.

Singapore’s new business class was designed with BMW’s Designworks and built by Recaro. It’s a bespoke seat, with a forward-facing, staggered 1-2-1 layout with doors and direct aisle access throughout. The biggest improvement is being able to adjust the seat continuously from upright to flat, choose a comfortable lounging position, and sleep without angling my body across the seat.

The A350 seat goes from 28 inches wide to 22 inches. On the wider Boeing 777-9, it’ll be 24 inches. So that’s a real tradeoff in seat width. Singapore’s old seat was exceptionally wide, but short and you had to angle your feet. A350 business class gets a 22-inch OLED screen, while the new 777-9 gets a smaller 20-inch screen without OLED.

The new first class, designed by PriestmanGoode and manufactured by Collins Aerospace, will have four seats on the ultra-long-range A350 and six on the 777-9.

The center pair can remain two independent suites or open into one shared space. Each passenger still has their own entrance, screen and table. Those seats can form a sofa for two or an 80-by-60-inch double bed. That’s the size of a standard U.S. queen mattress. Singapore calls it the largest double bed in commercial aviation. Individually, the beds measure 80 by 30 inches. The seats are 23 inches wide with the armrests raised.

Curved sliding doors, warm colors, Poltrona Frau leather and batik details make this look much more like Singapore Airlines than the new business cabin.

Companion dining is available at every first class seat, using the ottoman, which restores something missing from the current A380 Suites experience. The joined center suites can accommodate four people dining together.

Other features include a personal wardrobe, an illuminated vanity drawer, carry-on storage beneath the ottoman, wireless charging and a 32-inch 4K screen. Bang & Olufsen wireless headphones are supplied, and you can pair your own headphones. A small information panel shows flight details and lavatory availability without requiring you to turn on the main screen. Seat and lighting preferences can be saved for future flights.

This isn’t the A380’s separate armchair-and-bed concept. The chair becomes the bed. It’s a massive improvement over today’s 777 first class, while the A380 retains its current expansive Suites layout. There is only one center pair on each aircraft. Six first class seats on the 777-9 means four window singles and one potential double suite, not three double beds.

The announced program covers 41 existing A350s and Singapore’s 31 ordered Boeing 777-9s. Only the 777-9 gets all four new seat designs.

The A380, existing 777-300ER, medium-haul A350, 787-10 and 737-8 aren’t included in this seat program. Those aircraft keep their current cabin products under the announced plan. The A380 is separately getting Starlink.

The rollout has already slipped twice: the first refurbished long-haul A350 was originally due in the second quarter of 2026, then the first quarter of 2027. Now it’s the second half of 2027. The airline still targets the end of 2030 to complete the A350 retrofits.

Boeing’s delays explain why seats originally intended for the 777-9 are going onto A350s. But seat certification is also holding things up: the 777-9 seats have been certified, while the airplane hasn’t. The A350 seats still need certification. The ultra-long range A350 doesn’t have a firm separate debut date or announced launch route for its new first class.

The new premium economy seat offers 40 inches of pitch, up from 38, and nine inches of recline instead of eight. It’s 19 inches wide, in a 2-4-2 cabin, with adjustable leg and footrests.

777-9 economy cabin goes to 3-4-3 and 31 to 32 inches of pitch. It’s a wider cabin, but Singapore’s current 777-300ERs are 3-3-3. There are redesigned cushions, adjustable headrests and a revised recline mechanism intended to improve knee and shin clearance, plus 13-inch 4K screens, Bluetooth and USB-C.

Meanwhile, an A350 retrofit won’t bring these new premium economy or economy seats. Those cabins get refreshed upholstery and an updated entertainment interface, while keeping their existing seat hardware.

There will even be two hardware versions within the 777-9 fleet. Premium economy and economy on the first 12 aircraft get conventional 4K screens. The later 19 get OLED screens but lose USB-A. Economy also loses universal power outlets on those 19 aircraft, retaining USB-C. Premium economy keeps universal power. On those later jets, coach will have OLED while first and business won’t.

The early reaction is much warmer toward first class than business. In the FlyerTalk discussion folks like the larger bed, the return of companion dining and the ability to separate the middle pair into two proper suites. That’s a better arrangement for unrelated passengers than Lufthansa’s shared center suite. The business class thread is much rougher. Gray surfaces and bright yellow trim draw comparisons to Scoot, car interiors and a loss of Singapore’s warmth. Reddit reactions echo the complaints about generic styling and lost identity. Still, folks like the doors, storage and companion beds. Several Other Changes Arrive Before The Seats Singapore’s broader announcement bundles together upgrades with different schedules: Sleepwear and amenity kits. New kits begin rolling out this month on flights over six hours: Sisley in Suites and first, Byredo in business, INK & WATER in premium economy, and travel essentials in a batik pouch in economy. Business class gets pajamas for the first time, on all long-haul flights and selected overnight medium-haul flights over six hours. First class and Suites get new cotton sleepwear. Dining. The package includes more than 100 new or refreshed dishes, expanded drinks and Christofle serviceware in Suites, first and business. Lounge and ground-service improvements are also part of the broader investment. Entertainment and internet. The next KrisWorld system adds easier navigation, personalization, a wellness planner and more than 2,500 entertainment options, with hardware varying by cabin. Starlink begins rolling out from early 2027 on the A380 and long-haul and ultra-long-range A350s. The announced Starlink list doesn’t include the 777-9. The Biggest Commercial Change Is At The Back Of The Longest Flights The ultra-long-range A350 goes from 67 business and 94 premium economy seats to four first, 70 business and 58 premium economy. That’s 36 fewer premium economy seats or a 38% cut. Total passenger capacity falls from 161 to 132, or 18%. Singapore is replacing a substantial portion of its lowest-priced cabin on these aircraft with space it expects to sell for more. First class provides a new way to monetize the nonstop flights. Net net I expect this to mean tougher award space overall (certainly in premium economy). #6262. Livery of the Week: JetBlue’s Florida Panthers Design

Editor’s Note: AirlineGeeks is proud to present our ‘Livery of the Week’ series. Every Friday, a team member will share an airline livery, which can be from the past, present, or even a special scheme. Some airline liveries are works of art. The complexity associated with painting around critical flight components and the added weight requires outside-the-box thinking from designers. The average airliner can cost upwards of $200,000 to repaint, creating a separate aircraft repainting industry as a result.

Have an idea for a livery that we should highlight? Drop us a line.

Since the beginning of its operations in 2000, New York-based airline JetBlue has always considered South Florida as one of its primary markets, with a presence at Fort Lauderdale-Hollywood Airport that has grown during the past 25 years to include up to 25 aircraft based overnight at the airport and over 2,000 people supporting its operations in Broward County.

As a sign of its commitment to the South Florida community, JetBlue has announced a multi-year extension for an expanded partnership with the Florida Panthers, the NHL’s southernmost franchise that captured back-to-back Stanley Cups in 2023-24 and 2024-25. The partnership will see JetBlue present a newly redesigned Champions Club at the Amerant Bank Arena in Sunrise, Florida, home of the Panthers, and to celebrate the announcement, the airline unveiled a special Panthers-themed livery for one of its Airbus A320 aircraft.

The new livery draws its inspiration from the Panthers’ jersey, therefore sporting the iconic Panthers’ red across the entire fuselage, with the outline of a golden panther all across the central part of the fuselage, right next to JetBlue’s logo. The Panthers’ shield logo is on the aircraft tail in navy and gold.

Bold red letters spelling FLORIDA appear on the bottom of the aircraft, where there’s also a leaping cat, the team’s logo. More symbols of the Panthers and the State of Florida appear in other parts of the fuselage: a simplified Florida flag appears near the front of the aircraft together with a palm tree and a hockey stick, which represent the secondary logo for the team.

“South Florida has been part of JetBlue’s story since our very first flight more than two decades ago, and we’re continuing to build on that history in a big way as Broward County’s largest airline,” said Marty St. George, JetBlue’s president, in a press release. “The Panthers know a thing or two about winning in South Florida, and we’re bringing that same energy as we expand our network, elevate the customer experience and deepen our commitment to the community. ‘Go Cats Go’ is a fun way to celebrate our shared passion for South Florida and team up with a franchise that knows how to make some noise.”

The aircraft chosen to display this special livery is an Airbus A320, registered as N784JB, delivered to the airline on Feb. 11, 2011.

The original name of the aircraft was “Blue And Infinity And Beyond,” which has been changed to “Go Cats Go” following the repainting in this new livery.

#6261. Good Riddance: The Worst Airport Lounge In The United States Closes

The Swissport Lounge at Chicago O’Hare Airport (ORD) Terminal 5 has just quietly closed. I’m about as sad as I’ll be on the day when Delta retires its latest Boeing 767-300ER…

Historically, Chicago O’Hare Terminal 5 has been a pretty lousy facility, though it has started to get better in recent years, thanks to an expansion to the terminal, and also thanks to the opening of new lounges.

Arguably the single most disappointing thing about Terminal 5 was the Swissport Lounge, which I’ve labeled the worst lounge in the United States — clearly many people agreed with me, since my review of the lounge had over 200 comments. It’s just truly one of those facilities that makes you wonder why we even bother using lounges.

The lounge had no windows, the most random collection of furniture, and a very limited selection of drinks and snacks. Unless you wanted to just guzzle alcohol, you’d be better off sitting in the terminal, in my opinion. Unfortunately for all too long, many premium airlines sent their customers here, given the lack of other lounge options. It’s quite underwhelming to be flying business class on a carrier like Etihad Airways or Qatar Airways, and then be sent here.

That brings us to the interesting update — the Swissport Lounge Chicago has closed as of October 31, 2026, so passengers are no longer being subjected to this facility.

It remains to be seen what happens with this lounge space, as that hasn’t been announced one way or another. In April 2025, Swissport’s head of North America lounges said that the company had “submitted a proposal to the Chicago Department of Aviation (CDA) for a multi-million-dollar renovation and expansion of our current Terminal 5 lounge at O’Hare International Airport.” However, I haven’t been able to find any updates on that, so I’m not sure what the latest is there.

It’s worth acknowledging just how much better the lounge situation at Chicago O’Hare Terminal 5 has gotten in recent years:

If we get another lounge at Terminal 5, that would of course be awesome, so I’m curious to see how this evolves. Chicago O’Hare is the biggest airport in the country to not have any sort of a credit card branded lounge, so I hope that eventually changes. The issue is the extent to which the terminals are dominated by their primary tenants (American and United), combined with the lack of airside connections to Terminal 5.

The Swissport Lounge Chicago O’Hare Terminal 5 has suddenly closed. I’m not sad to see the United States’ worst airport lounge close, though I am curious to see what is next for this space. Fortunately the Terminal 5 lounge situation has improved nicely in recent years, and there are now several solid new options. I do wish we’d still see a proper credit card lounge, though.

What do you make of the Swissport Lounge Chicago closing? Are you happy or elated?

#6260. Southwest 737 Flew 44 Times Before Wind Damage Was Found

A Southwest Boeing 737 MAX 8 flew 44 times before maintenance crews discovered tail damage that investigators traced to a thunderstorm more than a week earlier. In a final report released Thursday, the National Transportation Safety Board said the damage went undetected through a scheduled maintenance check and caused a standby rudder control unit to operate abnormally.

The damage came to light after Southwest flight 746 experienced unexpected rudder movements on May 25, 2024, while flying from Phoenix to Oakland, California. All 175 passengers and six crew members were uninjured. The aircraft, registered N8825Q, sustained substantial damage.

The NTSB traced the damage to the night of May 16, when the jet was parked in New Orleans, and thunderstorms brought gusts of up to 73 knots, or about 84 mph. Investigators said the wind likely moved the rudder enough to damage ribs inside the vertical stabilizer where the standby rudder control unit was mounted.

At the time, Boeing’s 737 maintenance manual called for a special inspection after an extreme wind event but gave no wind speed at which the check was required. The manual listed signs such as an aircraft moving over its wheel chocks or leaving tire skid marks.

Southwest also lacked a process to notify maintenance control when a parked aircraft had been exposed to extreme winds. The jet flew the next morning without the inspection.

Over the next week, the aircraft completed 38 flights with no reported rudder or yaw damper problems. It then underwent scheduled maintenance in Houston on May 23, including a test of the standby hydraulic system. The procedure required a mechanic at the tail to verify that the rudder moved in response to pedal inputs.

Hangar video showed the rudder moving to the right but failing to move to the left. Investigators said no one was at the tail to verify the movement. Southwest’s maintenance records showed the test was signed off as passed, and the aircraft returned to service. The NTSB could not determine whether the test worsened the existing damage.

On the fourth flight the next day, a crew disconnected the yaw damper after reporting that it was overcorrecting in turbulence. The yaw damper uses the rudder to counter side-to-side motion.

The jet flew one more leg with the system listed as inoperative. It then passed a functional test, and the yaw damper was returned to service before Flight 746.

On the Oakland flight, the captain noticed momentary stiffness in the rudder pedals while turning onto the runway. Shortly after reaching 34,000 feet, he felt what he described as “a small amount of Dutch roll.” Both pilots felt the pedals move, and the oscillations recurred after the crew descended to 32,000 feet.

Flight data showed one episode of rudder and pedal oscillations lasting about 20 seconds, with no significant change in heading or bank angle. Investigators found that the abnormal movement appeared in the data from the first flight after the Houston maintenance check, before crews reported it. They observed it only when the yaw damper was engaged.

Southwest removed the aircraft from service after it landed in Oakland. The airline later inspected the rudder control unit mounting areas across its 737 MAX fleet and found no similar damage. It also added individual mechanic sign-offs to the hydraulic test and set up a process to alert maintenance control after extreme winds. Boeing revised its maintenance manual to require the special inspection at a wind threshold of 65 knots, or 75 mph.

#6259. Flights In Europe Face Endless Bomb Threats: “This Is Only The Beginning”

It has been a rather rough week for many airlines in Europe, as dozens of flights have been diverted, canceled, or delayed, due to bomb threats. There’s obviously some sort of a coordinated effort here, but it’s hard to know what exactly is going on, beyond just the desire to create chaos (thanks to 1990_ for flagging this)…

The concept of bomb threats being called in on flights is nothing new. Sometimes people are dumb enough to call in a bomb threat because they’re running late for a flight, and think that’s the best way not to miss it. Other times people will call in bomb threats as a prank.

Rarely is a bomb threat actually called in on a flight where there’s a bomb. That comes down to two reasons — it’s exceedingly rare for flights to be bombed (thank goodness), and if someone actually wants to take down a plane, they wouldn’t issue a warning, since that kind of defeats the purpose.

So that brings us to what has gone on in Europe this week, particularly on Tuesday, Thursday, and again today (Friday). Dozens of flights across airlines have had bomb threats called in on them, and airlines generally have to take these seriously. This has now happened to over 50 flights, departing from roughly a dozen countries.

In some cases the bomb threats were called in before takeoff, so passengers could be deplaned, allowing a search to happen before departure. In other cases, the threats came in mid-flight, leading to diversions, and even fighter jet escorts, in some situations.

In no case were any credible threats found, though. It goes without saying that this is incredibly frustrating for all parties. This is a massive waste of time and resources, given that these kinds of threats are consistently fake. At the same time, governments and airlines have to take these threats seriously, because imagine what would happen if a threat were proven to be real, and it was ignored (personally I think they should just be ignored, but that’s neither here nor there).

It’s not known for sure who is behind this attack, or just how centrally coordinated it is, rather than there being a copycat element to this.

Some emails taking credit for these attacks were signed as being from “the fighters of the Male State,” referencing a Russian far right, ultra nationalist movement that was founded in 2016. However, in a Telegram post today, the group’s founder denied involvement in this, and said the group hasn’t even existed since 2021.

Another email sent to media outlets regarding these attacks said that “this is only the beginning,” and threatened further attacks (or at least threats of attacks) across European transport.

The timing of this is likely not a coincidence, as Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky is currently visiting Europe for a series of meetings regarding the war with Russia.

It goes without saying that this could get messy. If this is really coming out of Russia, it’ll be hard for European authorities to hold them accountable. And it’s also easy enough for the culprits to try to mask where their threats come from.

If the threats keep coming, then one wonders how this will be handled — will this all just continue, or will the threats be ignored at some point?

Dozens of flights across Europe have been impacted by bomb threats this week, which is obviously incredibly frustrating. None were found to be credible, but they’ve all been taken seriously, with everything from aircraft evacuations, to diversions, to fighter jet escorts.

It can be hard to track down the source of these threats, especially if it’s some tech-savvy, foreign operation. An email claiming to be associated with the group behind these threats suggest that this is only the beginning. Only time will tell how this plays out, because if the threats continue and authorities have no way to take action against the foreign culprits, their options might be limited.

What do you make of this Europe airplane bomb threat situation?

#6258. Inside The B-2 Spirit Bomber’s Secret Crew Rest Areas

The Northrop B-2 Spirit is not designed for comfort; it is designed survive the first night of war. It is designed to be one of the first aircraft to kick in the proverbial door and carry out some of the operation's opening strikes. Unlike other bombers in service with the US, Russia, and China, it is able to penetrate enemy air defenses.

To avoid the risk of being struck on the ground and to maximize surprise and uncertainty, these bombers often take off directly from their home base at Whiteman AFB, Missouri. However, regardless of how spartan the aircraft may be, it still has to cater to the needs of human pilots on missions that can last over 40 hours in the air.

Even the most fit and experienced pilots can start losing concentration during these long missions. Let's examine the not-so-secret crew rest areas on the B-2 Spirit and how they are intended to be functional, not comfortable.

The Northrop B-2 Spirit is an extremely valuable aircraft. Not only because of the cost of acquiring the aircraft, but also as a prestige icon. It would be a major symbolic victory for an adversary to destroy one of them. However, these are incredibly difficult to hit while in the air; it is easier to destroy them on the ground.

The world was reminded of how vulnerable bombers are on the ground in 2025 when Ukraine's Operation Spiderweb destroyed around 20% of Russia's strategic bombers on the ground. Repeated war games show that in a high-end peer-to-peer conflict, most of the aircraft the United States would lose would be on the ground.

As such, while the US does forward-deploy its B-2s to bases like Guam and Diego García, these are typically in the context of military exercises or as a show of force. When the time comes to actually use the B-2s in an operation against a noteworthy opponent, the US Air Force often elects to fly them nonstop from their home bases in the United States.

The US is uniquely able to do this thanks to a massive network of air bases around the world that allow aerial tankers (KC-135s and KC-46s) to take off and refuel the bombers along the way. Flying them nonstop from the US and back eliminates the risk of them being destroyed on the ground.

Flying these long missions from the B-2's Whiteman Air Force Base in Missouri results in some very long missions. The longest was in October 2001 during Operation Enduring Freedom. That mission took around 44 hours. The aircraft took off from Whiteman and struck targets in Afghanistan. After 40–44 hours, they stopped over to change crew at an overseas base before returning home.

In total, the mission lasted 70 hours. In June 2025, the US Air Force launched Operation Midnight Hammer against Iran's Fordow nuclear facility. The aircraft took off from Whiteman, flew across the Atlantic and Europe to Iran, and back. A diversionary group of B-2s flew the other way from Whiteman across the Pacific to Guam. The operation lasted around 37 hours in the air.

In 2017, B-2s flew 34 hours in Operation Odyssey Dawn against Libya. In 1999, they flew around 31 hours to Kosovo and back, and the aircraft flew around 33 hours as part of Iraqi Freedom in 2003. While many of the Iraqi flights were from forward-deployed bases (like Diego Garcia), the first flights were ones designed to 'knock the door in' and flew directly from Missouri.

When missions are this long, the aircraft require rest areas for the crew. While the B-2 is subsonic, all bombers are subsonic in the real world. The B-2 relies on stealth to remain hidden, not outrunning threats. In the real world, supersonic aircraft like the B-1B, T-22, and Tu-160 almost never fly supersonic, and if they do, it's for dashes, not marathons.

The B-2 is famous for its stealth, but how much punch does it pack? Let’s find out.

The B-2 features a fold-down sleep cot located behind the cockpit area, mounted along the cockpit bulkhead, and is only enough for one pilot at a time. It is fairly limited and isn't long enough for tall pilots to fully stretch out. It is not designed for deep rest, only functional naps. The pilots also bring pre-packed meals on board.

It should be noted that while a bomber like the B-52 has a crew of five (pilot, copilot, weapon systems officer, navigator, electronic warfare officer), the B-2 only has two. These are the pilot in the left seat and the mission commander, seated in the right seat. The cockpit is reported to be high enough for a 6-foot-tall pilot to stand up

It is widely reported on the internet that the B-2 Spirit has a mini-fridge and a microwave on board. Most of these articles are tabloid sources repeating other secondary sources, and the truth is somewhere close to the claim. In a 2023 interview with YouTube channel Whayman College of Aeronautics, B-2 pilot Tim Sutton said that "we got an upgrade to a microwave so (...) we have a microwave on board for food."

Sutton also noted it was "nothing like the C-17." Regarding the claim that these aircraft have a mini-fridge, it depends on what one's definition of a mini-fridge is. According to The Atlantic, the mini-fridge is "typically a couple of Styrofoam coolers containing food the pilots pack for themselves."

40,000 lbs (official), 60,000 lbs (reality with reduced fuel)

30+ hours when taking off and returning to Whiteman

Sleeping cot, coolers, microwave, basic toilet

Meanwhile, the Atlantic reported that pilots "stretched out on the floor in the back of the cockpit" to take a nap. It also spoke of a pilot on the return flight stripping down to nothing, sponging himself with camping towelettes, washing his face, brushing his teeth, putting on a fresh flight suit, and making sure that his hair looked good.

The aircraft might be the Air Force's deadliest weapon.

In 2019, Defense News spoke with Chris Beck, a former B-52 pilot who had graduated from B-2 pilot school. He spoke about how once one gets used to these ultra-long missions, anything under 20 hours doesn't seem like a big deal. He said that "when you get started in that mission, [it’s important] to not get lulled into a false sense of security because you feel like you have 12 hours or more to get over to the target area."

Beck added that "you’ve got to be productive and get things done, so you can start taking turns taking naps and getting ahead of that, because as soon as you get behind the power curve, it's kind of hard to recover." Typically, pilots take naps for a couple of hours, although it depends on the route and when the refuelings are to take place. Pilots bring plenty of water (even Gatorade), toiletries, spare clothes, and light snacks on the flight.

In fact, Whiteman Air Force Base even has doctors and physiologists who specialize in how prolonged flying can impact the human body. They help new pilots learn techniques to improve their endurance and how to prevent fatigue. Doctors will even prescribe medication for especially long missions intended to help pilots get a "little bit of extra push" and help them stay focused on the mission.

The Northrop B-2 Spirit is notable for being the only de facto penetration strategic bomber remaining in service in the world, at least until the Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider enters service. Meanwhile, the B-1B Lancer was designed as a low-flying, map-of-the-earth supersonic bomber with a dramatically reduced radar cross-section.

However, the proliferation of threats like look-down radars has rendered it unacceptably vulnerable in contested airspace. The B-52 was designed for a different era, and direct bombing runs (like Operation Linebacker II over Vietnam in 1972) are not likely to be repeated. Russia's Tu-95MS is somewhat comparable to the B-52.

The Tu-22M3 was designed to attack allied shipping, particularly aircraft carriers, but those days are long gone. The massive Tu-160 is also now considered unsurvivable in contested airspace. China's Xi'an H-6 bombers are also modernized variants of the old Soviet Tupolev Tu-16 and are not stealthy.

All this means that the US Air Force now uses its B-52s and B-1Bs, and Russia uses its Tu-95s, Tu-22s, and Tu-160s as de facto missile trucks launching their munitions from outside contested airspace. The B-2 Spirit is the only bomber realistically able to carry out penetration strikes with actual bombs in contested environments, such as what was seen in Iran in 2025.

#6257. Denver Airport Taco Bell Worker Sues For Pay While Waiting At Security — And They May Win

A former Taco Bell food preparer at Denver International Airport is suing the restaurant’s operator for pay for time spent going through security and getting to the restaurant before clocking in. According to Law360, the Colorado state court lawsuit also alleges that hourly employees weren’t provided paid rest breaks. I’d normally be skeptical of a claim for pay while passing through an airport checkpoint. Government-required screening looks like part of getting to work. However, Colorado law is unique and more generous here than even California. This Wouldn’t Fly In California In January, I wrote about a Delta Sky Club worker at Los Angeles International Airport seeking pay for time spent going through TSA. A similar claim by an Admirals Club employee had already lost. In Cazares v. Host International, the Ninth Circuit upheld dismissal because the employee hadn’t alleged facts showing employer control during federally mandated screening. Federal law is also favorable to employers here. The Supreme Court’s Integrity Staffing Solutions v. Busk decision held that warehouse workers didn’t have to be paid for certain employer-required security searches. Simply requiring an activity doesn’t automatically make it paid work under federal law. Colorado Specifically Includes Security Screening As Work Colorado’s wage rules list “security or safety screening”, including waiting for it, among activities that can count as paid work. The state’s labor department explains that screening required to work for an employer can qualify “whether discretionary with the employer or legally required.” Its example is federally required radiation screening for nuclear plant guards. In Rael v. Q3 Contracting in 2024, a federal judge dismissed claims involving vehicle inspections and commuting under federal law, while allowing claims for that same time under Colorado law. The Taco Bell concessionaire’s best argument is that a shared airport checkpoint remains part of the commute: it serves aviation security generally, outside the restaurant’s premises and supervision. The worker’s answer is that this is a required screening to reach the assigned workplace, exactly the sort of activity Colorado treats as work. It’s not a frivolous theory the way it was for California airport lounge employees. Interestingly, the time security to the restaurant could count as work, too. Colorado generally excludes ordinary commuting and the initial trip to a workstation. However, its travel rule includes an exception once compensable work has begun. If the security checkpoint is work, then travel from that work location to the next one can be work, too. The state’s travel time guidance even discusses walking from an entrance to a workstation after paid activity starts. I’ve written plenty about the time it takes to get around Denver airport. So this could be a lot of time. My bet is that this dispute is more likely to produce a negotiated payment than a clean employer win based on who runs the checkpoint. But that’s just going to encourage more similar suits. I’ve held the (see rates and fees) for eight years, and despite carrying more than 25 credit cards, it’s one I’ll continue renewing year after year.

The reason is simple: World of Hyatt is my favorite hotel loyalty program, and this card makes it even more rewarding to stay with the brand. Between an annual free night, automatic elite status and the ability to earn valuable Hyatt points on spending, I consistently receive far more value than the card’s affordable $95 annual fee.

It isn’t the right fit for everyone. Hyatt has a much smaller global footprint than Marriott, Hilton and IHG, so travelers who rarely stay at Hyatt hotels may be better served by a more flexible travel rewards card. However, if Hyatt is already part of your travel plans — or you’d like it to become one — the World of Hyatt card is one of the best mid-tier hotel cards on the market. Card rating*: ⭐⭐⭐⭐

*Card rating is based on the opinion of TPG’s editors and is not influenced by the card issuer.

If you’re comparing several hotel credit cards, here’s what you need to know at a glance:

Unlike cards that earn transferable rewards, this is very much a Hyatt-focused product. If you’re loyal to Hyatt — or want an affordable way to accelerate your progress toward higher status — it deserves serious consideration.

If there’s one reason why I continue paying the World of Hyatt card’s annual fee, it’s the anniversary free night certificate.

Each cardholder anniversary, you’ll receive a free night award valid at any Category 1-4 Hyatt hotel or resort. Since Hyatt prices these properties between 3,000 and 25,000 points per night, there’s plenty of opportunity to extract well over $95 in value. Free nights expire 12 months after issuance.

I’ve redeemed my certificates at The Standard, Brussels, Hyatt House Manchester in the U.K. and Andaz Mexico City Condesa. In each case, paying cash would have cost considerably more than the card’s annual fee.

Even better, you can earn a second Category 1-4 certificate after spending $15,000 on the card in a calendar year.

That’s the spending threshold I personally target each year. It unlocks another free night and an additional six elite night credits toward Hyatt status for even more value beyond the points you'll earn from that spending.

Related: The best Hyatt Category 4 hotels to maximize your free night award certificates

Simply holding the card gives you complimentary Discoverist status.

While Discoverist isn’t Hyatt’s most rewarding elite tier, I still appreciate benefits like preferred room upgrades and late checkout (when available) and a 10% bonus on eligible Hyatt spending.

That said, for frequent Hyatt guests, this perk probably won’t be all that enticing since they’re likely to earn Discoverist status organically. The card becomes more valuable when working toward a higher status level.

Every calendar year, you’ll receive five qualifying night credits automatically, and you’ll earn another two qualifying night credits for every $5,000 spent.

I’ve found those elite night credits incredibly valuable. By combining the five annual elite nights from the card with my Hyatt stays and strategic spending to earn an additional six nights, I qualified for top-tier Globalist status in August 2025, which I’ll enjoy through February 2027.

Related: Was going all-in on Hyatt Globalist worth it? My honest take

Chase issues this card, so you'll receive several useful travel protections, including:

These protections aren't as extensive as those you'd receive with a premium travel card, but that's to be expected given this card's modest annual fee.

Related: Is the World of Hyatt credit card worth the annual fee?

One of my favorite things about the World of Hyatt program is that earning and redeeming points is refreshingly straightforward.

Unlike most major hotel loyalty programs, Hyatt still publishes an award chart, making award pricing more predictable.

When you stay at Hyatt hotels, these earnings stack with the points you earn as a World of Hyatt member. Since cardholders receive complimentary Discoverist status, you’ll also earn a 10% bonus on your base points, meaning you can earn up to 9.5 total points per dollar spent on eligible Hyatt purchases. That represents a solid 16% return on Hyatt purchases, per our November 2026 valuations.

I generally use this card for Hyatt stays and tax payments that help me reach the $15,000 annual threshold for the second free night certificate.

Otherwise, I typically use my  (see rates and fees) for most travel and dining purchases, then transfer those Chase Ultimate Rewards points to my Hyatt account whenever I need to top up my balance for an award stay.

That gives me the best of both worlds: I earn more rewards on everyday travel and dining while keeping my points flexible until I’m ready to book. If I don’t end up needing Hyatt points, I can always transfer them to one of Chase’s 13 other airline or hotel partners instead.

Related: 6 of the best credit cards for travel purchases — beyond flights and hotels

In my opinion, Hyatt points remain among the most valuable hotel points due to their flexibility.

Award nights start at just 3,000 points for a Category 1 property at the Lowest rate and range up to 75,000 points for a top-tier Category 8 property under Hyatt’s five-tier standard award chart.

I’ve used Hyatt points for everything from inexpensive city breaks to luxury resorts. Some of my favorite redemptions include:

Hyatt also lets you redeem points for Points + Cash stays, suite upgrades, club lounge access and Find experiences. While those options can make sense occasionally, I almost always get the best value by redeeming points for standard award nights.

Related: 22 best Hyatt hotels in the world to book with points

Despite being one of my favorite hotel credit cards, the won’t be the right fit for every traveler.

The biggest drawback is Hyatt’s relatively small footprint. While Hyatt has more than 1,500 hotels and all-inclusive properties across 80-plus countries, that’s still far fewer than Marriott or Hilton. If you frequently travel to destinations without a Hyatt, you may struggle to maximize the card’s benefits.

Those who prioritize earning the highest possible rewards on everyday spending will likely find better options elsewhere. Beyond Hyatt purchases and spending toward the $15,000 threshold for a second free night certificate, this card isn’t particularly rewarding for dining, travel or everyday purchases.

Finally, travelers looking for premium perks like airport lounge access, annual travel credits and luxury benefits across multiple hotel brands should consider a premium travel rewards card instead.

For most travelers, I think the personal World of Hyatt Credit Card is the better choice than the (see rates and fees).

Both cards help you earn Hyatt points and elite status, but the business version is designed primarily for business owners. It offers bonus categories geared toward business spending and additional benefits for companies, while the personal card provides better long-term value for most travelers, thanks to its annual Category 1-4 free night certificate.

By comparison, I think the World of Hyatt Business card's $199 annual fee is harder to justify year after year because it lacks an anniversary free night. It does offer up to $100 in Hyatt statement credits each anniversary year, but that requires Hyatt spending and there's no way to get outsized value like you might with a free night.

Unless you own a business and can maximize the business-specific earning categories, I’d start with the personal card.

Related: World of Hyatt card vs. World of Hyatt Business card: 2 valuable hotel earners

The currently offers new cardholders four free nights (at Category 1-4 Hyatt hotels) after spending $5,000 on purchases in the first three months from account opening.

These are hotels that would ordinarily require 3,000 to 25,000 points per night, depending on the property and stay dates. Someone who uses all four free night certificates at the highest-priced properties would save up to 100,000 World of Hyatt points, making this offer worth up to $1,650 (based on TPG valuations).

This is a very strong bonus compared to other historical welcome offers, though not the absolute all-time highest offer for new cardmembers. The best-ever welcome offer included five free-night awards (offer no longer available). Having said that, if you max out the four certificates, this would be considered the most lucrative offer since February.

Despite being a great offer right now, some travelers may prefer to wait until the introductory bonus is awarded in points instead. Unlike free nights, there are no hotel category restrictions for redeeming points. The expiration date for free nights is also stricter.

Related: Your guide to the World of Hyatt award chart

If you’d rather earn more flexible rewards that are transferable to a number of travel partners, including Hyatt, one of these cards may be a better fit:

For additional options, check out our lists of the best hotel rewards credit cards and the best travel credit cards.

I’ve carried the World of Hyatt Credit Card for eight years, and it’s one of the few hotel credit cards I have no intention of canceling.

The annual Category 1-4 free night certificate has consistently offset the card’s $95 annual fee, while the elite night credits helped me qualify for Globalist status last year. Add in Hyatt’s strong redemption value, and it’s easy to see why this remains my favorite mid-tier hotel credit card.

If you regularly stay at Hyatt properties, I think the World of Hyatt card deserves a place in your wallet. If you rarely stay with Hyatt, though, you’ll probably get more long-term value from a flexible travel rewards card.
