#6255. Singapore Airlines’ New Business Class Finishes Look Cheap, Mismatched

Earlier I covered how Singapore Airlines unveiled its new first & business class, which should enter service in 2027 (hopefully). These products look like very nice improvements over the existing cabins, even if they’re not revolutionary.

That being said, I have to give Singapore Airlines some tough love on the new business class seats. Let me acknowledge that I’m a huge fan of Singapore Airlines as a brand. Any list I keep of the best airlines in the world (whether it’s the best airline brand, best first class, best business class, best inflight service, best inflight entertainment, etc.) has Singapore Airlines on it… that’s how highly I think of the brand!

But I’m also honest, regardless of how it fits my preconceived notions of a brand. I feel like I’m saying what everyone else is thinking, seemingly except for most influencers who are in Singapore for the launch event, who are just casually glossing over this… so much for attention to detail!

When I think of Singapore Airlines, the first thing that comes to mind for me is how deliberate the airline is. I don’t think there’s an airline that’s more intentional with every aspect of its guest experience, from the tone of voice with which staff speak, to warm and elegant design.

I’d say Singapore Airlines’ new first class actually looks really on brand. It’s a nice evolution of what the carrier has historically offered — it’s warm and elegant without being outdated.

And then you move to business class, and it looks like Scoot and Spirit Airlines had a baby. The gray and black is generic, the yellow accents look cheap, and then there’s so much going on with the blue and white bulkheads (if that’s actually how they’ll look).

And the Scoot reference isn’t even sarcastic. For those not familiar, Scoot is Singapore Airlines’ low cost carrier, and look at the seat finishes you’ll find there!

Usually there’s some consistency between seat finishes and wider branding, including the livery, flight attendant uniforms, etc. In this case, it’s not only not aligned, but they seem at odds with one another. There’s otherwise not a hint of yellow (or neon green, or whatever that is) in Singapore Airlines’ branding.

What so bizarre to me is how the first and business class finishes are completely mismatched, and you wouldn’t assume they belonged to the same airline. That’s because Singapore Airlines worked with different design firms (separate from the seating manufacturers as such) for the two cabins.

BMW Designworks was behind the business class seats, while PriestmanGoode was behind the first class seats. I think it’s safe to say there was no coordination between the two. I guess the argument from executives is that they want the cabin to look more modern and high tech, and go after a younger crowd, but I just don’t follow the logic.

It’s clear that Singapore Airlines put many years of effort into this product, and frankly I’m just surprised that Singapore Airlines executives signed off on this. Am I just in the minority in thinking this isn’t a good look for the airline? Did some marketer assure Singapore Airlines executives this was great branding, and they were wrong? Or did everyone just independently decide that this looks great?

If they at least eliminated the yellow stripes, it would no longer look cheap, but would instead look generic. I’m just surprised that this is the conclusion they came to.

Singapore Airlines of course had a big media event in Singapore to celebrate the launch of this product. I don’t attend media events, just as a general policy, because I don’t find them to be a great use of time. But I certainly do enjoy seeing the coverage from others.

What I find fascinating is the inherent bias that exists when someone is invited to something. For example, if you look at the comments on my post about the new cabins, the single thing most commented on by OMAAT community members is how bad the business class colors look.

If you watched the videos on social media about this, there’s oddly no commentary on that. Admittedly I haven’t seen all the coverage, but the worst coverage I’ve seen is someone saying they “don’t mind” the colors, and that it’s a “big departure” from the old look. Okay, that’s not exactly an endorsement.

I also haven’t found a single person who attended the event who said “I love the new colors,” which probably tells you everything you need to know. For that matter, it’s one thing if people acknowledged “I realize the colors might not look good in pictures, but in person, it’s a different story.” But I haven’t heard that either.

To me this gets at the rather complicated relationship between so many brands and influencer types. If you can say all the things you love about the product, shouldn’t you also feel totally comfortable criticizing the parts of the experience you don’t like, though?

While we’re on this topic, let me add one more point. Being able to sit in seats at media events like this is of course cool, but it really doesn’t actually give you an impression of what it’s like to fly in a product, and that’s why it’s not something I particularly value, as an experience.

Of course a big business class seat is comfortable when you sit in it for a minute, and you’re filming content. But the real test of a product is when you spend hours in the seat, when you recline the seat into a bed, when you try to move your laptop around while you’re being served a meal, etc.

I once had the opportunity to spend a night in an aircraft seat on the ground (I can’t really say more, since I signed an NDA, but it was to provide feedback to a seating manufacturer). To me that was fascinating, because it really gives you an understanding of what the experience is like. My feeling about the seat was very different after being in the seat for many hours vs. when I sat down.

Singapore Airlines has unveiled its new cabins, and there’s a lot to be excited about, as the hard products look very nice. However, Singapore Airlines’ new business class cabin finishes are a real mystery to me, because the yellow stripe looks cheap (I mean, it seems to be inspired by the carrier’s low cost subsidiary), and completely mismatched with first class.

The airline used different design firms for first class and business class. For an airline so focused on attention to detail and being very deliberate in terms of design, this strikes me as a misstep. Anyway, Singapore Airlines, I still love you and think you’re one of the best airlines in the world…

Where do you stand on Singapore Airlines’ new business class seat finishes? Does anyone love them?

#6254. “The sitting president doesn’t win”: Ahead of midterms, Trump reflects on himself

On the last day before the 2026 midterm elections, President Donald Trump gave a speech before the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, a site of considerable scandal in his second term. He joked it should be renamed after him and spent considerable time discussing Washington, D.C. construction projects and resurrecting conspiracy theories about monument vandals. When the president did turn to the elections, more than 23 minutes into an hour-long speech, he seemed to foreshadow major Republican losses in the House and Senate, describing it as “The most important midterm, I believe, in our lifetime.”

“When you vote, remember a party that hates America cannot be allowed to rule over the people who built our country,” Trump said, referring to Democrats, whom he said want to “blow all of this up by electing communist jihadists.”

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” Trump said midway in his speech. “Now that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is, Republican or Democrat, uh, good or bad, good president, great president, bad, for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot.”

The last day of polling indicates that Democrats have odds that are better than good to flip control of the House and Senate. The final results from the New York Times/Siena University polls report “The party is ahead in all seven states likeliest to decide control of the Senate: Michigan, Kansas, Texas, Maine, Ohio and, more narrowly, Alaska and Iowa.” The final predictions in the Cook Political Report included five additional shifts for Democrats in North Carolina, Florida, Tennessee and Virginia, projecting “that Democrats will win 15 to 25 seats, putting them at a 230- to 240-seat majority.” If a sweep happens in the toss up races, it’ll give Democrats their strongest majority since 2009.

Meanwhile, early voting records have been smashed around the country, in places like South Carolina and Ohio. In Texas, more than 7.7 million voters did so early, surpassing the record turnout for a midterm election set in 2018. Across the nation, about 50 million ballots have already been cast so far, with the share of registered Democrats notably increased in several key state races. But according to the New York Times, around half the expected votes will come on Election Day itself, making it difficult at this point to determine how big a role early votes will play in the outcome.

#6253. British Airways $710 Million Tax Fight Could Leave Members With Less Valuable Points

British Airways’ parent has €638 million tied up in a fight over taxing Avios. The government wants 20% value added tax when the points are issued. For members, that creates a risk of fewer points for their spending, weaker bonuses or more expensive redemptions (even if the tax authority never sends them a bill). IAG’s November 6 financial results update a dispute with the British tax authority over how its loyalty business should have been taxed going back to March 2018. While IAG is the legal taxpayer, a tax on the business selling your rewards can reduce what those rewards deliver. And VAT is something ultimately passed onto the consumer but collected throughout the value chain. What Britain Wants To Tax IAG historically accounted for value added tax based on what members redeemed their Avios for. Most redemptions were flights attracting a zero rate. The tax authority’s position is that IAG Loyalty is being paid to develop, administer and maintain a loyalty program. On that interpretation, the issuance of Avios attracts 20% tax regardless of what the member eventually books. IAG’s more detailed half-year disclosure says its treatment relied on an earlier ruling from the same tax authority and existing case law. It’s challenging the assessment and whether the government can reverse that treatment retrospectively. And the November filing identifies two amounts: €516 million of historical payments, net of input-tax recoveries, recorded as an asset IAG expects to recover if it wins. €122 million of subsequent payments disclosed as a contingent asset. Some of these amounts reduce the revenue IAG ultimately recognizes from Avios. Together that’s €638 million (US$710 million). IAG expects a tax tribunal hearing during the remainder of 2026 and a decision in 2027. Members Can Pay Without Receiving A Tax Bill Suppose a bank buys Avios to give customers for using its credit card. If supplying those Avios becomes more expensive, several things can happen: IAG receives less after tax. Existing contracts may prevent it from immediately charging partners more, leaving shareholders with lower profits. The bank pays more. It can absorb that cost, buy fewer Avios, reduce earning or initial bonuses, raise card fees, or steer spending toward a different rewards product. The member gets less from the points. Changes to award prices, cash charges or redemption availability can lower the cost of honoring rewards—but also make the currency less attractive to collect. IAG’s disclosure flags payments it doesn’t consider recoverable from commercial partners. That leaves IAG holding those costs initially. But it forces a reevaluation prospectively of those agreements, or revaluing the points themselves. In other words taxing the creation of rewards makes it more expensive to offer the same rewards. IAG’s November 6 financial results update a dispute with the British tax authority over how its loyalty business should have been taxed going back to March 2018. While IAG is the legal taxpayer, a tax on the business selling your rewards can reduce what those rewards deliver. And VAT is something ultimately passed onto the consumer but collected throughout the value chain.

IAG historically accounted for value added tax based on what members redeemed their Avios for. Most redemptions were flights attracting a zero rate. The tax authority’s position is that IAG Loyalty is being paid to develop, administer and maintain a loyalty program. On that interpretation, the issuance of Avios attracts 20% tax regardless of what the member eventually books. IAG’s more detailed half-year disclosure says its treatment relied on an earlier ruling from the same tax authority and existing case law. It’s challenging the assessment and whether the government can reverse that treatment retrospectively. And the November filing identifies two amounts: €516 million of historical payments, net of input-tax recoveries, recorded as an asset IAG expects to recover if it wins. €122 million of subsequent payments disclosed as a contingent asset. Some of these amounts reduce the revenue IAG ultimately recognizes from Avios. Together that’s €638 million (US$710 million). IAG expects a tax tribunal hearing during the remainder of 2026 and a decision in 2027. Members Can Pay Without Receiving A Tax Bill Suppose a bank buys Avios to give customers for using its credit card. If supplying those Avios becomes more expensive, several things can happen: IAG receives less after tax. Existing contracts may prevent it from immediately charging partners more, leaving shareholders with lower profits. The bank pays more. It can absorb that cost, buy fewer Avios, reduce earning or initial bonuses, raise card fees, or steer spending toward a different rewards product. The member gets less from the points. Changes to award prices, cash charges or redemption availability can lower the cost of honoring rewards—but also make the currency less attractive to collect. IAG’s disclosure flags payments it doesn’t consider recoverable from commercial partners. That leaves IAG holding those costs initially. But it forces a reevaluation prospectively of those agreements, or revaluing the points themselves. In other words taxing the creation of rewards makes it more expensive to offer the same rewards. #6252. How Many Crew Members Does It Take To Fly On Project Sunrise?

The debut of 'Project Sunrise' next year is one of the most anticipated developments in the history of Australia's flag carrier, Qantas Airways. The landmark new route will establish the longest nonstop air bridge in history when flights commence to connect the East Coast of Australia to London and New York. To make the 22-hour flights possible, Airbus has been developing a special ultra-long-range Airbus A350-1000 variant, which will be staffed by 18 crew members on every flight.

Just like the mission, the new A350-1000ULR will be the first of its kind when it debuts in October 2027. Project Sunrise marks the realization of a century-old aviation dream to span the final frontier of global distance without intermediate stopovers. The Sydney–London route will eliminate stops on the iconic Kangaroo Route for the first time since 1947. That spans close to 9,200 nautical miles (17,038 km) and will make it the longest scheduled passenger service in the world when it opens.

To ensure that such an ambitious new program will launch smoothly, the aircrew will be composed only of fully qualified and experienced captains and first officers, with no junior aircrew. The pilots rotate in pairs between active cockpit duties and scheduled rest breaks. Meanwhile, in the cabin, to ensure that flight attendants are not overworked and flyers receive the standard of care that Qantas is famed for, the aircraft will have the largest cabin complement of any twinjet in the fleet.

A 22-hour continuous flight pushes the limits of human endurance. Qantas spent years collaborating with medical researchers at the University of Sydney’s Charles Perkins Centre, aviation unions, and Airbus to tailor the workforce precisely to the flight profile, layout, and in-flight service. Qantas negotiated a historic pact with the Australian and International Pilots Association to mandate two full captains and two first oficers. On typical long-haul routes, airlines use two senior pilots in command and two junior second officers who only take the controls for cruise.

While a standard A350-1000 holds roughly 350 to 410 passengers, Qantas dramatically cut this down to just 238 seats to reduce weight and enable the ultra-long range. However, more than 40% of the plane is dedicated to high-tier seating: 6 first class Suites, 52 business class seats, and 40 premium economy seats. To support the additional strain of the extremely long flight and provide the elevated experience expected of premium airfare, the FA-to-passenger ratio is higher than the rest of the fleet.

Flight tracking data and sleep science dictate that human alertness drops significantly after 10 hours. The four pilots operate in rigid, alternating shifts. To maximize space on the main deck for passengers, Airbus designed overhead crew rest compartments nestled in the ceiling of the fuselage. While two handle the flight deck, the other two sleep in a pod above the front cabin, which features two full-length lie-flat beds.

Airbus' A350-1000ULR begins testing as Project Sunrise moves closer to reality.

Many long-haul airlines add a third pilot on very long flights so that rest can be shared, and the pilots’ union at Qantas has also argued for that model in early planning rounds. The AIPA has said its preferred arrangement for flights of about 20 hours is three pilots who are each qualified to land the aircraft. However, Qantas’s chief medical officer insisted from 2024 that the airline would begin with a more conservative approach to crewing.

In a three-pilot operation, the cockpit relies on a rolling cycle. While many ULH flights spanning 12 to 15 hours operate safely with three pilots, stretching a flight to nearly a full day changes the biology of human fatigue. If you divide 20 hours of cruise time evenly among three pilots, each gets roughly 6.5 hours of bunk time. However, as they swap out, that rest must be broken up into short, fragmented rest.

A flight that takes 22 hours leaves very little margin for error if something goes wrong late in the journey. If a pilot becomes incapacitated or falls seriously ill 18 hours into a flight, a three-pilot crew is immediately reduced to two. Those remaining two pilots would be forced to fly the rest of the mission with zero opportunities for further rest, driving fatigue levels to dangerous extremes.

With four pilots, the crew splits cleanly into two independent, two-pilot teams: Team A and Team B. This allows for a clean break in shifts. Instead of catnapping, a pair of pilots can sleep in a cycle that aligns with normal human sleep patterns. While adding a fourth pilot increases crew costs, beyond improving safety, it also pays off in fuel efficiency during the flight.

A well-rested air crew can actively work to optimize the flight path, finding better tailwinds, or adjusting speeds to save fuel. A heavily fatigued three-pilot crew is more likely to default to passive, rigid flight paths to minimize their workload. On a plane carrying massive fuel loads, a sharp crew's micro-adjustments save enough fuel to easily offset the cost of the extra pilot.

A closer look at why the Boeing 777X lost the Project Sunrise order.

Since its airframes are still under construction at Airbus's factory in Toulouse, France, Qantas has performed research on other ULH itineraries flown by its Boeing 787-9 Dreamliner Fleet. Monash University researchers tracked pilot brainwaves and alertness levels across the 19-to-20-hour test runs. These test flights have successfully demonstrated that both the human body and the aircraft's custom engineering can withstand the extreme limits of 22-hour continuous flight.

By tracking passengers using wearable devices, sleep diaries, and melatonin monitoring, researchers from the University of Sydney's Charles Perkins Centre proved that jet lag could be severely minimized. Changing the cabin lighting, meal schedule, and serving protein-rich meals aligned with the destination's time zone after boarding showed dramatically improved post-flight recovery. Meanwhile, feedback from test passengers emphasized that having space to move and stretch is an absolute necessity on flights this long.

On July 23 to 28 a skeleton crew of six test pilots from Airbus made the first historic, record-shattering marathon round trip between Toulouse, France, and Melbourne, Australia. Prototype MSN707 was packed with over five tons of custom Flight Test Instrumentation and 1,000+ advanced sensors wired throughout the cabin to stream real-time engineering data. The aircraft flew from Melbourne back to Toulouse via the Pacific, crossing the US and Atlantic. Pushed by specific testing parameters, it stayed airborne for an incredible 24 hours and 23 minutes.

From a capital and corporate perspective, the successful flights also de-risked one of the largest capital deployments in Qantas' modern history. The test flight confirmed that the physical airframe modification, the 5,283-gallon (20,000-liter) Rear Center Tank, could deliver the required range without a payload penalty. The tests verified that skipping hubs like Singapore or Dubai saves up to four hours of travel time to justify the planned 20% fare premium. That will make Project Sunrise profitable as well as pioneering.

The ultra-long 22-hour journey from Toulouse will be the longest flight of the test campaign to date.

Even though there is great promise in the testing results, the current delivery timeline is already a far cry from the original 2026 window. It hopes to receive its first A350-1000ULR in April next year in order to complete the training and preparation necessary to commit service in October. The airline will need to complete an intensive proving campaign with the Civil Aviation Safety Authority in Australia after they receive that first aircraft, the jet nicknamed 'Vega.'

Ticket sales are currently expected to begin in February, two months before the first jet is slated to be on the ground 'down under.' Operating a daily ultra-long-haul route requires a minimum of three functioning aircraft to handle maintenance cycles and continuous rotations. If a single software bug, supplier delay for cabin interiors, or unexpected maintenance variance pops up during proving flights, the late October launch slips.

For its part, Airbus has promised to deliver the four follow-on airframes that will come after the first jet is delivered in a faster time frame. Meanwhile, it remains to be seen what the actual scheduled routes will be, as advertising has shifted over time as the project has gone on. While the Sydney to London route is confirmed for the debut, the parallel Sydney to New York itinerary has been confirmed for a much later launch in mid-2028, according to AeroTime.

Similarly, Qantas has completely dropped references to direct Melbourne-to-London or Brisbane-to-London legs from its short-term strategy. This will leave the airline with only one route to rely on for economic stability when Project Sunrise kicks off. Although this could be a cost-saving measure that pays off by concentrating all of the assets on one high-demand market, if traffic falters, it could potentially slow the addition of the other highly anticipated destinations expected to follow on later.

#6251. Sacha Baron Cohen reveals “Who Is America?” and the answer is terrifying

Showtime debuted Sacha Baron Cohen’s latest series on Sunday, finally providing a partial to the question its title poses. “Who Is America?” The answer, on its face, will not surprise you: we are a nation of easy marks. Not merely easy, but willing.

Baron Cohen bases his career on that knowledge, but watching it in action was much more entertaining two decades ago in the heyday of “Da Ali G Show.” His HBO prank show became a cultural phenomenon before the omnipresence of social media and its accelerated mainstreaming of conspiracy theory as news, before a sitting president began making the denigration of objective journalism into a sport and before the proliferation of junk science as fact.

Back then cameras were not so prevalent as to persuade everyone that they were only one turned corner away from stardom. But today, being on camera is so natural and desirable to most of us that we are willing to say or do just about anything for a few of the 15 minutes we believe to be our birthright.

“Ali G” and the characters the show introduced, including Borat Sagdiyev and Brüno Gehard, also were born years before Project Veritas and InfoWars and other right-wing vehicles of disinformation made hidden camera hoaxing into something sinister.

All of which is to say, “Who Is America?” is not, as Showtime would like you to believe, “the most dangerous show in history.” At best, it is an occasionally funny one.

But to anyone who mourns the collective deterioration of our population’s capacity to engage in critical thought, but has no idea of how urgent of a crisis that happens to be, Baron Cohen’s new endeavor is less of a comedy than a fright show. “Who Is America?” A nation of pliable dullards ripe for the hacking.

“Who Is America?” was produced in secret, and its pre-show marketing largely consisted of publicized declarations of outrage by such right-wing figures as Joe Walsh, Sarah Palin and Roy Moore. Each attempted to transform their extreme embarrassment at having been duped by a British clown hiding behind layers of latex and spirit gum into some approximation of righteous anger at said comedian’s dishonesty.

Showtime, meanwhile, maintained the aura of mystery surrounding the series almost to the brink of its debut, revealing the title only a little more than a week prior. The network released the briefest of clips featuring one famous interview subject, Dick Cheney.

This in itself was a bit of flimflam Showtime’s part: “Hope you’ll tune in next week for an interview with me,” Cheney says in the video, only to be a no-show in the premiere.

You can’t blame “Who Is America?” for saving its biggest fish for later, because the famous politicians in the opener prove the problem of our collective gullibility just fine by themselves. In fact, although liberals may have gotten a hearty guffaw out of hearing Palin’s wailing about having been faked out by Baron Cohen, the very same character — Dr. Billy Wayne Ruddick Jr. PhD of Truthbrary.org — sat down for a conversation with none other than the honorable junior senator from Vermont, Bernie Sanders.

Prior to the premiere Billy Wayne tweeted a response to Palin’s accusation that he made fun disabled veterans. “I did NOT say I was a War Vet,” Ruddick’s “official” response reads, going on to explain that the service was in was “not military, but United Parcel”.

Nor does he make such assertions to Sanders, with whom he debates the merits of a universal healthcare plan. And when I say debate, what I mean is that Sanders very calmly shares statistics with Billy Wayne long after the interviewer’s line of questioning stops making sense. And when Sanders asks Billy Wayne to confirm that he is disabled, given that he is conducting the interview while seated on a motorized scooter, Baron Cohen’s character replies that no, he is not. “This here scooter is to preserve my body’s finite energy,” Billy Wayne says.

READ MORE: That viral “strangers on a plane” Twitter story: Not a rom-com but a horror show

One may be tempted to qualify Sanders’ appearance by pointing out that he acquitted himself well in the face of a person best be described as a few coconuts short of a beach vacation in Binomo.

But this fails to answer the question of why Sanders signed a release, allowing this interview to be broadcast. Did anyone on Sanders’ team vet Truthbrary.org the moment Billy Wayne mentioned it? Even if they thought he was genuine, what is to be gained from being seen in a televised debate with a guy whose site includes a page titled  “Obamanoids — For Real!”?

(To be fair, reportedly Baron Cohen almost fooled veteran news anchor Ted Koppel as part of his project. Koppel told The Hollywood Reporter that he was contacted to appear in a Showtime project titled “Age of Reason,” said to feature “conversations with distinguished experts in science and public policy, highlighting the brightest and most reputable minds on today’s most important topics.” Koppel, perhaps receiving brainwaves from his colleague Sam Donaldson, wised up before Baron Cohen could pull him too deeply into his game.)

A second character introduced in the premiere, an NPR shirt-wearing hyper-liberal named  Nira Cain-N’Degeocello, visits the opulent South Carolina home of wealthy Trump supporters he says are  “afflicted with white privilege.” But it soon becomes clear that his marks’ problem isn’t close-mindedness but over-correcting in the acceptance department. When Baron Cohen’s interviewer waxes on about encouraging his daughter Malala to “free bleed” on the American flag as a lesson, they simply nod and listen; when he chats about his wife’s ongoing affair with a dolphin, they don’t have any questions like, say, whether what they’re hearing is real.

This brings us to another answer to “Who Is America?”: we’re so aware of cameras, and desperate to have its focus upon us, that we will do and say anything without thinking of its possible permanence.

Demonstrating this is Baron Cohen’s third character Rick Sherman, an ex-con turned TV host who visits a Laguna Beach, California gallery to show his work, which is a series of capable but otherwise unextraordinary portraits rendered in feces and ejaculate.

Now, it’s entirely possible that the woman who runs the gallery might have been thinking she could have the next Andres Serrano on her hands. On the other hand, please.

This is a subject entirely aware of being on view, so obsessed with appearing erudite that while Rick is off camera, having excused himself to the facilities to commit another brown-and-white vision to paper, she addresses the camera like the host she was born to be.

“Who knew the world was capable of such oxymoronic paradoxical juxtapositions?” she muses. And this is before the homemade pubic hair paintbrush comes out.

Baron Cohen has pushed the limits of tolerant everyday people many times in the past, mostly in a way that makes them look reasonable or, at the very least, more intelligent than the put-ons he inflicts upon them. And this is perhaps one of the most depressing aspects about “Who Is America?”, its demonstration of how endemic our lack of analysis truly is. I’m not saying that gallery owner is a stupid woman, understand.

But her interview is an example of prizing exposure over lasting consequence. By that I’m not merely referring to the fact that she placated a man who not only handed her pieces of cardboard purportedly smeared with his own dried excrement, or waited to receive a fresh sample of his work, but that she decided she needed to share her expert observation as to why she needed to do so by uttering a sentence full of five dollar words that add up to absolute nonsense.

(Either that or she’s a friend of Baron Cohen’s and in on the gag. I hope it’s option two, as opposed to her actually legitimizing the artistic relevance of number two.)

A number of reviews of “Who Is America?” have pointed out that Baron Cohen’s sneaky deceit is no longer funny because the formerly insane viewpoints Baron Cohen’s tactics expose have been normalized.

This has always been the danger, but it’s one every sort of parody or satire contends with in the current climate. It’s difficult to lampoon leaders seeking to legislate ludicrous patches to crises like gun violence instead of adopting common sense solutions like stricter regulation.

Which brings us to the portion of “Who Is America?” guaranteed to dominate Monday’s gallery of crazy clips, fronted by Baron Cohen’s Col. Erran Morad, a self-styled Israeli anti-terrorism expert who calls himself “the terrorist terminator.”

The fake Mossad officer is there to promote his “Kinderguardians” program, a proposal that aims to train and arm toddlers in the classroom because, Moran says, arming teachers is crazy.

And this is the portion that has Walsh’s boxers in a bunch, because he joins House representatives Dana Rohrabacher and Joe Wilson in lending on-camera endorsements. Walsh’s comments are interwoven with a series of fake testimonials from the likes of Larry Pratt, executive director emeritus of the lobbying group Gun Owners of America and rape joke enthusiast.

Nobody forced Walsh to say, with gusto, “The way to stop a bad guy with is a good child with a gun. Happy shooting, kids!” If he didn’t want to say it, he wouldn’t have.

What Walsh might be upset about is being upstaged by Pratt, who earns some of the episode’s biggest laughs by reading the “science” behind the effectiveness of the fake program, revealing he doesn’t know the difference between human anatomy and hitmakers who grace Billboard’s pop charts.

Yes, “Who Is America?” gets mileage out of highlighting the callousness, sexism and extraordinary gullibility of conservatives, as Baron Cohen always has. But the things they say to him in disguise aren’t all that different than what they’d say on CNN, Fox, MSNBC or talk radio. Whatever power his comedy used to reveal is diminished by the fact that the charlatans no longer operate in secret.

Next week’s episode introduces one or two new characters, although I don’t imagine they do anything more “dangerous” than the four we met on Sunday. For a number of viewers who love Baron Cohen’s schtick, that won’t matter.

To them “Who Is America?” is precisely on brand, showing Americans famous and everyday reacting to bizarre situations with varying degrees of what we consider to be normalcy in a time where the baseline version of normal is constantly morphing and shifting.

To other viewers, however, “Who Is America?” is a confirmation that Baron Cohen has run some tests and can confirm there is limited and ever decreasing brain activity in this worsening patient we know as America. It is something to behold, that’s for sure. But I’m not sure it’s the stuff of groundbreaking comedy. It’s not even really news.

#6250. When Is An Airport Lounge Visit Not Worth It? Here’s How I Decide…

It goes without saying that a lot about the passenger experience when traveling by air has changed over the decades, both for better and worse. I think perhaps one of the most fascinating transformations we’ve seen over the years involves airport lounges, and how their purpose has completely flipped.

I’d like to talk about that in a bit more detail in this post, and share my approach to using lounges. Let me emphasize that there are of course all kinds of lounges out there, from international first class lounges, to international business class lounges, to Priority Pass, membership, and credit card lounges. This post is primarily about lounges that fall into that last category, in terms of being pretty widely accessible.

Look, I’m not trying to sound like some boomer talking about how things were in “the good old days” (nothing against boomers… hi, dad!), but I think it’s interesting to compare how things were 15-20 years ago, to how they are today.

Back in the day, airport lounges — even the most basic ones — were primarily about escaping the hustle and bustle of the terminal, and having a quiet place from which to work, with free Wi-Fi and easy access to charging ports. At the time, free Wi-Fi and charging ports in terminals were incredibly rare. The food in most standard domestic lounges sucked — it was typically cubed cheese, snack mix, and not a whole lot else.

It also goes without saying that lounges were mostly very poorly monetized. Airport real estate is incredibly expensive, and lounges were primarily a cost center for their operators, as part of an overall value proposition for travelers.

Fast forward to today, and look at the state of lounges in the United States. Lounges have much better food than they used to, and they also have much better amenities than they used to. Also, exponentially more people have access to the lounges than they used to. They’re actually pretty nice destinations in airports.

The catch is that they’ve completely lost their initial purpose — they’re no longer a place you go to escape the crowds, and quite to the contrary, they’re often the most crowded place in a terminal. In many lounges you’ll find every single seat occupied, and even a very long waitlist to get in.

Obviously this is great for monetization, since lounge operators maximize their return by having the lounges utilized as much as possible, so that the cost can be divided by the highest number of people possible. Ironically, we’ve also seen terminals largely get much nicer over the years. It’s nowadays common to see free Wi-Fi and charging ports throughout terminals, and it’s usually not too hard to just find a quiet place to sit, with more peace than you’d find in a lounge.

Back in the day, if I had lounge access, my obvious move was always to use the lounge if I had time. I mean, that seems like a pretty obvious move, right? After all, you get access to something “premium,” so you want to make the most of it. Most people with TSA PreCheck don’t say “meh, you know, I think I’ll skip that today and go through the regular line.”

At the same time, I think one has to step back and look at things objectively. At times it almost feels like people use lounges religiously in order to justify the annual fees on their credit cards, and so they can talk about how they’re eating for “free.”

You’ll often see people on social media essentially call airport lounges upper middle class airport cafeterias, and that’s probably not actually too far off in terms of how they’re practically used… and there’s nothing wrong with that!

Personally, for places with consistently crowded lounges, my approach to lounge use is pretty straightforward:

Honestly, this is one of the reasons I really love grab & go lounges, where you can pick up something to take with you. To me that’s the ideal setup, since it serves the purpose I’m actually looking for from lounges — if a lounge is going to be crowded, I’d rather just be able to grab what I’d like, and head somewhere quiet.

As someone who loves coffee, it’s why I also appreciate when lounges have great coffee to go. It’s typically the item I most want to consume at airports, and the wait for a cup of coffee at an airport can often be quite long early in the morning.

The lounge crowding issue nowadays is only made worse by the number of people who are watching videos and making calls with no headphones in lounges.

The whole concept of airport lounges has changed massively over the years. Monetization of lounges has largely gotten better, as they’ve become a key component of the credit card race that we’re seeing between airlines and card issuers.

That’s a double edged sword. On the one hand, lounges have become higher quality, on average. On the other hand, demand for them has also increased massively.

For the most part, lounges are no longer a place you go to escape the bustle of the terminal, and to use free Wi-Fi and charge your electronics. Now they’re a place you go to eat, drink, and wait in line.

The way I’ve used lounges has definitely evolved over the years, and it’s one of the reasons I appreciate the grab & go concept that we’re increasingly seeing. Unless I’m hungry or thirsty, I prefer just finding a quiet gate area.

What do you make of how airport lounges have evolved, and has your approach to using them changed?

Basically, 2 factors: 1) How long is the line to get in? and 2) How crowded is it once I am in (regardless of how long it took to get in)?

Well, 30 year user of lounges here... paid for Admirials club for decades, and used it multiple times a week if the airport actually had one.... Lifetime multiple million miler on AA, completely useless now. Have moved to United/Star, and now have PP, UA Club and Amex club. Its still worth it more often than not depending on where I/we are in the world. There are certainly many times where there are a gazillion credit card holder people in line, for sure, but more often than not, I find some lounge at most airports and its at least a place to sit without all the noise and chaos of the main terminal. I for one, do not understand the maniacal obsession with eating in airport lounges. People stock up on food likes its their last meal they'll ever eat, I just don't get it....

I do not see the point of cc lounges anymore. Amex has lost all the sheen. The lines are long, the crowds are massive and the food is a degree better than gas station food. And given the fact they have been chipping away at the benefits, pretty much every month, sometimes multiple times in a month, it no doubt that anecdotally i have been hearing a lot of people leaving that universe or on verge of leaving that universe. Cap 1 has very limited lounge coverage. Chase seems to have overtaken them in lounge network. There tapas style food is frustrating, even their a la carte options are in tiny portions, like one chicken meatball, yeah that ought to do it for me. Its just not fulfilling although the quality is decent.

My rule of thumb for going to an airport lounge is pretty simple: If I can get in with sufficient time to enjoy it and it isn't inconvenient to my gate, I will generally use the lounge. Why? Because the food tends to be pretty good at my favorite lounges and, despite their sometimes loud, overcrowded conditions, they are still more comfortable, quieter, and less crowded than other areas of my home airport. My favorite lounges at SEA are Amex Centurion (a real coffee bar with real baristas), the Delta SkyClub, and the Alaska Airlines lounge in the N concourse (great airport operational views). One issue with many airport lounges is the restrooms, where the men's room typically only has 2 stall toilets. It's often faster and easier to use the restrooms in public areas of the airport.

I have access to a variety of lounges and I'll stop by one if it's convenient to my gate. If it's busy or there's a line then I just keep it moving. I'm certainly not going out of my way to visit a lounge (I'm looking at you DFW Centurion Lounge) unless I have a lengthy layover. Maybe my luck has been good recently but I've found that Admirals Clubs and United Clubs, while busy, haven't been overflowing so I tend to stop by one of those rather than a credit card lounge.

#6249. Dallas Wants More Gates At Love Field—And To Give Southwest Airlines A Bigger Monopoly

Dallas is opening the door to more gates at Love Field airport. Two things stand in the way. Federal law caps the airport at 20 gates, and Dallas has already negotiated a lease that would offer most of the additional gates to Southwest Airlines if the law were to change. Southwest already controls nearly all of the gates there. More room for adding Southwest flights is different than more competition for Southwest. Dallas needs a larger airport and to open itself to competition. The Dallas City Manager raised the prospect of additional gates at an aviation event last week. The airport is undergoing a $2.5 billion redevelopment that doesn’t include more gates. Former American Airlines Chairman and CEO Doug Parker defended the existing arrangement on this week’s Airlines Confidential podcast. His argument rests on the existing five-party agreement, federal law and investments made in reliance on both: “agreements are agreements.” That’s only why changing the rules will be difficult, not a reason to keep limits on competition forever. Why Dallas Can’t Just Build More Love Field Gates Southwest Airlines had to fight to operate from Dallas Love Field when it first launched. It flew its first flight in 1971 after being tied up in the courts. Existing airlines agreed to leave Love Field for DFW airport. Southwest wasn’t a party to that agreement. In 1979, the Wright Amendment was passed to limit competition from Southwest Airlines. Deregulation meant that Southwest could fy beyond the state of Texas, and other carriers feared that the close-in airport they operated from would be more desirable than DFW. The upstart Southwest that fought for the right to fly was mature and pivoted to using government to its own advantage by the time they succeeded in securing the Wright Amendment Reform Act of 2006. It was a compromise among Dallas, Fort Worth, DFW Airport, American Airlines and Southwest Airlines. Southwest gained the ability to sell connecting service beyond the old geographic limits, followed by nationwide domestic nonstop service in October 2014. Love Field’s gate count had to be reduced from 32 to 20. Southwest kept most of the gates. The airport couldn’t offer nonstop international passenger service. Basically Southwest got more flying from Love Field and a monopoly there, while American Airlines got a monopoly on international service from Dallas and a cap on how much service could compete from Love Field. Initially, Southwest effectively couldn’t even fly out of Dallas – Fort Worth offering direct competition with American. The five party agreement specified that any gate Southwest operates at DFW (or another airport within 80 miles) would require giving up a Love Field gate, up to 8 total gates. That restriction ended in 2025. The provision even covered affiliates and flights carrying Southwest’s code, with exceptions for existing DFW–Midway codeshare service. Southwest couldn’t even codeshare with partners who flew to DFW, and could set up a regional affiliate to operate there. Dallas Already Gate Southwest An Option On More Love Field Gates The city council approved Southwest’s October 1, 2028 – September 30, 2040 Love Field lease covering 18 of the existing 20 gates. One gate is under Delta’s control and the final gate is under city control and can (theoretically) be used for new service. Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field Delta Air Lines Gate At Dallas Love Field The lease anticipates what happens with a change in federal law: Southwest and the airport both agree not to oppose an increase in gates at the airport. Dallas can then seek or support the effort. If the law changes, Dallas can pursue four, eight or twelve additional gates without the usual review by major incument airlines (‘majority-in-interest’ airline review, effectively Southwest) as long as each new gate won’t cost more than $50 million in 2025 dollars. Southwest receives an option on three of four, five of eight, or eight of twelve new gates. Even after changing a law that protects incumbents, Dallas would offer most new gates to its dominant airline. Parker Explains Why American Would Fight This Parker attributed two percentage points of Delta’s margin advantage, in an internal analysis from his American tenure, to Atlanta’s lack of a competing airport like Love Field or Midway. American has a lot to lose if some Dallas travelers gain better alternatives to DFW. Parker acknowledges his bias. American has made enormous investments at DFW, and predictable rules matter when financing airports. But I’d note: The agreement is more than 20 years old. Investors who bet on government keeping out competition also take the risk that the government changes its mind. Twenty years of protection is a substantial benefit, not a guarantee of protection in perpetuity. American hsa benefited from other subsidies, too. Parker was a prime mover behind American’s receipt of $12.8 billion in pandemic payroll support, the vast majority of the second and third tranches displacing payroll the airline was going to pay anyway. American chose not to fly from Love Field. American ended service in 2009 and subleased its gates to Delta. Its later merger settlement required divestiture of the gates, but American had already stopped operating. American preferred concentrating its network at DFW but that shouldn’t give them a permanent veto over competitors serving a different airport. The Government Destroyed Gates To Make This Deal Work Parker correctly recalls the demolition of six gates at the former Legend Airlines terminal. The overall reduction was twelve gates from 32 to 20. Six of those were at the separate Lemmon Avenue facility. I covered the litigation over that terminal and its leases. The Court of Federal Claims awarded the owners $133.5 million when the city took it back through eminent domain. The Federal Circuit reversed in 2018 arguing that the fact the gates couldn’t legally be used meant it had no value. It might soon have had value. The terminal was turned into a Lincoln dealership. North Texas Has Outgrown This Bargain DFW is growing. Its new Terminal F is planned for 31 gates, all serving American, with the first 15 expected to open in 2027. Meanwhile, McKinney is preparing to launch scheduled commercial service on November 11. Different parts of the Metroplex support different airport choices. DFW, Love Field and McKinney aren’t interchangeable for a passenger near downtown Dallas. Noise and road access are real though anyone living near the airport knew there was an airport there. Additional gate construction would necessarily involve an operational, environmental and access plan. American Airlines certainly didn’t walk away from the Naples, Florida airport just because residents there don’t like commercial air service! Love Field should be allowed to grow. The additional preferential gates should be open to airlines that bring new competition, rather than committing ex ante to enlarging Southwest’s existing control. These lease commitment is an impediment to that, and actually gives American Airlines its strongest argument against expansion. Southwest built its business by fighting attempts to keep it out. American chose to leave Love Field. Neither of those things justifies keeping other competitors out of the Dallas market, or serving each of the local markets in North Texas separately. #6248. “Borat 2” makes an America slathered in misogyny and disinformation reckon with itself

On Wednesday multiple news outlets revealed the purported headliner of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to be none other than Rudy Giuliani, President Donald Trump’s trusted lawyer and cable news’s favorite nutcase.

Compared with the mock attempted kidnapping Pamela Anderson, Borat’s ultimate get in 2006’s “Borat: Cultural Learnings of America for Make Benefit Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan,” the pranking of America’s mayor does not make for a grand climax or even an affectionate one. Instead, it more or less confirms what we already know about Rudy Giuliani: his corruptibility makes him shockingly easy to dupe.

All it took for the producers of “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” to succeed in their mission was a simple honeytrap, presented in the form of Baron Cohen’s exceptional co-star Maria Bakalova dressed as a right-wing fake news Barbie. By the time we get to that scene the Bulgarian actor has solidly established that she is the reason this feminist-themed sequel works as well as it does.

Performance-wise, Bakalova fully commits and never breaks, keeping pace with Baron Cohen in every shared sequence and commanding every scene she pilots solo. If Baron Cohen were to ever greenlight an inheritor to his Borat franchise, she would more than do it justice.

And this illustrates the subtextual call to action throughout “Subsequent Movefilm” for women of good conscience to reclaim their power, not only at the polls but in the realm of social equity. Baron Cohen and his writers cloak this in slapstick from the moment we’re introduced to Bakalova’s Tutar, the 15-year-old daughter Borat never realized he had.

Tutar is filthy and coarse, raised in a pen and guided by a book given to her by the Kazakh government that insists that women cannot drive, own businesses or even touch their privates without causing great disaster on par with the sinking of the Titanic. Her highest aspiration is to live in a golden cage like Queen Melania, “the happiest wife in the world,” emboldening her to join Borat’s latest trip as a stowaway.

Similarly life, and Borat’s government, have not been kind to him since “Cultural Learnings” conquered America with great success – high five! – 14 years ago.

America may have loved Borat but his countrymen, neighbors and family in his home village of Kuzcek felt great shame at how his documentary portrayed them (a nod, perhaps, at the Romanian villagers angered at being misrepresented in the 2006 film, who unsuccessfully sued its producers). In reaction he was sentenced to a life of hard labor in a gulag.

When Kazakhstan’s current Premier Nazarbayev (Dani Popescu) realizes the regime has a use for Borat, he’s hauled out of prison, shaved into a familiar form – ill-fitting grey suit, walrus mustache, puffy hairstyle and all – and given a new mission to smooth glorious leader’s entry into the world’s strongman club. How? By presenting to”Vice Premier Mikhail Pence” valuable offering: Johnny the Monkey, “Kazakhstan’s Minister of Culture and No.1 porno star.”

This is why the Giuliani spoiler leaking before the film’s release fails to ruin “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” because, like old Johnny would do in a room full of bananas,  plunking Giuliani into a situation like the one announced in the film’s full title: “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” merely yields the expected results. Giuliani was hoodwinked not by a monkey but old-fashioned monkey business. Wa-wa-wee-wa!

In the main, the humor driving “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” is a continuation of what Baron Cohen does in his 2018 Showtime series “Who Is America?” – which is to say that he functions more as a prodding force these days than a hard crowbar. Long ago the Borat character functioned as a truth serum, the kind of amiable ignoramus people were inclined to countenance or forgive either out of politeness or a sense of superiority. Bigots would meet his bigotry with their own, perhaps, in a gesture of finding common ground, while others put up with him out of kindness.

Now, as father and daughter embark travel through the good old U.S. of A, 2020 edition, they encounter a place where the rampant racism, anti-Semitism and Islamophobia Borat unearthed in 2006 is now on proud display across the land and slathered in misogyny.

The sexism, though, is the road by which Borat and Tutar find their way into the psyche of the ugly American – enabling them to infiltrate a debutante ball where Borat gets a father to admit he’d pay $500 for Tutar within earshot of his own child, and another man, hopelessly drunk, slurs out unbidden that men love pretty girls in South. “They’re fun!”

Following a span of time in which Borat keeps Tutar in a cage while he sleeps in the relative luxury of a horse trailer he drags behind a jalopy, “Subsequent Moviefilm” makes Tutar’s empowerment the centerpiece of the movie’s second half.  Baron Cohen’s signature obviousness and a style reminiscent of director Jason Woliner’s past TV work (which includes series such as “Nathan for You”) shapes how this transpires, and the audience either accepts this for what it is or may cringe at its clunkiness.

Either way, the fact that “Borat Subsequent Moviefilm” and Baron Cohen need Bakalova is indisputable.

There’s the practical matter that the character of Borat is famous, for one. Back in 2007 Baron Cohen announced that he was retiring two of his alter egos, Borat and Ali G, acknowledging to The Daily Telegraph that “the problem with success, although it’s fantastic, is that every new person who sees the Borat movie is one less person I ‘get’ with Borat again, so it’s a kind of self-defeating form, really.”

What he could not have predicted back then was how thoroughly the fabric of reality would be torn by the disinformation flood plaguing us today. However, he’s right about the problem of Borat’s fame. “Subsequent Moviefilm” confronts this early in the film when Borat sets down in America once again, only to be instantly recognized and pursued by crowds of thrilled Texans. This necessitates a trip to a local costume shop to purchase prosthetics and disguises.

Nonetheless, Borat’s relevance in 2020 is debatable. Since the anti-Semitism and sexism at his heart are defining traits in a nation seized by white nationalism, that either makes him redundant or highly relevant — except for when he revealshis subjects’ prejudices.

But then, the laugh-until-you-cry parts of the original “Borat” don’t involve, say, the Islamophobic, homophobic rodeo organizer mouthing off or those Southern frat boys wishing aloud that slavery was still legal. The best antics involve Borat’s stupidity crashing against the patience and politeness of typical Americans, or ludicrous moments like the nude wrestling match between him and his producer Azamat (Ken Davilian) that spills out of their hotel room and well into public spaces.

Fewer of those sight gags exist in “Subsequent Moviefilm.” Save for an extended segment in which he quarantines with a pair of right-wing QAnon adherents, they have been replaced instead by situational humor, such as when Tutar swallows a plastic baby cake decoration and Borat rushes her to what he believes to be a doctor’s office. Naturally they land in crisis pregnancy center where father and daughter are counseled, not by a doctor but by Pastor Jonathan Bright. This evolves precisely as one expects it would.

Then there are the bits that have already made the news: Baron Cohen’s infiltrating the Conservative Political Action Conference in February dressed as Trump? They work their way to that, and a scene from a right-wing militia gathering in Washington state where Borat performed as Country Steve and got the audience to sing along to a racist ditty, starting with lyrics about injecting Obama “with the Wuhan flu.”

Gotcha moments like this and the Giuliani business don’t tell us anything we don’t already know. Instead, it’s what the context implies about America’s psychological state. The cringe comedy in the crisis center isn’t merely in the pastor’s misunderstanding about the nature of the baby inside Tutar’s stomach. It is his calm insistence in her keeping it there even after Tutar’s father tells him that he put it there. (He bought the cupcake, OK?)

But this is part of an escalating series of moments that show us who America is: a nation of very fine people who live and let prejudice flourish so long as it doesn’t disturb the status quo.

There’s the Texas baker who uses icing to pipe the words “Jews Will Not Replace Us” on a chocolate cake without batting an eyelash. There’s the shop owner who guffaws along with Borat when he asks that Tutar be directed to the “no means yes” dress section. There’s the spray tanning salon technician who, in response to Borat asking, “What color is best for racist family?” says without pause or reaction, “I wouldn’t go any darker than a six or a seven.”

This leads up to savior in this narrative: Jeanise Jones, a Black woman Borat hires to look after Tutar and who ends up talking some sense in to her, starting with waking her up to the fact that her father has been lying to her. (And how.) Jones is the level-headed figure in a vast land of fools; she’s also playing to the trope of the Black woman savior utilized in the first “Borat” and touted in this election cycle. Placed in the context of everyone else Borat and Tutar encounter, though, she’s a cool clarifying drink in a desert of dumb and therefore welcome.

Evaluating the comedy value of “Subsequent Moviefilm” relative to the first “Borat” sets it up to lose, sad to say. It is enormously entertaining and, for the reasons listed above, a healthy treatment to whatever anxieties may be plaguing us a little more than a week leading up to the election. Whatever faults it has aren’t deadly, although it’s plain to see that the pandemic may have shifted the film’s ending in ways that don’t feel fully baked.

The most prominent difference between the “Borat” of 2006 and the 2020 “Subsequent Moviefilm” is in who America is now. Our inability to agree on basic facts has only worsened since Trump’s election in 2016, to say nothing of how decline and fall of basic critical thought has left us vulnerable to benevolent pranksters like Baron Cohen and outside forces who would mean us harm.

At the same time, there’s simply no getting around the fact that Kazakhstan receives little in the way of an image acquittal in this follow-up, an unavoidable and miserable result of alloying a problematic character to a place. If there’s a salvageable component to this, it is in how differently the sequel leaves us. When we first met Borat we comforted ourselves with the first-world notion that somehow we are better than people of so-called “lesser” nations.

Now it doesn’t allow the audience to be so sure of itself, implying in the final scene that we aren’t merely ugly Americans. We’re a once glorious nation being led by goons who are sliding us backward into diminishment, and dangerously so. That is nothing to laugh about.

“Borat Subsequent Moviefilm: Delivery of Prodigious Bribe to American Regime for Make Benefit Once Glorious Nation of Kazakhstan” is currently streaming on Amazon.

As High As 300,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

As High As 175,000 points. Find Out Your Offer.

If you’re a frequent traveler, scoring elite status with a major carrier like Delta Air Lines can make your journeys more relaxing and rewarding.

However, deciding which airline loyalty program benefits you the most is difficult. This is mainly due to the variations between complimentary upgrades, bonus points or miles, lounge access and other valuable perks. Plus, is it even worth pursuing elite status?

This guide breaks down Delta’s SkyMiles Medallion program, including its four public elite status tiers, how to earn status in 2027 through both travel and non-travel expenses, and the benefits of each level.

Here is everything you need to know about elite Medallion status in the Delta SkyMiles program.

Delta awards elite status to qualifying SkyMiles members each year. Elite status offers a range of benefits — from seat selection to priority boarding — that make travel more comfortable and convenient.

The airline has four published tiers of elite status:

Delta also has an invite-only status tier called Delta 360. While the airline doesn't publish its standard qualification criteria, big spenders could get an invitation to this very special club. Delta also says, “Members that have reached the 5 Million Miler milestone will receive an annual complimentary invitation for Delta 360° Membership.” That's a pretty sweet perk.

Visit our Delta Medallion glossary page for more details.

Flyers earn Medallion status based on their eligible activity during the preceding calendar year. Delta tracks travelers' activity through Medallion Qualification Dollars, which they earn by flying with Delta and its partner airlines, spending on select Delta SkyMiles American Express cards and booking Delta Vacations packages.

For Delta-marketed flights operated by Delta or a partner airline, members generally earn 1 MQD for every dollar spent on the eligible ticket price (including the base fare and carrier-imposed surcharges but excluding government-imposed taxes and fees). For eligible partner-marketed flights, MQD earnings are generally based on a percentage of the distance flown and the purchased fare class, according to Delta's published partner earning charts.

Note: Delta Main Basic tickets generally don't earn MQDs or qualify for Medallion upgrades.

Related: Your guide to Delta Air Lines Million Miler status

You can also earn MQDs on eligible award tickets and through everyday spending on the Delta SkyMiles Platinum, Platinum Business, Reserve and Reserve Business American Express cards. All four cards offer an annual 2,500-MQD Headstart, while eligible spending earns 1 MQD per $20 on Platinum cards and 1 MQD per $10 on Reserve cards.

Your status is valid through Jan. 31 of the following year. For example, travelers who qualify in 2026 will earn 2027 Medallion status, which would be valid through Jan. 31, 2028.

You must meet the applicable Medallion Qualification Dollar thresholds each calendar year to maintain that status.

Delta used to have several ways to earn status, but now the carrier uses only MQDs as qualification criteria. Below are the requirements to obtain 2027 Medallion status:

Delta did not raise the status requirements for 2027 status.

Here are some key benefits of each of Delta’s status tiers.

This is the entry tier in Delta’s program, and you’ll receive benefits like:

Delta’s mid-tier status includes Silver Medallion benefits, plus:

In addition to the Gold Medallion perks, you’ll also get the following:

You’ll get everything detailed above, plus some even better perks:

Check Delta’s website to review the full list of benefits available to SkyMiles Medallion members.

To make it easier to earn elite status, Delta gives eligible frequent flyers who also hold the following cobranded cards a head start on MQD metrics with a boost of 2,500 MQDs (per eligible card type) toward status qualification at the start of the year (and each year thereafter, until further notice):

Since the MQD head start is awarded per eligible card type, you’ll enjoy more than one 2,500 MQD boost if you have multiple eligible cards. Additionally, you’ll be able to enjoy bonus MQDs based on everyday spending on these cards.

Specifically, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Reserve Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $10 spent. Meanwhile, the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Amex and the Delta SkyMiles Platinum Business Amex will accrue 1 MQD for every $20 spent.

Technically, you could earn Delta Medallion status without ever stepping on a plane, simply by putting enough eligible spending on a cobranded credit card. But that doesn't necessarily make it a good strategy,

Even with the MQD Headstart, reaching the higher status tiers through credit card spending alone requires a large financial commitment. Before putting everyday purchases on a Delta card to chase status, consider whether the rewards and benefits justify the cost, when there are lots of other travel credit cards that could offer better returns for you personally.

If you earned Delta elite status in 2025, it’s valid through Jan. 31, 2027. If you qualify in 2026, your status will last until Jan. 31, 2028.

It’s critical to consider how much you’ll be traveling in the future to decide if Medallion status is worth it. If you push hard to reach Diamond Medallion status, the valuable perks outlined above apply only when traveling.

With the high MQD requirements, you would need to spend a significant amount of money with the airline or on a cobranded card to earn this top-tier status. So, you should ensure you're traveling enough to enjoy it.

That said, if you wind up within striking distance of the next tier, consider whether the benefits are worth it for you personally. There’s no reason to go out of your way for perks that don’t matter to you. Pursuing elite status with an airline you can’t realistically fly regularly isn't a great move. Look at Delta’s offerings from your home airport and whether it would be feasible to rely on that airline.

This elite-status hobby has many trade-offs, and one of the most common is deciding whether to use your preferred airline or hotel chain when neither is the most convenient nor the cheapest. Would you book a one-stop Delta flight if Southwest Airlines had a cheaper, nonstop option? If the answer is no, it may not be worth going out of your way to earn Delta elite status (or any elite status, for that matter).

The final consideration involves travel rewards credit cards. Many airline cobranded cards offer perks that mirror what you’d enjoy as an elite member. For example, the includes a free checked bag worldwide and a second checked bag when flying domestic, priority boarding and a 20% inflight savings in the form of statement credit. The card has no annual fee for the first year, then a $150 annual fee (see rates and fees).

Meanwhile, when you fly with Delta, the Delta SkyMiles Reserve American Express Card provides 15 Sky Club lounge visits each year (Feb. 1 through Jan. 31). Cardmembers also qualify for various complimentary seat upgrades and receive an annual companion certificate (valid for round-trip domestic and short-haul international flights to Mexico, the Caribbean and Central America in economy, Delta Comfort, Delta Premium Select or first class). To earn unlimited Sky Club visits each year, the total eligible purchases on the card must equal $75,000 or more between Jan. 1 and Dec. 31 each calendar year.

If you can pay a flat annual fee for one of these cards and gain access to perks that matter to you without going out of your way to earn elite status, that may be a good plan.

Delta Medallion status can make flying more comfortable, particularly if you're a frequent Delta customer who can take advantage of all the perks. But the value of those perks really depends on how often you fly and how much you're willing to spend to earn them.

For most travelers, the goal shouldn't necessarily be "reach Diamond Medallion." Instead, focus on the status tier that offers benefits you'll actually use and avoid spending more or booking less convenient flights just to earn a higher level of status.

If you’re considering switching your loyalty, we hope this detailed review of Delta’s elite status program has helped you make your decision.

#6246. The GOP’s midterm plan: Make America hate Muslims again

With less than a week to go before the midterms, the Republicans’ desperation is becoming obvious. Donald Trump is stumping in Mississippi, where Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith is locked in a tight race, and half the Cabinet is running around giving speeches to people who don’t know who they are. But the biggest sign of the GOP’s anxiety is the resurrection of a tried-and-true tactic: racism.

Only months ago, the party went all-in on red-baiting, accusing mainstream Democrats of being communist sympathizers, a reaction to the 2025 victory of New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani and the primary wins of a few democratic socialist candidates. This came alongside the now perennial attacks on transgender Americans, led by the president who continues to insist that elementary schools are performing gender-affirming surgeries in the nurse’s office without parental consent.

We knew they would rely on xenophobia, which has  been the central organizing principle of Trump’s decade of political dominance. He may not have kept most of his promises, such as “no new wars” and “bringing prices down on day one,” but he has delivered magnificently on his pledge to incarcerate and deport as many immigrants, undocumented and otherwise, as humanly possible. In fact, he’s even exceeded expectations.

Since they make up the largest share of immigrants, Latinos have been hit the hardest by this cruel policy, and Trump has long asserted that they are all violent criminals. But as we were warned in the 2024 presidential campaign, Haitians have also been among the top immigrant groups targeted by MAGA leaders, with Vice President JD Vance homing in on the racist right-wing id by declaring that these Black immigrants were eating the household pets of their Real American white neighbors.

For a moment, there seemed to be a new target when a social media post by Bo French, the GOP’s nominee for Texas Railroad Commissioner, went viral, exposing a growing conservative antipathy to Indian Americans. This was somewhat surprising since Vance, one of the party’s leading race-baiters, is married to the daughter of Indian immigrants, and Vivek Ramaswamy, another child of Indian immigrants, is Ohio’s Republican nominee for governor.

But none of these attacks and lies has gotten the traction they were hoping for, so the party has gone back to the deep well to draw up a big bucket of Islamophobia.

In the wake of 9/11, some in the GOP became infected by a strain of anti-Arab bigotry that, to his credit, George W. Bush attempted to fight. It waxed and waned as the attacks grew more distant. Then came Trump, whose demonization of Muslims goes back to the 2016 campaign. At that time, the U.S. was in the midst of an outbreak of “lone-wolf” terrorist attacks, and his violent rhetoric really got the crowds going.

Trump famously said he wanted to take up waterboarding “and worse,” and told lurid stories about dipping bullets in pigs blood to scare terrorists. Declaring that he would ban all Muslims from coming to America “until we can figure out what the hell is going on,” he executed his infamous “Muslim ban” days after taking office in 2017, an order that became the focus of legal challenges and, after some re-tooling by the administration, was ultimately upheld by the Supreme Court in 2018.

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., has long been a particular focus of Trump’s ire. As a progressive, she has been a fierce critic of the administration, but no more than most other Democrats. But she’s a Black woman, an immigrant and a Muslim who wears a hijab. Omar, who fled Somalia with her family at eight and lived for years in a Kenyan refugee camp, represents Minnesota, which became one of Trump’s bete noirs after Kamala Harris chose the state’s governor, Tim Walz, as her running mate. Trump began attacking Minnesota’s community of Somali Americans with some of the most bigoted comments in American history, and that’s saying something.

Somalia, he said, is “garbage, a “sh*thouse country” that “stinks.” He has even claimed that 98% of Somali immigrants don’t work and that they are all criminals driving around in Mercedes-Benz and BMWs. Reprising his role as inciter-in-chief, the president called for (white) Minnesotans to “fight back” against the state’s Somali population, writing that they “view you as weak and stupid people.”

Another target of MAGA’s anti-Muslim bigotry is Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan-born Democratic nominee for the Senate. Earlier this week, Vance referred to him as “very, very evil,” a “psychopath” who pushes “anti-white racial hatred.” This charge of reverse racism is one of the favorite tropes of the modern right, guaranteed to draw cheers at a MAGA rally. Trump called El-Sayed a violent jihadist, and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. expanded the attacks, saying that the one billion Muslims worldwide contribute nothing to society, having never won the Nobel Prize or any other prestigious awards, an easily disprovable lie.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people.

The blatant bigotry of these latest attacks is enough to take your breath away, not because they are unprecedented; this is America, after all, and racism is one of our “exceptional” characteristics. But until the last decade, Republicans had learned that it was far better for them to obscure their racism with dog whistles and code words so as not to scare the suburban white people. The famous quote from the notorious GOP strategist Lee Atwater, who recommended referring to “welfare” and “busing” to stand in for overtly racist language, held true for years.

Republicans stuck with that tactic for decades, starting with Richard Nixon, who used the term Trump thinks he invented, “law and order,” as a code word for cracking down on Black protests in inner cities. Ronald Reagan famously talked about “welfare queens” during his 1976 primary bid for president, and four years later he opened his presidential campaign by declaring his belief in states’ rights — another dog whistle — in Mississippi, near the spot where white civil rights workers were killed. Three decades later, Trump turned even more creative with his “birther” campaign against President Barack Obama, combining the party’s burgeoning Islamophobia with classic All-American racism. To this day, Trump refers to Obama using his full name — Barack Hussein Obama — with a childish glee.

I don’t think claiming that a whole African country is a “sh*thouse” or saying that Black immigrants are barbecuing their neighbors’ cats for dinner is the kind of subtlety Atwater was talking about. In fact, I will not be surprised to see Trump, who has lost virtually all rhetorical restraint, drop the ugliest epithets of all someday soon. It’s just a matter of time. And if he does, I’m sure JD Vance and all the rest of MAGA’s staunchest loyalists will find a way to rationalize it as something the other side is responsible for.
